title: Marriage Allowance

figures.what: Personal Allowance the lower earner transfers to their spouse or civil partner
Maximum Income Tax saving for the couple in one tax year
Earliest tax year a claim can be backdated to — four tax years back from 2026/27

scope.who: Married couples and civil partners where one pays no Income Tax and the other pays basic rate (starter, basic or intermediate in Scotland)
scope.excluded: Couples living together but not married or in a civil partnership. Anyone already claiming Married Couple's Allowance. A higher earner above the basic rate — above £50,270, or above £43,662 for a Scottish taxpayer.
scope.from_when: Current for 2026/27; backdating to 2022/23
scope.how_to_claim: The LOWER earner applies, free, on gov.uk. It then renews automatically until cancelled.

notes: The claim is made by the lower earner, not the higher — the commonest error. Scotland: the test is the Scottish band, so a Scot on £46,000 does NOT qualify while someone on £46,000 in England does. No Budget 2026 change.

title: The Trading Allowance

figures.what: Trading allowance for the current tax year, 2026/27
New trading allowance and reporting threshold from 6 April 2027, announced at Budget 2026
Deadline to register for Self Assessment, in the tax year after the one you went over

scope.who: People with trading income from self-employment, casual work such as babysitting or gardening, or hiring out their own equipment
scope.excluded: Anyone whose trading income comes from a company they control, a partnership they are in, or their own or their partner's employer. It cannot be combined with claiming actual expenses — it is one or the other.
scope.from_when: £1,000 now; £3,000 from 6 April 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Automatic below £1,000 gross. Above it, register for Self Assessment by 5 October in the following tax year.

notes: The test is GROSS income, not profit: £1,200 earned with £400 of costs is over the threshold even though the profit is £800. Budget 2026 raised it to £3,000 from 6 April 2027 — that does NOT apply to this tax year.

title: Business mileage rates for your own car

figures.what: 2026/27 rate for the first 10,000 business miles — raised from 45p, backdated to 6 April 2026
2026/27 rate for every business mile after the first 10,000
The old first-10,000 rate, which applied from 2011/12 to 2025/26

Rate for every business mile after the first 10,000, from 6 April 2027 - up from 25p, the first move in that band since 2011/12. Announced at Budget 2026 (OOTLAR section 2.7) and to be delivered by statutory instrument later, so ANNOUNCED BUT NOT YET LEGISLATED. The first-10,000-mile rate is not changed by this measure and stays at 55p

The 2026/27 rates, already in primary legislation not an SI: Taxation (Energy and Vehicles) Act 2026 s.2 amends ITEPA 2003 s.230(2) and ITTOIA 2005 s.94F(2), substituting 55p for 45p, in force at Royal Assent 15 July 2026 and having effect for 2026-27 and subsequent tax years

scope.who: Employees and directors using their OWN car or van for business journeys, and the self-employed using the simplified rates
scope.excluded: A company car or any vehicle the employer provides — those use Advisory Fuel Rates instead. Ordinary commuting from home to a permanent workplace never counts. Where the employer pays less than the approved rate, you claim tax relief on the shortfall, not the full pence per mile.
scope.from_when: 55p for the first 10,000 business miles applies for the whole of 2026/27, backdated to 6 April 2026, and 25p above 10,000. From 6 April 2027 the over-10,000 rate is announced to rise to 35p, with the first-10,000 rate staying at 55p.
scope.how_to_claim: Normally paid by the employer. Where they pay less, claim Mileage Allowance Relief through Self Assessment or form P87.

notes: HIGHEST-RISK FIGURE: almost all third-party material still says 45p. The 10,000-mile counter resets each tax year and is per person, not per vehicle. Do NOT state a 2027/28 first-10,000 rate — only the over-10,000 rate rising to 35p has been announced. The over-10,000 band rises to 35p from 6 April 2027 (Budget 2026 OOTLAR 2.7) but that is ANNOUNCED ONLY, to be legislated by statutory instrument - it must not be stated as law. The 2026/27 55p is law, in the Taxation (Energy and Vehicles) Act 2026 s.2, not an SI; the gov.uk 'Increasing mileage rates' note is stale on legislative status and still says 'Bill', so cite the Act. This is NOT a change to Advisory Fuel Rates for company cars, which are revised quarterly and are routinely confused with AMAPs. Motorcycles stay at 24p and bicycles at 20p for both bands.

title: The High Income Child Benefit Charge

figures.what: Adjusted net income above which the charge starts
How the charge builds, for every £200 of income above £60,000
Income at which the charge equals all of the Child Benefit received

scope.who: Whichever partner has the higher adjusted net income, where that is over £60,000 and someone in the household receives Child Benefit
scope.excluded: Anyone with adjusted net income of £60,000 or less. Where both partners are over £60,000, only the higher earner pays it. A household where nobody receives Child Benefit at all.
scope.from_when: £60,000 threshold applies from 2024/25 onwards, including this year
scope.how_to_claim: Claim Child Benefit to keep the National Insurance credits, then opt out of the payments to avoid the charge. The charge itself is paid through Self Assessment.

notes: The real story is the opt-out: staying registered but stopping the payments keeps the National Insurance credits that count towards the State Pension, and the child still gets a National Insurance number at 16. Not claiming at all forfeits those credits. The test is ADJUSTED net income, so pension contributions reduce it. The threshold is per person, not per household: two people on £59,000 pay nothing.

title: The Personal Savings Allowance

figures.what: Tax-free savings interest for a basic rate taxpayer
Tax-free savings interest for a higher rate taxpayer
The starting rate for savings — a separate band taxed at 0%

scope.who: Individuals with interest from bank, building society and credit union accounts
scope.excluded: Additional rate taxpayers get nothing at all — zero, not a reduced amount. The separate £5,000 starting rate is not available to anyone whose other income reaches £17,570. Interest inside an ISA is already tax-free and does not use the allowance.
scope.from_when: Current for the 2026/27 tax year
scope.how_to_claim: Automatic. Banks report interest to HMRC and any tax due is usually collected through the tax code.

notes: It is a 0% band, not a deduction: going £1 over does not tax the whole amount. Budget 2026 did not change the allowance, but raised the tax rates charged above it to 24/44/49% from 6 April 2027.

title: Small Business Rate Relief (England)

figures.what: Rateable value at or below which 100% relief applies — no business rates at all
Taper band — relief falls gradually from 100% to 0%
gov.uk's own worked examples inside the taper
Limits on other properties if you are to keep relief on the main one

scope.who: Businesses using one property with a rateable value under £15,000, and some with more than one property within the limits above
scope.excluded: Properties with a rateable value of £15,000 or more. Businesses whose other properties breach the £2,899 or £20,000 limits. Businesses already receiving charitable rate relief.
scope.from_when: Ongoing. Second properties taken on from 27 November 2025 keep relief for 36 months rather than 12.
scope.how_to_claim: Apply to the billing authority — Birmingham City Council for Birmingham.

notes: England only — Scotland and Wales run different schemes on different thresholds. Relief is based on RATEABLE VALUE, not turnover or profit; that is the commonest misunderstanding. The £12,000 headline is misleading without the taper band beside it.

title: £100 Household Energy Payment (England, from January 2027)

figures.what: One-off payment per eligible household, for this financial year only, announced at the Autumn Budget 2026
Council tax bands covered by the core scheme, in England
When payments begin. Councils are expected to start making payments from January 2027, with scheme funding provided to them in advance and a reconciliation process afterwards

Number eligible in England - the government says this includes an estimated 83% of fuel-stressed households in England and 88% of households in the bottom three income deciles. The MHCLG letter to councils puts it as 'over 20 million households'

Separate discretionary fund given to councils in England to support households that are not eligible for the £100, including some in bands above D. Councils set their own criteria and publish their own application details

figures.value: No action needed if you pay by Direct Debit
figures.what: The payment mechanism, now confirmed on gov.uk: 'If you pay by direct debit and live in bands A to D, you don't need to do anything - the rebate will be paid directly into your bank account.' For everyone else: 'If you don't pay by direct debit, your council will invite you to apply for the rebate directly'
The Warm Home Discount, which gov.uk flags as separate support for households on means-tested benefits - it is not the same thing as the £100 Household Energy Payment and the two are not alternatives

scope.who: Households in England that are liable for council tax on, and live in, a property in council tax bands A to D as their main home. Most households exempt from council tax are included. Delivered through the council tax system by local authorities.
scope.excluded: Second homes, empty properties, and households where the householder is not responsible for paying council tax (so many people in houses in multiple occupation, and tenants whose landlord pays the council tax, get nothing). Bands E to H are outside the core scheme, though the separate £100 million discretionary fund lets councils reach some of them. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are outside the scheme entirely - they receive additional funding instead and their own governments decide how to use it, so there is no guarantee of a £100 payment there. Northern Ireland has domestic rates rather than council tax, so a band-based council tax scheme could not run there as designed.
scope.from_when: Payments from January 2027. One-off, for the 2026-27 financial year only.
scope.how_to_claim: It depends on how you pay your council tax, and this is the single most important thing to get right. If you pay council tax by Direct Debit and live in a band A to D property, gov.uk says you do not need to do anything and the money will be paid straight into your bank account. If you do NOT pay by Direct Debit, your council will invite you to apply for it directly - so a sizeable minority must act. For the separate £100 million discretionary fund, every council sets its own eligibility criteria and publishes its own application route on its website once local arrangements are in place. gov.uk also warns that nobody other than your council should contact you asking you to claim, and to double check with the council if a message looks doubtful.

notes: RE-CHECKED 17 November 2026 and this entry has CHANGED materially: the payment mechanism is now confirmed at primary source, which it was not at the last check. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero page 'What the Autumn Budget 2026 means for your energy bills' (gov.uk, published 28 October 2026) states that Direct Debit payers in bands A to D need do nothing and will be paid straight into their bank account, and that anyone not paying by Direct Debit will be invited by their council to apply. That is why 'automatic' is set to false rather than true: it is automatic for Direct Debit payers only, and copy that just says 'it's automatic, you don't need to do anything' will cause non-Direct-Debit households to miss out. The second piece of newly confirmed detail is the exclusions - second homes, empty properties, and households where the householder is not responsible for paying the council tax - plus the fact that most council-tax-exempt households ARE included. Still NOT published, checked again today: MHCLG's detailed delivery guidance. Council tax information letter 6/2026 (published 29 October 2026, unchanged) says the department 'will shortly publish detailed guidance' covering eligibility criteria, payment arrangements, monitoring and assurance, and expectations of the discretionary fund. So the full eligibility criteria are still described on gov.uk as 'to be published in due course', and anything beyond the outline above is not yet verifiable. Naming traps: gov.uk calls it both the Household Energy Payment and, in the consumer questions, 'the rebate' - it is not a Winter Fuel Payment, not the Warm Home Discount (that is a separate £150 for people on means-tested benefits) and not a general council tax rebate. Nation trap: this is England only. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland get additional funding and decide for themselves, so do not promise readers outside England a £100 payment, and remember Northern Ireland has domestic rates rather than council tax bands. Band trap: band A to D is the property's band, not an income test, so a high earner in a band C flat qualifies and a low earner in a band E house does not - the £100 million discretionary fund is the only route for the latter. Scam trap worth repeating in any copy: gov.uk says nobody other than your council should get in touch asking you to claim.

title: Employment Allowance

figures.what: Maximum reduction in employers' Class 1 National Insurance for 2026/27
An employer doing less than half its work for the public sector can claim

scope.who: Businesses and charities with employer Class 1 National Insurance, where less than half the work is in or for the public sector
scope.excluded: A limited company where the sole director is the only employee paid above the Secondary Threshold. Public authorities that are not charities. Employers of a nanny, cleaner or gardener, unless that person is a care or support worker. All but one company in a group of connected companies. Payments caught by the off-payroll working rules.
scope.from_when: £10,500 for 2026/27. The old £100,000 eligibility cap was removed from April 2025.
scope.how_to_claim: Through payroll software, by sending an Employment Payment Summary. Must be claimed again every tax year.

notes: The single-director exclusion catches a large share of small limited companies. The claim does not roll forward — it is re-made each year. Do not assert anything about de minimis state aid; it was not on any page that loaded.

title: National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage from 1 April 2027

figures.what: National Living Wage, 21 and over, from 1 April 2027 (up from £12.71)
Ages 18 to 20, from 1 April 2027 (up from £10.85)
Under 18 and the apprentice rate, from 1 April 2027 (up from £8.00)

scope.who: Workers of school leaving age and over; the National Living Wage applies from age 21
scope.excluded: Anyone aged 20 or under does not get the National Living Wage — they get the lower age rate. Apprentices under 19, and those 19 or over in their first year, get the apprentice rate instead of their age rate. Genuinely self-employed contractors are not covered at all.
scope.from_when: 1 April 2027; the April 2026 rates apply until then
scope.how_to_claim: A statutory entitlement — nothing to claim. Enforced by HMRC.

notes: UK-wide, not devolved. The National Living Wage starts at 21 — not 18, not 23. Entirely separate from the voluntary Real Living Wage set by a charity, which is higher and is NOT a legal rate.

title: Council Tax Reduction

figures.what: Maximum reduction of a council tax bill under a local scheme

scope.who: People on a low income or on benefits who are liable for council tax where they live, whether they own or rent, whether working or not
scope.excluded: People subject to immigration control, and people not habitually resident in the UK, Ireland, the Channel Islands or the Isle of Man, are excluded by law from every council's scheme. Beyond that each council sets its own working-age rules, so income and savings limits differ by council.
scope.from_when: In force since April 2013. Local rules usually change each 1 April.
scope.how_to_claim: Apply to your own council. It is not applied to the bill automatically.

notes: Not a single national scheme — Birmingham, Solihull, Sandwell, Dudley and Walsall genuinely differ. Never quote one council's rules as regional, and never state a national savings cut-off. Distinct from the Single Person Discount and the Disabled Band Reduction. Replaced Council Tax Benefit in 2013; never use the old name.

title: Self Assessment: 31 January 2027

figures.what: Deadline to file the 2025/26 return online AND to pay the tax owed for it
How each payment on account is calculated
No payments on account if last year's Self Assessment bill was under this
No payments on account if more than this share of last year's tax was collected at source

scope.who: Anyone issued a notice to file, plus sole traders with gross trading income over £1,000, partners, those with Capital Gains Tax, and those with untaxed income such as rent or dividends
scope.excluded: Anyone who meets none of the criteria and has had no notice to file. No payments on account are due where last year's bill was under £1,000, or where more than 80% of last year's tax was already collected at source. The paper deadline was 31 October 2026 and has passed.
scope.from_when: For the 2025/26 tax year
scope.how_to_claim: File online and pay by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027.

notes: THREE obligations fall on 31 January 2027, not one: the return, the balancing payment for 2025/26, and the first payment on account for 2026/27. Payments on account include Class 4 National Insurance but not Capital Gains Tax or student loan repayments. Budget 2026 changed nothing here; more frequent in-year payments start only from April 2029.

title: VAT registration and deregistration thresholds

figures.what: Registration threshold — taxable turnover in any rolling 12 months
The forward-look test, which triggers immediate registration
Deregistration threshold — you may ask HMRC to cancel below this
Time to register after the end of the month you went over

scope.who: Any business whose taxable turnover exceeds £90,000 in any rolling 12-month period, or which expects to exceed it in the next 30 days alone
scope.excluded: Businesses selling only goods or services that are VAT exempt or outside the scope of VAT, whatever their turnover. Businesses at £90,000 or below, who may still register voluntarily. Businesses whose supplies are wholly or mainly zero-rated can apply for exemption from registration.
scope.from_when: Unchanged since 1 April 2024, and confirmed unchanged for April 2026 and April 2027 at Budget 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Register online with HMRC within 30 days of the end of the month the test was breached.

notes: ROLLING 12 months — any consecutive twelve, checked monthly. NOT the tax year, NOT the accounting year, NOT profit. Turnover is sales value before costs. Zero-rated sales count; exempt and out-of-scope sales do not. The forward-look test is the next 30 DAYS, so one large contract can trigger it.

title: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax

figures.what: Qualifying income in 2024/25 — in scope since 6 April 2026
Qualifying income in 2025/26 — in scope from 6 April 2027
Qualifying income in 2026/27 — in scope from 6 April 2028

scope.who: Sole traders and landlords in Self Assessment whose qualifying income — gross self-employment and property income added together, before expenses — exceeds the threshold for the year
scope.excluded: Anyone with qualifying income of £20,000 or less is automatically exempt with nothing to apply for. Partnerships are not in yet. Employees and company directors with no self-employment or property income are outside it entirely, and limited company profits stay under Corporation Tax. Various further exemptions exist, including for foster and kinship carers.
scope.from_when: Live since 6 April 2026 for the first tranche
scope.how_to_claim: Sign up through HMRC's service and use compatible software for quarterly updates and a final declaration.

notes: Qualifying income is GROSS, not profit, and the two sources are added together. The look-back is two years, so the 6 April 2027 start is set by the 2025/26 return being filed now. Being exempt does NOT remove the duty to file an ordinary Self Assessment return. Budget 2026 added a penalty easement for the April 2027 cohort and new exemptions, but did not move the thresholds.

title: CIS monthly returns

figures.what: The return must REACH HMRC by the 19th of the month after the tax month
Deduction for a subcontractor registered for CIS
Deduction where the subcontractor is not registered, or HMRC cannot match their details
Penalties at 1 day, 2 months, and 6 and 12 months late

scope.who: Every CIS contractor — construction businesses paying subcontractors, and businesses outside construction spending over £3 million on construction in the previous 12 months
scope.excluded: Householders having work done on their own home are not contractors and file nothing. Subcontractors do not file these returns at all — the duty is the contractor's. A contractor who has notified HMRC of a period of inactivity, up to 6 months.
scope.from_when: Ongoing, every tax month
scope.how_to_claim: File the CIS300 online by the 19th. With no payments made, file a nil return or notify inactivity by the same date.

notes: The 19th is a RECEIPT deadline and does not move for weekends or bank holidays. Penalties stack. The 30% rate also applies when HMRC simply cannot match the subcontractor's details. Deductions come from the LABOUR element only — materials and VAT are excluded. Budget 2026 contained no CIS measure.

title: Companies House confirmation statement

figures.what: How often a confirmation statement must be filed
Filing window after the end of the review period
The fee
Fine for failing to file, and the company may be struck off

scope.who: Every company on the register, including dormant and non-trading companies
scope.excluded: Sole traders, ordinary partnerships and unincorporated bodies file nothing, because they are not registered companies. A company already dissolved and removed from the register. No fee is due on a second statement filed within the same 12-month payment period.
scope.from_when: First review period ends 12 months after incorporation
scope.how_to_claim: File online within 14 days of the end of the review period, or by paper form CS01.

notes: NOT the annual accounts and NOT the Corporation Tax return — a separate, third filing, and a company that files accounts on time can still be struck off for missing this. There is no 'nothing to report' exemption: the duty is to CONFIRM. Failure is a criminal offence and directors can be prosecuted. Companies House fees are set administratively, not by the Budget.

title: Payments on Account

figures.value: 2 payments a year, due by midnight on 31 January and 31 July
figures.what: the payment-on-account deadlines; the instalment due 31 January 2027 is the first payment on account for 2026/27, paid alongside the 2025/26 balancing payment

each payment on account is usually half of the tax you owed the previous year; HMRC manual: 50% of the 'relevant amount' for the preceding year, being income tax assessed less tax deducted at source (s.59A(2) TMA 1970)
de minimis: no payments on account are due if the amount of tax you owed last year was less than £1,000 (HMRC manual: 'less than a fixed amount of £1,000')

deducted-at-source test: no payments on account are due if last year you paid more than 80% of the tax you owed outside Self Assessment (HMRC manual: the relevant amount bears a proportion to the assessed amount of less than 1 to 5)
deadline for the balancing payment, worked out by deducting the payments on account already made from the total tax owed
how to claim to reduce payments on account if you expect your tax to be lower than last year

scope.who: Self Assessment taxpayers whose last year's Self Assessment tax bill was £1,000 or more and who paid 20% or more of that tax through Self Assessment rather than at source. The payment due by midnight on 31 January 2027 is the first payment on account towards 2026/27, calculated as half of the 2025/26 'relevant amount' (income tax assessed less tax deducted at source), and falls due at the same time as the 2025/26 balancing payment.
scope.excluded: No payments on account are due if EITHER the amount of tax owed for the previous year was less than £1,000, OR more than 80% of the tax owed for the previous year was paid outside Self Assessment (e.g. through a PAYE tax code or tax already deducted by a bank). Per HMRC manual SALF303 the statutory tests are the £1,000 fixed de minimis and the 'less than 1 to 5' proportion test under s.59A(1) TMA 1970. Payments on account also do not cover Capital Gains Tax or Class 2 National Insurance, which are collected in the balancing payment.
scope.from_when: Standing rule under s.59A Taxes Management Act 1970; the next instalment is due by midnight on 31 January 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — HMRC calculates the instalments from your previous year's return and they are due without demand. To REDUCE them, sign in to your online account, select the option to view your latest Self Assessment return and select 'Reduce payments on account', or send form SA303 to your tax office, stating the amount you expect to owe. If you reduce them and your actual bill turns out higher, HMRC charges interest on the difference.

notes: Verified against both the gov.uk guidance page and HMRC manual SALF303 (which cites s.59A TMA 1970 and the limits originally set by SI 1996/1654 as amended). Both the £1,000 and 80% tests are alternatives — either one removes the obligation. SALF303 confirms payments are 'due without demand'.

title: Self Assessment Late Filing Penalties

figures.what: initial fixed late filing penalty, charged as soon as the return is late, regardless of whether any tax is owed

figures.value: £10 per day, up to a maximum of £900
figures.what: daily penalties once the return is more than 3 months late (HMRC manual: £10 a day over a period of 90 days); HMRC must decide that a daily penalty is payable and give notice to the taxpayer

figures.value: 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater
figures.what: further penalty after 6 months (HMRC manual: the greater of 5% of the tax liability which would have been shown in the return, and £300)

figures.value: 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater
figures.what: further penalty after 12 months; can rise to 70% of the tax due where information is deliberately withheld, and 100% where that withholding is concealed

the replacement penalty for taxpayers inside Making Tax Digital for Income Tax — a points-based system where each missed return deadline earns one point and a £200 penalty is charged at 4 points, and for each further missed deadline

scope.who: Anyone required to file a Self Assessment tax return who misses the filing deadline. For the 2025/26 return the online filing deadline is 31 January 2027. The penalties stack: £100 immediately, then £10 a day from 3 months late (max £900), then the greater of 5% of the tax due or £300 at 6 months, and the same again at 12 months. All partners are charged a penalty if a partnership tax return is late.
scope.excluded: No liability to a late filing penalty arises where the taxpayer shows a reasonable excuse (HMRC manual SALF208A, para 23) — but an insufficiency of funds is not a reasonable excuse unless attributable to events outside the taxpayer's control, and reliance on another person is not a reasonable excuse unless the taxpayer took reasonable care to avoid the failure. Daily £10 penalties are not automatic: they are not due unless HMRC decides a daily penalty should be payable and gives notice to the taxpayer. Separately, these fixed penalties do NOT apply to taxpayers within Making Tax Digital for Income Tax for the tax years they are in MTD — they get a points-based regime instead (£200 at 4 points). The MTD penalties also do not apply to non-resident company returns, trust or estate returns, or partnership returns.
scope.from_when: Schedule 55 Finance Act 2009, in force for returns from 2010/11 onwards. For someone joining MTD for Income Tax on 6 April 2026, the penalties on this entry still apply to the 2025/26 return due 31 January 2027; the MTD points system applies from the 2026/27 return onwards.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — the £100 and the 6/12-month penalties arise automatically and HMRC issues a penalty notice. To challenge one, appeal to HMRC on the ground of reasonable excuse (form SA370 or online); appeals go on to the First-tier Tribunal and Upper Tribunal.

notes: Verified at both the gov.uk guidance page and HMRC manual SALF208A. SALF208A does NOT state any cap limiting the penalty to the tax liability. The MTD for Income Tax change is the live risk on this subject: anyone mandated into MTD from 6 April 2026 moves to the points system for their 2026/27 return (due 31 January 2028), so content must be clear which year it describes.

title: Self Assessment Late Payment Penalties and Interest

figures.what: First late payment penalty - 5% of the tax still unpaid 30 days after the due date. Statute: paragraph 3(2), Schedule 56 Finance Act 2009
Second late payment penalty - a further 5% of tax still unpaid at the end of the period of 5 months beginning with the penalty date (about 6 months late). Paragraph 3(3), Schedule 56
Third late payment penalty - a further 5% of tax still unpaid at the end of the period of 11 months beginning with the penalty date (about 12 months late). Paragraph 3(4), Schedule 56

figures.value: 5% at 30 days, 6 months and 12 months late
figures.what: The same three penalties as stated on the public guidance page: “You’ll get penalties of 5% of the tax unpaid at” 30 days, 6 months and 12 months, plus interest on the amount owed

Time limit to pay a penalty once charged - payment is due within 30 days of the date on the penalty notice, and late payment interest then runs on the unpaid penalty from the end of that 30-day period. Appeal is possible on reasonable excuse grounds and there is no obligation to pay the penalty before an appeal is determined
Late payment interest charged alongside the penalties - the rate in force today, 17 November 2026, applying from 9 January 2026 to 23 November 2026
Late payment interest rate from 24 November 2026, one week from today and not yet in force
Repayment interest rate in force today (from 9 January 2026), rising to 3.00% from 24 November 2026

figures.value: Bank of England base rate plus 4 percentage points
figures.what: Formula for the late payment interest rate from 6 April 2025; base rate is 4% following the MPC decision published 5 November 2026, with the next decision due 17 December 2026

figures.value: 3% at day 15, 3% at day 30, then 10% a year from day 31
figures.what: The DIFFERENT late payment penalties that apply instead for the 2026-27 tax year to taxpayers using Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - no penalty up to 15 days late; 3% of the tax owed at day 15 if 16 to 30 days late; 3% at day 15 plus 3% at day 30 if 31 days or more late, plus an annual rate of 10% charged daily from day 31 until the tax is paid, or for up to 2 years. For 2027-28 the two fixed charges are 4% each

In your first year of the new Making Tax Digital penalties you get 30 days, not 15, from the due date to pay in full or contact HMRC about a payment plan before penalties start. HMRC states you only get that 30-day period once: someone who volunteered early and is then mandated continues to have 15 days

The Making Tax Digital late SUBMISSION penalty, which is points based and separate from the late payment penalties: one point per missed quarterly update or tax return deadline, a £200 penalty at 4 points and a further £200 for each later miss. There are no penalties for missing a quarterly update deadline in the 2026-27 tax year. Points are separate from VAT penalty points

Who is pulled into Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, and so into the new penalty regime: qualifying self-employment and property income over £50,000 on the 2024-25 return, from 6 April 2026; over £30,000 on the 2025-26 return from 6 April 2027; over £20,000 on the 2026-27 return from 6 April 2028

figures.value: base rate minus 1 percentage point, 0.5% floor
figures.what: Repayment interest formula (late payment interest is base rate plus 4 percentage points from 6 April 2025). Repayment interest is paid at 0.5% until the Bank of England raises the base rate above 1.5%

scope.nation: Whole of the UK. Self Assessment late payment penalties and interest are UK-wide and identical in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland - Scottish and Welsh taxpayers are in the same system because HMRC collects Scottish and Welsh income tax.
scope.who: Self Assessment taxpayers - individuals, sole traders, partners (for their own tax), trustees - who still have Self Assessment tax unpaid after the due date. The manual confirms the penalty bites on Capital Gains Tax, on Class 4 National Insurance contributions (treated as income tax) and on student loan repayments collected through Self Assessment, as well as on tax shown as due in an amended self assessment or a discovery assessment. The penalties are charged on top of late payment interest, which runs from the due date.
scope.excluded: A late payment penalty is NOT charged where: (1) there is no tax unpaid at the relevant penalty date - the penalty bites only on what is still outstanding at 30 days, 5 months and 11 months from the penalty date, so paying before each date stops that penalty, and someone who owes nothing gets nothing; (2) a Time to Pay arrangement is requested and HMRC agrees to defer payment before the penalty date - no penalty arises on that amount for the deferral period, measured from the date of the request, as long as the plan is kept (break it, or miss a condition, and HMRC can serve notice charging the penalty); (3) the taxpayer has a reasonable excuse for the failure (paragraph 16, Schedule 56 FA 2009) - an insufficiency of funds counts only where it is attributable to events outside the taxpayer's control, and reliance on another person is not an excuse unless the taxpayer took reasonable care; (4) the tax is postponed pending an appeal in an enquiry; (5) additional tax arising from an amendment is paid within 60 days of the amendment (interest still runs from the original due date); (6) HMRC applies a special reduction for special circumstances (paragraph 9) - ability to pay does not count as a special circumstance; and (7) taxpayers inside Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, from the tax year they join - they are outside the three 5% penalties and get the reformed penalties instead. The reformed Making Tax Digital penalties themselves do not apply to payments on account, nor to non-resident company, trust or estate, or partnership returns, which keep the existing penalties. A further class never moves to the reformed regime at all: a taxpayer who is exempt from Making Tax Digital for Income Tax stays in Self Assessment and so stays on the three 5% penalties indefinitely. Digital exclusion is confirmed at primary source as a ground of exemption; the full list of exemption grounds sits on separate guidance that has NOT been verified, so cite digital exclusion only and do not list other grounds.
scope.from_when: The three 5% penalties apply to Income Tax and Capital Gains Tax for 2010-11 onwards under Schedule 56 Finance Act 2009. The reformed Making Tax Digital penalties apply from the tax year a taxpayer joins Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, mandation starting 6 April 2026 - so for someone mandated from 6 April 2026 the current penalties still apply to the 2025-26 return due 31 January 2027, and the new ones bite on 2026-27. The interest rate charged is 7.75% to 23 November 2026 and 8.00% from 24 November 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim - the penalties and interest are charged automatically by HMRC, which must serve a notice of assessment for each penalty. What the taxpayer has to do is act to avoid them: pay before each penalty date, or contact HMRC and agree a Time to Pay arrangement before the penalty date (penalties are paused from the date of contact if a plan is agreed and kept - the same rule is stated for the Making Tax Digital regime). A penalty already charged can be appealed on reasonable excuse grounds using form SA370, and HMRC can reduce a penalty for special circumstances.

notes: RE-CHECKED 18 November 2026: all penalty figures confirmed unchanged at SALF308A (page updated 13 October 2026) and on the public penalties page, and the Making Tax Digital penalty table confirmed unchanged. THE REGIME QUESTION, answered precisely: for Self Assessment returns due 31 January 2027 (the 2025-26 return) the three 5% penalties under Schedule 56 FA 2009 STILL APPLY, to everyone. The reformed Making Tax Digital penalties do NOT apply to that return for anyone - HMRC's own worked example states that 'current penalties will apply to your 2025 to 2026 tax return deadline of 31 January 2027'. The trigger is the tax year joined, not the filing date: someone mandated into MTD from 6 April 2026 is on the old regime for their 2025-26 bill due 31 January 2027, and on the new 3%/3%/10%-a-year regime for their 2026-27 bill due 31 January 2028. Both errors are equally easy - saying 'you get three 5% penalties' is wrong for the MTD cohort from 2026-27, and telling a mandated client the new penalties apply to their 31 January 2027 bill is wrong too. Second thing a reader would get wrong, the timing: the penalties are not at a tidy month 1, 6 and 12. The manual measures the second and third from the penalty date, at the end of 5 months and 11 months beginning with the penalty date, which lands around 6 and 12 months after the due date. Interest is separate from the penalties, runs from the due date, is not reduced for reasonable excuse, and does not change on the day the Bank of England moves: it is 7.75% today and becomes 8.00% on 24 November 2026, nearly three weeks after the 5 November 2026 Bank Rate rise. Interest also runs on an unpaid penalty itself from 30 days after the notice. No change to Schedule 56 Self Assessment penalties or the interest regime was found in Budget 2026 OOTLAR Annex A.

title: HMRC Budget Payment Plan

figures.what: the payment frequencies available under a Budget Payment Plan; you choose the frequency and the amount
how long you can pause payments under the plan if you need to

figures.value: 11 characters (your UTR followed by the letter K)
figures.what: the payment reference needed to set the plan up

scope.who: Self Assessment taxpayers who are up to date with their payments and want to pay towards their NEXT tax bill in advance by weekly or monthly Direct Debit. Payments are credited against the next bill, so there is less to pay at the payment deadline. Payments can be paused for up to 6 months. If the amount paid does not cover the whole of the next bill, the difference must still be paid by the deadline; if the account is in credit, a refund can be requested.
scope.excluded: You cannot set up a Budget Payment Plan unless you are up to date with any payments from your last Self Assessment tax bill — gov.uk states 'To set up a plan you must be up to date with any payments from your last Self Assessment tax bill.' It is therefore not available to anyone with an outstanding or overdue balance from their last bill, and it is not a route for paying off an overdue bill at all: anyone who has missed a Self Assessment payment deadline or cannot pay what they owe needs a Time to Pay arrangement instead. It also requires a Self Assessment online account and a Direct Debit, so it is not open to anyone who cannot or will not pay by Direct Debit.
scope.from_when: Standing HMRC facility, available now; payments count towards the next Self Assessment bill.
scope.how_to_claim: Sign in to your Self Assessment online account, select 'Direct Debit' and choose the Budget Payment Plan option, then decide whether to pay weekly or monthly and how much. You will need your 11-character payment reference (your UTR followed by the letter K).

notes: The gov.uk page lists only the one eligibility condition (being up to date with the last bill) — no minimum or maximum payment amount and no debt threshold are stated at primary source, so content must not invent one. The distinction from Time to Pay is drawn by the page's own structure (Budget Payment Plan = paying ahead while up to date; Time to Pay = an overdue bill you cannot pay) rather than by a single explicit sentence. Note a naming inconsistency on gov.uk itself: the page heading is 'Pay weekly or monthly' and the scheme is written 'Budget Payment plan' in the body.

title: Self Assessment Time to Pay Payment Plan

figures.what: maximum Self Assessment debt that can be arranged as an online payment plan without contacting HMRC directly; those owing more can still apply but must contact HMRC
the longest period over which the online Self Assessment payment plan spreads the payments
a Time to Pay arrangement cannot be set up until the Self Assessment return has been filed

scope.who: Self Assessment taxpayers who cannot pay their tax bill in full and who have already filed the return. A plan spreads the overdue amount into regular monthly instalments and, while it is kept to, avoids further late payment penalties. HMRC checks that the plan is affordable; where there are savings or assets, HMRC expects those to be used to reduce the debt as much as possible first. A missed instalment incurs interest as well as a penalty.
scope.excluded: You cannot use the ONLINE self-serve payment plan and must contact HMRC directly if: you owe more than £30,000; you need longer than 12 months to pay; or you have not yet filed your Self Assessment tax return (HMRC: 'A Time to Pay arrangement cannot be set up until a Self Assessment return has been filed'). Companies in tax debt face extra questions and are expected to reduce the debt as much as possible before a plan is set up. A payment plan is also not a route for a bill that is not yet due — paying ahead of the deadline is a Budget Payment Plan instead. Interest continues to run on the outstanding balance throughout a Time to Pay arrangement.
scope.from_when: Standing HMRC facility, available now; the current £30,000 online threshold was confirmed in HMRC's gov.uk release of 9 December 2025.
scope.how_to_claim: File the return first, then check eligibility and set the plan up through the 'Set up a Self Assessment payment plan' online service via gov.uk. If you cannot set one up online — because you owe more than £30,000, need longer than 12 months, or are otherwise ineligible — contact HMRC to agree a plan.

notes: SOURCING CAVEAT the content team must know: the current gov.uk guidance pages (/difficulties-paying-hmrc and /difficulties-paying-hmrc/pay-in-instalments) no longer state the eligibility figures — they defer to the online eligibility checker. The £30,000 ceiling, the filed-return requirement and the 'contact HMRC if you owe more or need longer' rule are taken from HMRC's own gov.uk news release of 9 December 2025; the 12-month maximum is from HMRC's gov.uk release of 10 December 2024. Both are HMRC publications on gov.uk but neither is live guidance, so this entry should be rechecked against the service itself before publication. The HMRC service pages at tax.service.gov.uk (which carry the full refusal reasons) could not be read without a session — they returned server errors. I also could NOT verify at primary source the commonly cited condition that you must be within 60 days of the payment deadline, so that must not appear in copy. One URL was blocked by a permission timeout and not read: https://www.gov.uk/pay-self-assessment-tax-bill/pay-in-instalments

title: Self Assessment Registration Deadline

figures.what: deadline to tell HMRC you need to complete a tax return for the previous tax year; the live gov.uk page currently states 'by 5 October 2026' for the tax year that started 6 April 2025 and ended 5 April 2026, so the equivalent deadline for the 2026/27 tax year is 5 October 2027

figures.value: six months from the end of the tax year
figures.what: the statutory time limit for notifying chargeability (HMRC manual: 'Notification must be received on or before 5 October'), under s.7(1)
failure to notify penalty range for a non-deliberate failure disclosed unprompted within 12 months of the tax being due
failure to notify penalty range for a non-deliberate failure disclosed unprompted 12 months or more after the tax was due, and for a prompted non-deliberate disclosure within 12 months
failure to notify penalty range for a non-deliberate failure disclosed prompted 12 months or more after the tax was due
failure to notify penalty range where the failure was deliberate but not concealed
failure to notify penalty range where the failure was deliberate and concealed

scope.who: Anyone who needs to complete a Self Assessment tax return for a tax year and has either never sent a tax return before, or registered before but did not need to send a return for the previous year. They must tell HMRC by 5 October following the end of that tax year — six months from the end of the tax year in which the liability arises. Penalties for failure to notify are a percentage of the tax unpaid, set by whether the failure was non-deliberate, deliberate, or deliberate and concealed, and reduced for unprompted disclosure and for disclosure within 12 months of the tax becoming due.
scope.excluded: HMRC manual SALF210 sets out the statutory exceptions to the requirement to notify (s.7(3) to (7)): a taxpayer is excepted where they have no chargeable gains, or their chargeable gains do not exceed the annual exempt amount, AND either they have no net liability to income tax for the year, or they have had sufficient tax deducted at source to meet their net income tax liability for the year. Anyone who has already been sent a notice to file, or who registered and filed for the previous year, does not need to re-register. On penalties: HMRC states 'If you have a reasonable excuse for a non-deliberate failure to notify, we won't charge you a penalty', provided the failure was not deliberate and HMRC was told without unreasonable delay once the excuse ended. There is also no failure-to-notify penalty where no tax is unpaid, since the penalty is a percentage of the unpaid tax.
scope.from_when: Standing rule under s.7 Taxes Management Act 1970; failure to notify penalties under Schedule 41 Finance Act 2008. The live gov.uk page currently states the 5 October 2026 deadline for the 2025/26 tax year; the deadline for the 2026/27 tax year is 5 October 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Use the 'Check how to register for Self Assessment' service on gov.uk to register and get a Unique Taxpayer Reference. gov.uk warns: 'If you tell HMRC after 5 October 2026, you could get a penalty.'

notes: DATING WARNING for the content team: the gov.uk registration page is written dynamically around 'the previous tax year', and as read on 14 November 2026 it shows the 5 October 2026 deadline for 2025/26 — a date that has already passed. Copy should give the rule ('by 5 October following the end of the tax year') and the concrete 5 October 2027 date for 2026/27 rather than lifting the page's current year wording. Note also that gov.uk says only 'you could get a penalty' and does not quantify it; the percentages come from HMRC factsheet CC/FS11. The penalty is a percentage of the tax unpaid, not a fixed sum — do not present it as a flat fee. The gov.uk page's second registration trigger is worded against 'the tax year 2024 to 2025', which appears to lag the page's own 2025/26 framing; treat that detail as unreliable and do not reproduce the year.

title: VAT return and payment deadlines (one month and 7 days)

figures.what: Deadline after the end of a VAT accounting period for submitting the online VAT Return and for the payment to reach HMRC's account

figures.value: last day of the month following the end of the return period
figures.what: Statutory return due date under regulation 25(1), VAT Regulations 1995, before the online extension

Extension for returns filed online and paid electronically, given by HMRC Direction under regulations 25A(20) and 40(3) and (4); the extended date is shown on the return and applies to nil and repayment returns too
Return due date for an annual return instead of one month
Period after the extended return deadline on which a Direct Debit is collected

scope.who: All UK VAT-registered businesses on standard (normally quarterly) accounting periods that file the return online and pay electronically: the return and the cleared payment are both due one calendar month and 7 days after the end of the accounting period. A return is due for every period even if there is no VAT to pay or reclaim.
scope.excluded: Payment on Account businesses and Annual Accounting Scheme businesses do not get the 7-day extension to either the return or the payment (VATAC1300); an annual return carries two months rather than one month. Businesses paying by cheque by post get no 7-day extension at all: the cheque is late unless it clears by the standard due date, even though the online return displays the extended date. Nil and repayment paper returns from businesses exempt from online filing must arrive by the standard due date.
scope.from_when: Current rule as read on 14 November 2026. Return due date set by regulation 25(1) and payment due date by regulation 40(2) of the VAT Regulations 1995; the 7-day online extension is given by HMRC Direction under regulations 25A(20) and 40(3) and (4).
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. The deadline applies automatically, and the 7-day extension applies automatically where the return is filed online and the payment is made electronically. The extended date appears on the return itself.

notes: There is no extension where the deadline falls on a weekend or bank holiday — the return and the cleared payment must arrive on or before the deadline (gov.uk/submit-vat-return). Faster Payments can be received on weekends and bank holidays. No Northern Ireland difference for deadlines: the rule is UK-wide.

title: VAT Flat Rate Scheme

figures.what: VAT-exclusive taxable turnover expected in the next year — the limit to join the scheme (VAT Notice 733 paras 2.5 and 3.1)
VAT-inclusive total income (taxable plus exempt supplies) in the year ending, above which you must leave the scheme (VAT Notice 733 paras 3.5 and 12.2(a))
HMRC may allow you to stay in the scheme after breaching £230,000 if satisfied your income in the next 12 months will not exceed this figure (VAT Notice 733 paras 3.5 and 11.2)
Flat rate percentage a limited cost business must use (VAT Notice 733 para 4.4)

figures.value: 2% of flat rate turnover, or over 2% but under £1,000 a year
figures.what: The limited cost business test: spending on relevant goods including VAT below 2% of flat rate turnover, or above 2% but under £1,000 a year (VAT Notice 733 para 4.4)

scope.who: VAT-registered businesses whose taxable turnover excluding VAT is expected to be £150,000 or less in the next year. A business whose spending on relevant goods (including VAT) is under 2% of its flat rate turnover, or over 2% but under £1,000 a year, is a limited cost business and must use the 16.5% rate instead of its trade sector rate.
scope.excluded: You cannot join if: you are not registered for VAT; you use the second-hand margin scheme or the auctioneers' scheme; you are required to use the Tour Operator's Margin Scheme; you are required to operate the Capital Goods Scheme for certain capital items; you stopped using the Flat Rate Scheme in the 12 months before the date of your new application; in the last 12 months you accepted a compound penalty offer or were convicted of an offence in connection with VAT; in the last 12 months you were assessed with a penalty for conduct involving dishonesty; you are, or in the last 24 months were, registered in a VAT group or as a division, or are eligible to join a VAT group (para 3.7); or your business is 'associated' with another one in the way set out in para 3.8. HMRC may waive the group and association restrictions in writing. You must also leave once total VAT-inclusive income exceeds £230,000.
scope.from_when: Current rule as read on 14 November 2026. Apply from the start of a VAT accounting period.
scope.how_to_claim: Must be applied for. Apply online, by post or by email (VAT Notice 733 para 2.6). If already VAT-registered, apply on form VAT600FRS (para 5.1); if joining when you register for VAT, apply as part of the registration.

notes: The £150,000 join limit is VAT-exclusive taxable turnover; the £230,000 leave limit is VAT-inclusive total income including exempt supplies — the two figures are measured on different bases, which is the most common error in commentary on this scheme. The 16.5% limited cost rate and the 2%/£1,000 test are stated in VAT Notice 733 section 4.4, not on the short gov.uk overview page. No Northern Ireland difference in the turnover limits or rates.

title: VAT Cash Accounting Scheme

figures.what: Estimated VAT taxable turnover, excluding VAT, expected in the next 12 months — the limit to join the scheme (VAT Notice 731 section 2.1)
Join limit as stated on the gov.uk eligibility page
Annual value of taxable supplies excluding VAT, over a 12-month period, above which you must leave the scheme (VAT Notice 731 sections 2.5 and 6.2)

scope.who: VAT-registered businesses expecting taxable supplies excluding VAT of £1.35 million or less in the next year. You account for VAT on sales when your customers pay you, and reclaim VAT on purchases when you have paid your supplier.
scope.excluded: You cannot use the scheme if: your expected taxable supplies for the next year exceed £1.35 million; you have VAT Returns outstanding; within the last year you were convicted of a VAT offence, accepted an offer to compound proceedings, or were assessed to a penalty for dishonest VAT evasion; you owe HMRC money and have no arrangement to clear it; HMRC withdrew your use of the scheme or denied you access within the last year; or you cannot meet the record-keeping requirements (VAT Notice 731 section 6.2). You also cannot combine it with the Flat Rate Scheme (section 2.8). Separately, specific supplies are outside the scheme and must be accounted for under normal VAT rules: goods bought or sold under lease purchase, hire purchase, conditional sale or credit sale agreements; goods imported or acquired from an EU member state, or removed from a customs warehouse or free zone; certain goods and services subject to a domestic reverse charge; supplies where payment of an issued VAT invoice is not due in full within 6 months; and supplies where you issue a VAT invoice before making the supply (sections 2.7, 2.8, 5.5).
scope.from_when: Current rule as read on 14 November 2026. You can start from the beginning of your next VAT accounting period; new registrants can use the scheme from their date of registration (VAT Notice 731 section 3.2). You cannot apply the scheme retrospectively.
scope.how_to_claim: No application and no notification to HMRC. VAT Notice 731 section 3.1 states there is no need to apply to use the scheme; you simply start using it at the beginning of a VAT accounting period if you are eligible, and the gov.uk join page confirms you do not have to tell HMRC you use cash accounting. You should leave at the end of a VAT accounting period.

notes: Northern Ireland difference: goods imported into Northern Ireland from the EU are outside the scheme and must be accounted for under normal VAT rules (gov.uk eligibility page; VAT Notice 731 section 2.7). A one-off breach of the £1.6 million limit does not force you out if the increase has not happened before and is not expected to recur (for example selling a capital asset), it arose from genuine commercial activity, and you have reasonable grounds to expect taxable supplies below £1.35 million over the next 12 months — you must record the decision (VAT Notice 731 section 2.6). If turnover exceeded £1.35 million in the last 3 months, outstanding VAT must be reported and paid straight away (gov.uk join/leave page).

title: VAT Annual Accounting Scheme

figures.what: Expected taxable supplies — the limit to join the scheme (VAT Notice 732 section 2.1); the figure excludes VAT, exempt supplies and sales of capital assets (section 2.2)
Taxable supplies per year above which you are withdrawn from the scheme, usually at the end of the annual accounting year in which it happens (VAT Notice 732 section 2.4)
Default monthly instalment pattern: nine payments, each 10% of the previous year's VAT liability (VAT Notice 732 sections 4.1 to 4.3)

figures.value: 3 instalments of 25%, due in months 4, 7 and 10
figures.what: Alternative quarterly instalment pattern available on request, each 25% of the previous year's liability (VAT Notice 732 section 4.5)
Period after the end of the annual accounting year within which the single annual VAT Return and the balancing payment are due (VAT Notice 732 sections 1.3 and 3.6)

scope.who: VAT-registered businesses expecting taxable supplies of up to £1,350,000 (excluding VAT, exempt supplies and capital asset sales). You submit one VAT Return a year instead of four, pay nine monthly instalments of 10% of the previous year's liability by default — or three quarterly instalments of 25% in months 4, 7 and 10 on request — and then make a balancing payment or claim a refund with the annual return.
scope.excluded: You cannot use the scheme if: you are registered for VAT as part of a company group or as a division; you stopped using annual accounting in the previous 12 months; your business is insolvent; or you have a growing VAT debt (a small debt with agreed repayment proposals may still allow entry) (VAT Notice 732 section 2.6). You must also leave once taxable supplies exceed £1,600,000 per year.
scope.from_when: Current rule as read on 14 November 2026. Where a part-year accounting period is under 4 months, the return and balancing payment are due 1 month rather than 2 months after the period end (VAT Notice 732 section 3.6).
scope.how_to_claim: Must be applied for on form VAT600AA (VAT Notice 732 sections 8.1 and 8.2). If you are not yet VAT-registered you can register and apply at the same time. To use annual accounting alongside the Flat Rate Scheme, complete both VAT600AA and VAT600FRS (section 9.1).

notes: Annual Accounting Scheme businesses do not get the 7-day online filing and electronic payment extension that applies to standard quarterly returns (HMRC VAT Accounting manual VATAC1300, read 2026-11-14) — the annual return and balancing payment are due 2 months after the year end. Annual Accounting instalments are also outside the late payment penalty regime (gov.uk late payment penalties guidance, read 2026-11-14). No Northern Ireland difference in the limits or instalment pattern.

title: VAT late submission penalty points and late payment penalties

figures.what: Penalty point thresholds for late submission, by return frequency

figures.value: 2 points (over 20 weeks), 4 points (over 8 and up to 20 weeks), 5 points (8 weeks or less)
figures.what: Penalty point thresholds for non-standard accounting periods
Penalty charged on reaching the points threshold, and again for each further late return while at the threshold
First late payment penalty, charged on the VAT outstanding at day 15 where payment is 16 or more days overdue
Added to the first late payment penalty, on the balance outstanding at day 30, where payment is 31 or more days overdue
Second late payment penalty, charged as a daily rate on the outstanding balance from day 31 until paid in full

Date from which the late payment penalty rates rose from 2 to 3 percentage points at 15 days, 2 to 3 percentage points at 30 days, and 4 to 10 percentage points per annum from day 31, for taxpayers already in the Schedule 26 regime including VAT-registered businesses
VAT accounting periods starting on or after this date are in the points-based late submission and late payment penalty regime; earlier periods fall under the VAT default surcharge

scope.who: All UK VAT-registered businesses, for VAT accounting periods starting on or after 1 January 2023. One penalty point is awarded for each late return until the frequency threshold is reached; at the threshold a £200 penalty is charged, and another £200 for each further late return while you remain at the threshold. Nil returns and repayment returns are covered. Late payment penalties apply to any VAT not paid in full by the due date.
scope.excluded: No penalty point is given for: your first VAT Return after becoming newly VAT registered; your final VAT Return after cancelling your registration; and one-off returns covering a period other than a month, a quarter or a year. For periods starting on or before 31 December 2022 the old VAT default surcharge applies instead, not this regime. The late payment penalties do not apply to payments on account or to Annual Accounting Scheme instalments (gov.uk late payment penalties guidance).
scope.from_when: Points-based regime: VAT accounting periods starting on or after 1 January 2023. Current late payment penalty rates of 3% / further 3% / 10% per annum: from 1 April 2025.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — points and penalties are issued automatically by HMRC. Points can be adjusted when you change accounting periods, and those adjustments cannot be appealed. Separate HMRC guidance covers removing penalty points.

notes: Submitting on time once at the threshold keeps you at the threshold without a further £200 charge; it does not clear the points. Late payment interest is charged separately, from the first day the payment is overdue until it is paid in full, in addition to any late payment penalty. The second late payment penalty runs from day 31 until the balance is paid or just before the 2-year assessment time limit. No Northern Ireland difference. The 1 April 2025 commencement of the higher rates is not stated on the gov.uk late payment penalties guidance page itself — its update history only records on 10 July 2025 that 'the value of late payment penalties charged has been increased' — so the date is cited to the HMRC policy publication instead.

title: VAT domestic reverse charge for building and construction services

figures.what: The charge applies to invoices with a tax point on or after this date; earlier tax points follow the normal VAT rules
The end user disregard: a predominantly end-user customer may re-supply a very small share of the services and still issue an end user declaration

scope.who: Supplies of standard-rated and reduced-rated building and construction services where the customer is VAT registered in the UK, the supply is reported within the Construction Industry Scheme (CIS), the supplier is not an employment business, and the customer has not given written confirmation that it is an end user or an intermediary supplier. The customer, not the supplier, accounts for the VAT on its own VAT Return.
scope.excluded: The charge does not apply where: the customer has notified the supplier in writing that it is an end user — a VAT and CIS registered business or group that does not make onward supplies of the construction services it receives (ending the reverse charge is optional for an end user); the customer is an intermediary supplier that has notified the supplier in writing — a VAT and CIS registered business re-supplying the services without material change to a connected or linked end user, connection being a relevant interest in the same land such as landlord and tenant, or membership of the same corporate group under section 1161 Companies Act 2006; the customer is not VAT registered, including private domestic customers; the supply is zero-rated (standard-rated items within a zero-rated supply of construction services, such as ovens and hobs, are excluded, as is scaffolding for a zero-rated construction project); the supplier is an employment business supplying staff or workers; or the supply is outside CIS. Specified services supplied on their own are also outside the charge: drilling for or extracting oil or natural gas; mineral extraction and related tunnelling, boring or underground works; manufacturing or delivering to site building or engineering components, equipment, materials, plant or machinery; manufacturing or delivering to site components for heating, lighting, air-conditioning, ventilation, power, drainage, sanitation, water supply or fire protection systems; professional work of architects or surveyors, or of building, engineering, interior, exterior decoration and landscape consultants; making, installing or repairing purely artistic works such as sculptures and murals; signwriting and erecting, installing or repairing signboards and advertisements; installing seating, blinds and shutters; and installing security systems such as burglar alarms, CCTV and public address systems. Where the charge does not apply, normal VAT rules apply.
scope.from_when: Tax points on or after 1 March 2021. Transitional rules apply to authenticated tax receipts and self-billed invoices.
scope.how_to_claim: The charge applies automatically where the conditions are met — it is not claimed. To disapply it, the customer must notify the supplier in writing that it is an end user or intermediary supplier: by post, by email, or within a contract the customer agrees to. The notice should be kept with normal business records and should make clear which supplies it covers. An intermediary supplier may describe itself as an end user in that notice. If the notification is invalid, the customer must account for the VAT that should have been charged under the reverse charge.

notes: The start date and the end user / intermediary supplier exceptions are not on the main 'Check when you must use' page — that page's main text gives no effective date and has no end user section, so both are cited to the HMRC VAT domestic reverse charge technical guide. The main page's update history records only that the start was moved from 1 October 2020 to 1 March 2021. The charge is UK-wide including Northern Ireland; no NI-specific difference was found at primary source. Note the interaction with the Cash Accounting Scheme: certain goods and services subject to a domestic reverse charge are outside cash accounting (VAT Notice 731 section 2.8).

figures.what: FPS deadline for an expense or benefit that attracts National Insurance but not Income Tax, and for certain non-cash payments

scope.who: All employers operating PAYE anywhere in the UK must send an FPS on or before each payday, reporting employees' pay, payrolled benefits and deductions. Penalties are charged per PAYE scheme, so an employer running more than one scheme can be charged for each.
scope.excluded: No late filing penalty is charged where: all reported payments on the FPS are within 3 days of payday; it is the employer's first failure in the tax year to send a report on time (this exception does NOT apply to employers registered as an annual scheme); or a new employer sent its first FPS within 30 days of paying an employee. No FPS is required for a tax month in which no employees were paid — an Employer Payment Summary (EPS) is sent instead. A late FPS is permitted without penalty in the specific listed situations (non-banking payday, PAYE reference not yet received, foreign tax still being calculated — all using late reporting reason code G; pay that cannot be calculated in advance; certain non-cash payments; NIC-only benefits). A penalty already charged can be appealed on reasonable excuse grounds (for example ill health, IT difficulty, or fire, flood or natural disaster) — this is an appeal ground, not an automatic exemption.
scope.from_when: Ongoing obligation; FPS 'on or before the payday' wording confirmed on guidance last updated 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim. The employer (or its agent) must submit the FPS through payroll software on or before payday. Where a permitted exception applies and the FPS is sent after payday, the employer must enter a late reporting reason on the FPS. If an FPS is not submitted on time and no EPS is sent to confirm no employees were paid, HMRC may issue a specified charge estimating what is owed, which is replaced by the actual amount once the missing return is filed.

notes: UK-wide PAYE obligation, so it applies to employers in Birmingham and the West Midlands and to Romanian-speaking employers anywhere in the UK on the same terms. The 5% extended failure penalty is from HMRC's Compliance Handbook (internal manual, primary source) and is discretionary rather than automatic. figures.value: At least one full working day

scope.who: Employees who have an employment contract, have done some work under that contract, have been sick for at least one full working day (a 'period of incapacity for work'), and give their employer notice and proof of illness when needed. From 6 April 2026 it is available to all eligible employees regardless of earnings. Agency workers may be entitled. The employer pays it through payroll for the employee's qualifying days.
scope.excluded: Employees who: have already received the maximum 28 weeks of SSP; are getting Statutory Maternity Pay or Maternity Allowance; are off work for a pregnancy-related illness in the 4 weeks before the week (Sunday to Saturday) the baby is due; were in custody or on strike on the first day of sickness (including any linked periods); are working outside the EU where the employer is not liable for their National Insurance contributions; or received Employment and Support Allowance within 12 weeks of starting or returning to work for that employer. Also excluded are employees with a continuous series of linked periods lasting more than 3 years, and anyone who is not an employee (no employment contract). An employee who fails to tell the employer within the notification deadline may lose some SSP.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 (rate and the removal of waiting days and the earnings test)
scope.how_to_claim: The employee must tell their employer they cannot work, usually by the employer's own deadline, or within 7 days if the employer has not set one, and provide proof of illness when required. The employer then pays SSP through payroll — the employee does not claim from HMRC. If the employee does not qualify, the employer must send form SSP1 within 7 days of the first day off sick. If SSP ends unexpectedly while the employee is still sick, SSP1 must be sent within 7 days of SSP ending; if SSP is expected to end before the sickness does, SSP1 must be sent on or before the beginning of the 23rd week.

notes: The SSP reform took effect on 6 April 2026: waiting days are abolished and the earnings test removed, with the rate now the lower of £123.25 a week and 80% of average weekly earnings. HMRC's employer rates page and the transitional guidance both present this UK-wide without a nation caveat. I verified the rate and the removal of waiting days only on those UK-wide HMRC pages; I did not separately verify Northern Ireland's devolved legislative position, so NI-specific content should be checked before publication. Daily SSP amounts depend on the number of qualifying days the employee works each week. UK-wide, so valid for Birmingham/West Midlands and for Romanian-speaking audiences across the UK. Where income tax arises in related content, Scotland sets its own income tax rates and bands.

scope.who: Employees who have been continuously employed by the same employer for at least 26 weeks continuing into the qualifying week (the 15th week before the expected week of childbirth), are on the employer's payroll in that qualifying week, have average weekly earnings at or above the Lower Earnings Limit applying at the end of the qualifying week, are still pregnant at the 11th week before the due week or have had the baby by then, have stopped working, have an employer in the UK with earnings attracting Class 1 National Insurance liability, and give the correct notice and medical evidence. The employee qualifies even if they do not plan to return to the employer after the birth.
scope.excluded: Employees who fail any of those conditions are not entitled: those with less than 26 weeks' continuous employment into the qualifying week; those not on the payroll in the qualifying week; those whose average weekly earnings are below the Lower Earnings Limit at the end of the qualifying week; those who do not give the required notice; and those who do not supply evidence of the due or birth date (the employer does not have to pay SMP if proof has not been received 13 weeks after the SMP start date). Anyone who is not an employee of a UK employer — including the self-employed — is excluded; they may be able to claim Maternity Allowance instead. Employees not entitled to SMP may be able to get Maternity Allowance. Special rules apply to agency workers, directors, educational workers, and where the employee leaves, becomes sick, or the baby is born before the qualifying week.
scope.from_when: SMP rate applies from 5 April 2026 (HMRC's rates page states the SMP rate as an exception to the 6 April 2026 start)
scope.how_to_claim: The employee must give their employer the correct notice (28 days' notice of when SMP is to start) and proof of pregnancy — usually a doctor's letter or MATB1 maternity certificate, normally issued 20 weeks before the due date — within 21 days of the SMP start date. The employer pays SMP through payroll and reclaims it from HMRC. If the employer refuses SMP it must give the employee form SMP1.

notes: FIGURE CONFLICT TO RESOLVE BEFORE USE: HMRC's employer eligibility page states the earnings condition as '£125 a week (gross)', while the HMRC Statutory Payments Manual states the condition as the Lower Earnings Limit applying at the end of the qualifying week, and the 2026/27 Lower Earnings Limit on the employer rates page is £129 a week. Part of the gap is genuine — the relevant LEL is the one in force at the end of the qualifying week, which for babies due early in 2026/27 is the 2025/26 LEL — but the £125 figure on the employer page may also simply not have been uprated. Safest copy states the condition as 'average weekly earnings at or above the Lower Earnings Limit in force at the end of the qualifying week' rather than quoting a single number. Note also that HMRC's rates page says the SMP rate applies from 5 April 2026, not 6 April 2026. UK-wide, so valid for Birmingham/West Midlands and Romanian-speaking audiences across the UK. Where income tax is relevant, Scotland sets its own income tax rates and bands.

scope.who: All employers operating PAYE anywhere in the UK, and their employees. Employee Class 1 NIC is deducted at 8% on earnings between the Primary Threshold and the Upper Earnings Limit and 2% above it; employer Class 1 NIC is 15% on all earnings above the Secondary Threshold with no upper limit. Rates differ by National Insurance category letter — the figures above are category A, the standard category.
scope.excluded: Employees whose earnings fall below the relevant threshold pay no employee Class 1 NIC (below the Primary Threshold) and attract no employer Class 1 NIC (below the Secondary Threshold). Employees who do not have to pay National Insurance at all — for example because they are under 16 — are reported under category letter X. Employees over State Pension age are category C, for which HMRC's rate table shows the employee rate as not applicable, so no employee contributions are due, while employer Class 1 NIC still applies. The employee rate is also shown as not applicable for categories K and S. Earnings below the Lower Earnings Limit do not count towards the employee's qualifying year for contributory benefits.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim. Employee and employer Class 1 NIC are calculated and deducted automatically through payroll each pay period on the correct category letter, and reported to HMRC on the Full Payment Submission on or before payday.

notes: UK-wide — National Insurance is not devolved, so these thresholds and rates are identical in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, which is why this is valid for Birmingham/West Midlands and for Romanian-speaking audiences across the UK. Income tax is different: Scotland sets its own income tax rates and bands, so any content pairing NIC with income tax must state the Scottish position separately. Note the Secondary Threshold (£5,000 a year) is far below the Primary Threshold (£12,570 a year), so employers pay NIC on earnings their employees pay nothing on. Employer Class 1 NIC has no upper limit. Category letters other than A carry different rates and should be checked on the same page. Rates page last updated 1 September 2026.

scope.who: All UK employers that provided taxable expenses or benefits to directors or employees in the tax year. A P11D is filed for each director or relevant employee with taxable benefits not taxed through payroll, and a P11D(b) is filed to declare the Class 1A National Insurance due for the year. Employers that voluntarily payroll benefits must still work out the Class 1A National Insurance and file a P11D(b) by 6 July after the end of the tax year.
scope.excluded: No P11D is required for an employee whose benefits are all being taxed through payroll — HMRC states 'You do not need to submit P11D for an employee if you're paying tax on all their benefits through your payroll.' A P11D should also not be completed where there are no taxable items for that person, or where all items were taxed through payroll. However, payrolling does NOT remove the P11D(b): a P11D(b) is still needed to pay any Class 1A National Insurance owed. A P11D is still required after the end of the tax year for any employee removed from payrolling part-way through. Employers that provided no taxable expenses or benefits in the year and owe no Class 1A National Insurance have nothing to file.
scope.from_when: 6 July after the end of each tax year (6 July 2027 for the 2026/27 tax year); Class 1A payment by 22 July, or 19 July by cheque
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim. The employer must submit P11D and P11D(b) to HMRC by 6 July, give each director and relevant employee their P11D information by 6 July, and pay the Class 1A National Insurance by 22 July (19 July if paying by cheque). To payroll benefits instead, the employer must register with HMRC before the start of the tax year concerned — until mandatory payrolling begins on 6 April 2027.
