scope.who: Employers must deduct student loan and postgraduate loan repayments through payroll from employees who are repaying, on earnings above the relevant plan threshold, at 9% (Plans 1, 2, 4 and 5) or 6% (Postgraduate Loan). Which plan applies depends on the funding body the borrower applied to and when their course started: Plan 1 — Student Finance England or Wales, course started before 1 September 2012, and Student Finance Northern Ireland (undergraduate or postgraduate); Plan 2 — Student Finance England for courses started 1 September 2012 to 31 July 2023 (undergraduate, PGCE, Advanced Learner Loans, short course loans), England for Higher Education Short Course Loans started on or after 1 August 2023, and Student Finance Wales for courses started on or after 1 September 2012 (undergraduate and PGCE); Plan 4 — Student Awards Agency Scotland (undergraduate or postgraduate); Plan 5 — Student Finance England for courses started on or after 1 August 2023 (undergraduate, PGCE, Advanced Learner Loans, Lifelong Learning Entitlement finance); Postgraduate Loan — master's or doctoral courses funded by England or Wales.
scope.excluded: No deduction is due on earnings at or below the relevant plan threshold. Employers are not responsible for deducting student or postgraduate loan repayments for off-payroll workers engaged through their own companies. Recipients of occupational pensions are not liable for student loan or postgraduate loan deductions. No deductions are made from payments made after an employee's date of death. Employers must stop deducting on receipt of an SL2 or PGL2 stop notice from HMRC, or when HMRC tells them to stop in writing. An employee cannot ask the employer to stop deductions — HMRC is explicit that 'You cannot stop making deductions because your employee asks you to'; an employee who thinks they have overpaid must request a refund instead.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim. Deductions are made automatically through payroll from the next available payday once the employer receives an SL1 or PGL1 start notice from HMRC, or where a new employee's P45 shows deductions should continue, or where a new employee tells the employer they are repaying a student loan. If the employee does not know which plan they are on, HMRC says to use Plan 5 until an SL1 notice is received. On an employee leaving, enter 'Y' in P45 box 5 even if the employee had not earned enough to make repayments.

notes: Plan 4 is the Scottish student loan plan — borrowers who applied through the Student Awards Agency Scotland. Plan 5 is the England-only plan for courses starting on or after 1 August 2023. Plan 1 is where Northern Ireland borrowers sit. Plan 2 covers Wales (from 1 September 2012) and the England 2012–2023 cohort. The thresholds and rates themselves are UK-wide payroll figures and apply identically to employers in Birmingham and the West Midlands and to Romanian-speaking employees anywhere in the UK, so the brand tags are correct even though the plan a borrower sits on depends on their funding nation. HMRC's rates page gives a single 9% rate for Plans 1, 2, 4 and 5 rather than a separate rate per plan, and 6% for the Postgraduate Loan. An employee can be repaying a student loan and a postgraduate loan at the same time, in which case both deductions run. Where income tax is relevant, Scotland sets its own income tax rates and bands. The 'which repayment plan you're on' page shows a visible last-updated of 18 October 2024 with page metadata of 10 November 2026; it loads and is live.

scope.who: Individuals who are taxpayers in England, Wales or Northern Ireland for the tax year 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027. The Personal Allowance of £12,570 itself is UK-wide and applies to Scottish taxpayers too; the 20%/40%/45% rates and the £37,700 basic rate limit shown here apply to non-savings, non-dividend income of taxpayers in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Savings and dividend income is taxed at UK-wide rates for taxpayers in all four nations.
scope.excluded: Scottish taxpayers do not get these bands and rates on their non-savings, non-dividend income — Scotland has its own starter (19%), basic (20%), intermediate (21%), higher (42%), advanced (45%) and top (48%) rates and its own thresholds. Anyone with adjusted net income of £125,140 or more gets no Personal Allowance at all, because of the taper. Dividend income is taxed at the separate dividend rates, not at 20/40/45%. Companies are outside income tax entirely (they pay Corporation Tax).
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: No claim needed. The Personal Allowance is given automatically through your PAYE tax code or in your Self Assessment calculation. The £100,000 taper is applied automatically by HMRC, but if your income is near or above £100,000 you may need to file a Self Assessment return or tell HMRC about changes in income so your code is right; a wrong code means an under- or overpayment to settle later.

notes: Income tax rates and bands on non-savings, non-dividend income are DEVOLVED to Scotland: the Scottish Parliament sets its own rates and thresholds, so this is not a UK-wide band structure and must not be presented as one. Wales has Welsh rates of income tax, but HMRC publishes Welsh rates together with England and Northern Ireland for 2026/27 at the same 20/40/45%. The Personal Allowance (£12,570), the £100,000 income limit, and the savings and dividend rates are reserved and UK-wide. Budget 2026 confirms the Personal Allowance, basic rate limit and £100,000 income limit are unchanged for 2027-28 as well; the maintained-thresholds policy runs to 5 April 2031.

scope.who: Any UK individual receiving dividend income from shares — including company directors and shareholders of their own limited company — in the tax year 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027. Dividend rates are reserved, so the same allowance and rates apply in England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland. The rate you pay depends on which income tax band the dividend falls into once dividends are added on top of your other income.
scope.excluded: Dividends from shares held in an ISA are not taxed and do not use up the dividend allowance. Dividends covered by your unused Personal Allowance are not taxed. Companies receiving dividends are outside this — they are within the Corporation Tax rules, not dividend income tax. The allowance is per person and is not transferable between spouses or civil partners, and it cannot be carried forward if unused.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: No claim needed — the £500 allowance is applied automatically in your tax calculation. You must, however, report dividends above your unused Personal Allowance plus the £500 allowance to HMRC. If you already file Self Assessment you include them on your return; otherwise you need to tell HMRC so they can collect the tax, which for smaller amounts can be done through your PAYE tax code.

notes: The dividend ordinary and upper rates rose by 2 percentage points from 6 April 2026 (from 8.75% to 10.75% and from 33.75% to 35.75%); the additional rate stayed at 39.35%. Do not quote the 2025/26 figures of 8.75%/33.75%. The allowance itself is unchanged at £500 and is confirmed at £500 for 2027-28. Dividend taxation is UK-wide and is not affected by the Scottish income tax bands.

scope.who: UK-resident individuals disposing of chargeable assets in the tax year 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027 — shares outside an ISA, second homes and buy-to-lets, business assets, crypto, valuables and so on. Also personal representatives of a deceased person and trustees, at their own exempt amounts and rates. CGT is reserved, so the same exempt amount and rates apply across England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland (including for Scottish taxpayers, whose Scottish bands do not change the CGT rate bands).
scope.excluded: Companies do not pay CGT — they pay Corporation Tax on chargeable gains and get no annual exempt amount. Trustees other than trustees for disabled people get £1,500, not £3,000. Gains on your own home are normally not chargeable at all because of Private Residence Relief, and gains on assets inside an ISA or a pension are exempt, so no exempt amount is used. The £3,000 is per person per tax year, is not transferable between spouses or civil partners, and cannot be carried forward if unused. Non-UK residents are generally outside the charge except on disposals of UK land and property and certain UK-property-rich company interests. Gifts and transfers between spouses or civil partners living together are on a no-gain-no-loss basis, so no exempt amount is used.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: The £3,000 annual exempt amount is applied automatically in the tax calculation — there is nothing to claim. You do have to report and pay: residential property disposals must be reported and the tax paid within 60 days of completion using HMRC's UK Property Account service, and other chargeable gains are reported either on a Self Assessment return or through HMRC's real-time Capital Gains Tax service. Reliefs such as Business Asset Disposal Relief must be claimed separately.

notes: Since 30 October 2024 the main CGT rates have been aligned with the residential property rates, so for 2026/27 residential property and other chargeable assets are both taxed at 18% within the basic rate band and 24% above it — there is no longer a higher separate residential rate. The 18%/24% split depends on your total taxable income: gains are stacked on top of income, and the part of the gain falling above the basic rate limit is taxed at 24%. Business Asset Disposal Relief rose to 18% for disposals on or after 6 April 2026 (it was 14% in 2025/26 and 10% before that), and Budget 2026 announced the BADR lifetime limit falls from £1 million to £500,000 from 2027-28 — that is a future change, not a 2026/27 one.

title: Rent a Room Relief

figures.what: Rent a Room Scheme tax-free threshold per year, per person
reduced Rent a Room threshold where the letting income is shared with someone else, for example a joint owner
Rent a Room limit and shared limit as set out in HMRC helpsheet HS223 (helpsheet text covers 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026; limit unchanged on the live guidance read in 2026/27)

scope.who: Resident landlords letting furnished accommodation in their only or main home — owner-occupiers and tenants alike, so you can use it whether or not you own the property. It also covers taking in a lodger, and lettings that amount to a trade such as running a bed and breakfast or guest house or providing meals and cleaning. The threshold is per person, so two people each letting rooms in the same shared home have £3,750 each.
scope.excluded: You cannot use the scheme where the accommodation is not part of your main home at the time you let it; where the accommodation is not furnished; where a home has been converted into separate flats that are let; where the accommodation is let as an office or for any business (HMRC allows two exceptions — a lodger who works at home in the evenings or at weekends, and a student given study facilities); or on a UK home let out while you live abroad. You also cannot use the exemption or Method B to create a loss, and if you use Method B you cannot deduct expenses or capital allowances. You cannot claim the £1,000 property allowance on the same Rent a Room income.
scope.from_when: Scheme in force and applies for the 2026/27 tax year (6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027); the £7,500 limit has applied since 6 April 2016
scope.how_to_claim: If your gross receipts from the letting are £7,500 or less (£3,750 if shared) the exemption is automatic — you are exempt from tax on that income and need do nothing. If your receipts exceed the threshold you must complete a Self Assessment tax return and choose between Method A (tax on your actual profit, which HMRC applies by default) and Method B (tax on gross receipts above the threshold, with no deduction for expenses). To use Method B, or to opt out of the exemption so you can claim a loss, you must notify HMRC within one year of the 31 January following the end of the tax year. Method B stops automatically if your rental income falls back below the threshold.

notes: This is a UK-wide income tax relief, reserved to Westminster, so it applies in England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland on the same terms. The £7,500 limit is a fixed statutory figure, not an annually indexed one, and has been unchanged since April 2016 — it is not restated in Budget rates tables, so verify it on the live guidance page each year. The threshold is on GROSS receipts, including any amounts your lodger pays for meals, cleaning or laundry, not on profit. The HS223 helpsheet carrying the fullest list of exclusions is the 2026-published version covering the 2025 to 2026 tax year; the £7,500 figure for the current year is taken from the live GOV.UK guidance page read on 14 November 2026.

title: Property Income Allowance

figures.what: property allowance — tax-free allowance per year for individuals with income from land or property
where you have both property income and trading income, a separate £1,000 allowance applies to each

scope.who: Individuals with gross income from UK or overseas land or property — a let room, a parking space, a holiday let, land. It is a per-person allowance, so where a property is jointly owned each owner can set their own £1,000 against their share of the gross rental income. It is separate from, and additional to, the £1,000 trading allowance: someone with both kinds of income gets £1,000 against each.
scope.excluded: You cannot use the property allowance against property income from a partnership in which you or a connected person are partners; against income from a company that you or a connected person owns or controls; or against income from your employer or from your spouse's or civil partner's employer. You cannot use it if you claim the tax reducer for residential finance costs such as mortgage interest. You cannot use it on income from letting a room in your own home under the Rent a Room Scheme, nor where you deduct expenses from that income instead of using the Rent a Room scheme. If you claim the allowance you cannot also deduct any other expenses or allowances against that income, and the allowance cannot create or increase a loss — so it is the wrong choice for a loss-making let. Companies cannot use it; it is an income tax allowance for individuals.
scope.from_when: Applies for the 2026/27 tax year (6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027); the allowance has applied since 6 April 2017
scope.how_to_claim: If your gross property income for the year is £1,000 or less the income is automatically exempt — you do not need to tell HMRC or declare it on a tax return, though you must keep records, and you can ask HMRC to stop issuing a return if you no longer need one. If your gross property income is more than £1,000 you must declare it, and you then choose on your Self Assessment return either to deduct the £1,000 allowance from your gross income instead of your actual expenses, or to work out your profit in the normal way by deducting actual expenses. It is a choice, so it is a claim rather than an automatic relief once you are above £1,000, and you should compare the two: the allowance only helps if your real expenses are less than £1,000.

notes: Distinct from the trading allowance, which is the same £1,000 amount but applies to casual self-employment and miscellaneous trading income; the two are separate allowances and a person with both types of income gets both. Also distinct from Rent a Room relief (£7,500) — you cannot use the property allowance on Rent a Room income, and for letting a furnished room in your own home Rent a Room relief is normally far more generous. The £1,000 is a fixed statutory figure, not indexed annually, and is not restated in Budget rates tables, so verify it on the live guidance page each year. The allowance applies to GROSS income before expenses. This is a reserved UK-wide income tax allowance.

title: Pension Annual Allowance 2026/27

figures.what: standard pension annual allowance 2026/27
standard annual allowance stated on the main GOV.UK guidance for the current tax year
Money Purchase Annual Allowance (MPAA) 2026/27, applying to members who have flexibly accessed their pension benefits
threshold income limit for the tapered annual allowance 2026/27
adjusted income limit for the tapered annual allowance 2026/27
minimum (floor) tapered annual allowance 2026/27
annual allowance, MPAA and tapered allowance adjusted income threshold confirmed for 2026-27 (and unchanged for 2027-28) at Budget 2026

scope.who: Members of UK registered pension schemes building up pension savings in the tax year 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027. The allowance is the total that can be paid in across all your schemes in the year — your own contributions, employer contributions and tax relief, plus the deemed value of defined benefit build-up — before an annual allowance charge arises. Pension tax relief is reserved, so the £60,000 and the taper apply across England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland.
scope.excluded: You do not get the full £60,000 if the taper applies: where BOTH threshold income exceeds £200,000 and adjusted income exceeds £260,000, the allowance is reduced, down to a floor of £10,000 for the highest earners. You do not get the full allowance for money purchase savings if you have flexibly accessed a defined contribution pension — for example taking cash or a short-term annuity from a flexi-access drawdown fund, or taking cash from an uncrystallised pot — because the Money Purchase Annual Allowance of £10,000 then caps money purchase contributions and no carry forward is available against it. Separately, tax relief on your own personal contributions is capped at 100% of your relevant UK earnings (or £3,600 gross if you have little or no earnings), so a high annual allowance does not by itself permit a large relieved personal contribution. Companies are outside this: the annual allowance is a member-level limit, not an employer one.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: There is nothing to claim for the allowance itself — it is a cap, applied automatically. You do have responsibilities if you exceed it: your scheme must send you a pension savings statement if your savings in that scheme exceed the standard allowance, you can carry forward unused annual allowance from the previous three tax years (not against the MPAA), and if a charge is still due you must report the excess on a Self Assessment tax return and pay the annual allowance charge, or in some cases ask the scheme to pay it under 'scheme pays'. If you are a high earner you need to work out your own threshold and adjusted income to find your tapered allowance — HMRC provides a calculator and scheme administrators can check a member's allowance.

notes: UK-wide and reserved. The £60,000 standard allowance, the £10,000 MPAA, the £200,000/£260,000 taper thresholds and the £10,000 taper floor are all unchanged for 2026/27 and are confirmed unchanged for 2027-28 at Budget 2026. The main GOV.UK guidance page states the £60,000 and the two taper thresholds but gives no figure for the MPAA or the taper floor, so those two come from HMRC's pension schemes rates publication, which tabulates them by tax year. Note the taper requires BOTH income tests to be met, not either. The lifetime allowance was abolished from 6 April 2024 and is replaced by lump sum allowances — a separate subject, not verified here.

title: Child Benefit rates 2026/27

figures.what: eldest or only child, 2026 to 2027 tax year
each additional child, 2026 to 2027 tax year

figures.value: £27.05 a week eldest or only child; £17.90 per child for each additional child
figures.what: same two rates as shown on the public Child Benefit guide

scope.nation: United Kingdom. GOV.UK sets the residence condition simply as living in the UK, and Child Benefit is administered by HMRC across the UK; there is no devolved replacement in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.
scope.who: Anyone responsible for a child under 16, or under 20 if the child stays in approved education or training, who lives in the UK. You are usually treated as responsible if the child lives with you or you pay at least the equivalent of Child Benefit towards their upkeep. Foster carers can claim provided the local council is not paying anything towards the child's accommodation or maintenance. Only one person can get Child Benefit for a child.
scope.excluded: Two people cannot get Child Benefit for the same child - if claimants cannot agree, HMRC decides. Foster carers cannot claim where the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance. Entitlement ends if the child starts paid work of 24 hours or more a week while not in approved education or training, starts an apprenticeship in England, or starts getting certain benefits in their own right. People with pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme qualify only in limited circumstances (for example working or earning above the National Insurance primary threshold for 3 continuous months, looking for work for up to 91 days, or having sufficient resources), and pre-settled status holders claiming Income Support, income-based Jobseeker's Allowance, Pension Credit or Universal Credit may not be eligible.
scope.from_when: Rates apply for the 2026 to 2027 tax year (from 6 April 2026).
scope.how_to_claim: Must be claimed from HMRC - it is never paid automatically. Claiming also gets the child a National Insurance number, and GOV.UK states you get National Insurance credits automatically if you claim Child Benefit and your child is under 12. Payment is usually every 4 weeks, and a claimant can claim but decline the payments to keep the other advantages.

notes: Northern Ireland: no separate scheme - HMRC pays Child Benefit at these rates across the UK. Scotland: no devolved replacement for Child Benefit itself. The same HMRC rates table also shows provisional 2027 to 2028 rates of £28.00 (eldest or only child) and £18.55 (other children), read 2026-11-14 at https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/rates-and-allowances-tax-credits-child-benefit-and-guardians-allowance/tax-credits-child-benefit-and-guardians-allowance - provisional, not yet in force. The High Income Child Benefit Charge threshold was NOT stated on any page read, so no figure for it is reported here.

scope.nation: Great Britain. The GOV.UK Universal Credit guide directs Northern Ireland residents to Universal Credit in Northern Ireland, which is run separately.
scope.who: People on a low income, out of work or who cannot work, who live in the UK, are aged 18 or over (with some exceptions for 16 to 17 year olds), are under State Pension age, and have £16,000 or less in money, savings and investments. Armed forces personnel stationed abroad can also apply. Couples claim jointly.
scope.excluded: People with more than £16,000 in money, savings and investments. Couples where both partners have reached State Pension age - the claim stops at that point (GOV.UK notes people on Pension Credit are usually better off staying on it). Most people in full-time education, unless they meet one of the listed exceptions (living with an eligible partner, responsible for a child, having reached State Pension age while living with a partner below it, having had a Migration Notice letter, or being 21 or under studying up to A level equivalent without parental support); students with a health condition must have been assessed as having limited capability for work before the course started and be entitled to a listed disability benefit. People who do not live in the UK. EU, EEA and Swiss citizens usually need settled or pre-settled status. Northern Ireland residents must use the separate Northern Ireland service.
scope.from_when: 2026 to 2027 rates, in force from April 2026 (DWP benefit and pension rates 2026 to 2027).
scope.how_to_claim: Must be claimed - the main route is an online Universal Credit account on GOV.UK, and existing claimants sign in to the same account.

notes: Northern Ireland: Universal Credit is a separate Northern Ireland scheme - the GOV.UK guide explicitly sends NI residents to 'Universal Credit in Northern Ireland', so the figures above should not be presented as NI figures. Scotland: covered by the GOV.UK scheme (Scotland has its own disability benefits, which feed into UC elements, but the standard allowance is the same).

figures.what: standard minimum guarantee, single person, 2026/27 - the level Pension Credit tops weekly income up to
standard minimum guarantee, couple, 2026/27 - the level Pension Credit tops joint weekly income up to
same standard minimum guarantee figures in the DWP benefit and pension rates 2026 to 2027 table
Pension Credit caseload take-up: 62% of pensioner families entitled to Pension Credit claimed it in the financial year ending 2025

available Pension Credit that went unclaimed in the financial year ending 2025
expenditure take-up: 74% of the total amount of Pension Credit that could have been claimed was claimed, financial year ending 2025

scope.nation: Great Britain. GOV.UK states plainly: 'This guide covers Pension Credit in England, Scotland and Wales' and links to nidirect.gov.uk for Northern Ireland.
scope.who: People who live in England, Scotland or Wales, have reached State Pension age and are on a low income. It can be claimed even if you have other income, savings or own your own home, and can help with housing costs such as ground rent or service charges. A couple qualifies if both partners have reached State Pension age, or if one partner gets Housing Benefit for people over State Pension age.
scope.excluded: Mixed-age couples where only one partner has reached State Pension age, unless one partner gets Housing Benefit for people over State Pension age. People moving permanently away from Great Britain, and people already outside Great Britain, cannot get or apply for it. EU, Swiss, Norwegian, Icelandic and Liechtenstein nationals usually also need settled or pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme. Northern Ireland residents are not covered by this guide. Savings and investments above £10,000 reduce entitlement - every £500 above £10,000 counts as £1 a week of income - so larger savings can remove entitlement altogether.
scope.from_when: 2026/27 standard minimum guarantee, in force from April 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Must be claimed - it is not awarded automatically, which is why take-up is only 62%. Routes are: online on GOV.UK if you have already applied for your State Pension, by phone on the DWP Pension Credit claim line, or by post on the claim form. You can start an application up to 4 months before reaching State Pension age, and a claim can be backdated by up to 3 months.

notes: Northern Ireland: Pension Credit exists but is run separately and the GOV.UK guide does not cover it - NI readers must be sent to nidirect.gov.uk. Scotland: Pension Credit has NOT been devolved, so Scottish pensioners claim the same DWP Pension Credit (unlike Carer's Allowance or Winter Fuel Payment). Take-up figures are DWP official statistics for the financial year ending 2025, first published 22 October 2026 and updated 28 October 2026.

scope.nation: England and Wales. The GOV.UK guide is written for England and Wales: it requires you to normally live in England or Wales, and tells Scottish residents to apply for Carer Support Payment instead. Northern Ireland is not covered by this guide.
scope.who: People aged 16 or over who spend at least 35 hours a week caring for someone who gets a qualifying disability benefit, who normally live in England or Wales (or live abroad as a member of the armed forces), have lived in England, Scotland or Wales for at least 2 of the last 3 years (not required for refugees or people with humanitarian protection), and whose earnings are £204 a week or less after tax, National Insurance and allowable expenses. Qualifying care includes help with washing and cooking, taking the person to medical appointments and household tasks such as managing bills and shopping. Some people moving to or living in an EEA country or Switzerland may still be eligible.
scope.excluded: Anyone under 16. Anyone in full-time education or studying 21 hours a week or more. Anyone subject to immigration control. Anyone earning more than £204 a week. Where care is shared, a second carer cannot also be paid for the same person if another carer already gets Carer's Allowance, Carer Support Payment or the Universal Credit carer extra amount for them - DWP decides if the carers cannot agree. Anyone whose State Pension is £86.45 a week or more (a top-up may be payable if the State Pension is lower). Scottish residents, who must claim Carer Support Payment instead. EU, Swiss, Norwegian, Icelandic and Liechtenstein nationals usually need settled or pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme.
scope.from_when: 2026/27 rate and earnings limit, in force from April 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Must be claimed - apply online on GOV.UK or by post using form DS700. GOV.UK warns that Carer's Allowance can affect the other benefits both the carer and the person being cared for receive.

notes: Scotland: Carer's Allowance has been replaced for Scottish residents by Carer Support Payment, delivered by Social Security Scotland - GOV.UK states directly that if you live in Scotland you need to apply for Carer Support Payment instead, so the £86.45 figure must not be presented to a Scottish audience as Carer's Allowance. Northern Ireland: runs its own social security system and its own Carer's Allowance via nidirect.gov.uk; the GOV.UK guide does not mention Northern Ireland at all, so NI rates were not verified here and must not be assumed to match. The earnings limit applies after tax, National Insurance and allowable expenses (which include 50% of pension contributions), not gross pay.

scope.nation: England, Wales and Northern Ireland. GOV.UK requires you to usually live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, and states that if you live in Scotland you cannot get the Winter Fuel Payment and may instead be eligible for Pension Age Winter Heating Payment.
scope.who: People born on or before 27 June 1960 who usually live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland during the qualifying week of 21 to 27 September 2026. Care home residents can get it, subject to the care home exclusion below. The amount depends on date of birth, who else eligible you live with, and whether you get Pension Credit, Universal Credit or income-related ESA.
scope.excluded: People who usually live in Scotland (Pension Age Winter Heating Payment instead) or outside England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Visitors who were in England, Wales or Northern Ireland during the qualifying week but usually live elsewhere. People in hospital getting free treatment for the whole qualifying week and the year before it. People who need permission to enter the UK and whose leave states they cannot claim public funds. People in prison for the whole qualifying week. Care home residents who both get Universal Credit, Pension Credit or income-related ESA and lived in a care home for the whole time from 29 June 2026 or earlier. And anyone whose total income is over £35,000 keeps nothing in the end: HMRC takes the payment back through the tax code or Self Assessment, so they can opt out instead.
scope.from_when: Qualifying week 21 to 27 September 2026; paid for winter 2026 to 2027, with most payments made and letters issued in October or November 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Most eligible people get it automatically and receive a letter in October or November showing the amount. A claim is needed only if you do not get State Pension or one of the other listed benefits and either you have never had a Winter Fuel Payment before, or you have deferred your State Pension since your last one. Claims can be made by post from 21 September 2026 or by phone to the Winter Fuel Payment Centre from 19 October 2026, with a deadline of 31 March 2027. People with income over £35,000 can opt out instead of having it recovered.

notes: This is the area to be most careful with. Scotland: Winter Fuel Payment does not apply - GOV.UK states you cannot get it if you live in Scotland, where the devolved Pension Age Winter Heating Payment applies instead, so never present these amounts to a Scottish audience. Northern Ireland: unusually for a DWP benefit, Northern Ireland IS inside this scheme - the GOV.UK eligibility page lists England, Wales and Northern Ireland together. The £35,000 recovery rule is individual: GOV.UK says a partner's income does not count towards your total income, and recovery is usually through the PAYE tax code, or through Self Assessment where that applies; it cannot be repaid through Making Tax Digital software, so HMRC writes with the amount instead. Recheck set to 2027-01-15 because these rules and amounts have changed repeatedly in recent years and are winter-specific.

scope.nation: United Kingdom. Tax-Free Childcare is an HMRC scheme applied for on GOV.UK; nidirect.gov.uk confirms Northern Ireland parents use it and apply through GOV.UK (Northern Ireland's own Childcare Subsidy Scheme requires parents to be claiming Tax-Free Childcare), and the GOV.UK eligibility page recognises Scottish disability benefits for the disabled-child route.
scope.who: Working parents - employed or self-employed, including those on parental, sick or annual leave - with a child aged 11 or younger (until the September after the 11th birthday), or 16 or younger if the child is disabled (until the September after the 16th birthday, where the child is certified blind or severely sight-impaired or gets DLA, PIP, Armed Forces Independence Payment, or in Scotland Child Disability Payment or Adult Disability Payment). You and your partner must each expect to earn at least the minimum amount above over the next 3 months, and each have expected adjusted net income of £100,000 or less. Self-employed people paid irregularly can use an average over the tax year, and there is no minimum if the business started less than 12 months ago. You need a National Insurance number (your partner too) and British or Irish citizenship, settled or pre-settled status (or a pending application), or permission to access public funds shown on an eVisa or UK residence card.
scope.excluded: You cannot claim if the child does not usually live with you; if you foster the child you are applying for; if you or your partner expect adjusted net income over £100,000; if you or your partner get a childcare bursary or grant; or if you claim Universal Credit or childcare vouchers at the same time (childcare vouchers are only available at all to people who had already joined a scheme). People below the minimum earnings threshold are excluded, and dividends, interest, property income and pension income do not count towards it. People without a National Insurance number or the required immigration permission are excluded. Payments can only be made to a childcare provider signed up to the scheme.
scope.from_when: Ongoing scheme; figures confirmed as at 14 November 2026 (GOV.UK pages last updated 9 November 2026).
scope.how_to_claim: Must be applied for - open a childcare account through the Tax-Free Childcare application on GOV.UK, then pay money in and the top-up is added. Check first that the childcare provider is signed up to the scheme.

notes: Northern Ireland: Tax-Free Childcare is available - nidirect.gov.uk describes it for NI parents and directs them to apply on GOV.UK, and NI's separate Childcare Subsidy Scheme requires a Tax-Free Childcare claim. Scotland: available, and the GOV.UK eligibility page lists Scottish Child Disability Payment and Adult Disability Payment as qualifying for the disabled-child route. Important interaction for client-facing copy: Tax-Free Childcare cannot be held at the same time as Universal Credit or childcare vouchers, and the £100,000 adjusted net income test applies to each partner individually. The funded childcare hours schemes referred to alongside it are England-only and were not verified here.

title: Corporation Tax Rates and Marginal Relief

figures.what: small profits rate — "you'll pay the 'small profits rate', which is 19%", on profits of £50,000 or less
main rate — "If your company made more than £250,000 profit, you'll pay the main rate of Corporation Tax"
Marginal Relief lower limit ("£50,000 (the lower limit)")
Marginal Relief upper limit ("£250,000 (the upper limit)")

HMRC rates-and-allowances table confirms small profits rate 19%, main rate 25%, Marginal Relief lower limit £50,000 and upper limit £250,000 are unchanged for the financial year beginning 1 April 2026 (table updated 1 April 2026)
standard marginal relief fraction
date the 19%/25% two-rate structure and Marginal Relief took effect — "From 1 April 2023"

figures.value: divided by the number of associated companies plus one
figures.what: both limits are reduced in proportion for accounting periods shorter than 12 months and divided by the number of associated companies plus one (with 3 associated companies the limits become £12,500 and £62,500)

scope.who: UK-resident companies and organisations chargeable to Corporation Tax. Profits of £50,000 or less are charged at the small profits rate of 19%; profits over £250,000 at the main rate of 25%; profits between £50,000 and £250,000 are charged at the main rate with Marginal Relief, which tapers the effective rate between 19% and 25%. Both limits are proportionately reduced for accounting periods of less than 12 months and divided by the number of associated companies plus one.
scope.excluded: Non-UK resident companies cannot claim Marginal Relief (gov.uk/guidance/corporation-tax-marginal-relief). Close investment-holding companies are excluded from both the small profits rate and Marginal Relief — CTA 2010 s.18N: close investment-holding companies "are chargeable at the CT main rate" and "are not eligible for the standard small profits rate or marginal relief" (HMRC CTM03951). Companies whose augmented profits, including certain distributions from unrelated, unassociated companies, exceed £250,000 get no Marginal Relief. Ring fence profits (UK/UK continental shelf oil rights or extraction) are outside the standard rates and have their own small ring fence profits rate of 19% with a ring fence fraction of 11/400 (CTM03910); CTA 2010 s.18A(1) applies the standard small profits rate only to profits "which are not ring fence profits". A company in liquidation is not treated as a close investment-holding company for the accounting period beginning when winding up commences, if it was not one in the prior period (CTA 2010 s.18N(5)).
scope.from_when: The two-rate structure with Marginal Relief applies from 1 April 2023. The rates and limits above are confirmed unchanged for the financial year beginning 1 April 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: No separate application. CTA 2010 s.18A(1) charges Corporation Tax at the standard small profits rate where the company is UK resident, is not a close investment-holding company, and its augmented profits do not exceed the lower limit. CTA 2010 s.18B(1) states "This section applies if—" the company is UK resident, is not a close investment-holding company, and its augmented profits exceed the lower limit but not the upper limit — so the relief operates as a statutory reduction rather than on application. The figures are self-assessed in the Company Tax Return; HMRC publishes a Marginal Relief calculator at gov.uk/guidance/corporation-tax-marginal-relief, which describes it as checking "how much Marginal Relief you may be able to claim".

notes: The GOV.UK guidance uses the language of claiming Marginal Relief, while the legislation (CTA 2010 ss.18A, 18B) frames both the small profits rate and the relief as applying automatically where the conditions are met — worth wording carefully in client copy. The associated-companies divisor is the commonest trap: a director with several companies loses the £50,000 band quickly. The gov.uk/corporation-tax-rates page itself does not mention the close investment-holding company exclusion; that comes from HMRC's Company Taxation Manual CTM03951 and CTA 2010 s.18N. CTM03910's published table runs to financial year 2025; FY2026 confirmation comes from the rates-and-allowances publication updated 1 April 2026.

scope.who: Every company registered at Companies House must deliver annual accounts for each financial year. A private company has 9 months from its accounting reference date. Where a company's first accounts cover a period of more than 12 months, the first accounts are due within 21 months of incorporation (private) or 3 months from the accounting reference date, whichever is longer. Dormant companies have the same deadlines as other companies.
scope.excluded: The 9-month deadline does not apply to public companies, which have 6 months from the accounting reference date and 18 months from incorporation for a first set of accounts covering more than 12 months. The 21-month first-accounts rule does not apply where the first accounts cover 12 months or less — the normal deadlines then apply instead. Dormant companies are NOT excluded: they have the same filing deadlines as other companies and face the same late filing penalties. The Companies House accounts deadline is separate from, and does not replace, the 12-month Company Tax Return deadline or the 9-months-and-1-day Corporation Tax payment deadline.
scope.from_when: Current Companies House guidance as at 14 November 2026 (guidance page updated 23 October 2026). The deadlines themselves are long-standing and were not changed by the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act.
scope.how_to_claim: No claim or application. The deadline runs automatically from the accounting reference date, and the directors are personally responsible for delivering the accounts on time. Small companies and micro-entities can file online using Companies House online services.

notes: ECCTA POSITION AS AT NOVEMBER 2026 — this is the material change worth banking. (1) The requirement for small companies and micro-entities to file a profit and loss account has been PAUSED. GOV.UK, 23 October 2026: "the government has decided to pause implementing the requirement for small and micro entities" — so as at November 2026 small companies "do not have to deliver a copy of the directors' report or the profit and loss account" and micro-entities are likewise not required to file "a directors' report or profit and loss account at Companies House" (life-of-a-company part 1, updated 23 October 2026). (2) ABRIDGED ACCOUNTS HAVE NOT BEEN ABOLISHED — the earlier plan to remove them has been reversed: the government will "continue to allow companies to file abridged accounts" (gov.uk/government/news/companies-house-update-to-accounts-filing-from-april-2028, published 23 October 2026). Where abridged accounts are filed, the balance sheet must state that the members have agreed to them. (3) What IS still coming from April 2028: all UK registered companies must "file their accounts in Inline eXtensible Business Reporting Language (iXBRL) format" using commercial software, and web and paper accounts filing closes on that date. Smaller companies keep the option to remove, or 'fillet', their profit and loss information from accounts filed after 1 April 2028. (4) The earlier 9 June 2026 notice announcing the P&L requirement and the removal of abridged accounts was WITHDRAWN on 23 October 2026 — do not cite it. (5) The ECCTA company accounts factsheet at gov.uk/government/publications/economic-crime-and-corporate-transparency-act-2023-factsheets/economic-crime-and-corporate-transparency-act-company-accounts still displays the old position (small and micro-entities must file a P&L, abridged accounts removed) and shows a visible date of 1 March 2024 with no commencement dates — it is out of date on these points and must not be used as the current position.

title: Corporation Tax Payment and Company Tax Return Deadlines

figures.what: Corporation Tax payment deadline — "You must pay your Corporation Tax 9 months and 1 day after the end of your accounting period"
Company Tax Return (CT600) filing deadline — "The deadline for your tax return is 12 months after the end of the accounting period it covers"
the separate payment deadline, as stated on the Company Tax Returns page — "It's usually 9 months and one day after the end of the accounting period"

figures.value: 9 months and 1 day after your 'accounting period' for Corporation Tax ends
figures.what: deadline to pay Corporation Tax or tell HMRC the company does not owe any, as stated in the GOV.UK deadlines table

figures.value: 12 months after your accounting period for Corporation Tax ends
figures.what: deadline to file a Company Tax Return, as stated in the GOV.UK deadlines table
taxable profits above which Corporation Tax must be paid in instalments rather than in one payment 9 months and 1 day after the period end

scope.who: Companies and unincorporated associations within the charge to Corporation Tax. Payment is due 9 months and 1 day after the end of the accounting period; the Company Tax Return (CT600) is due 12 months after the end of the same accounting period — two different dates for the same period. A company or association must file a Company Tax Return if it receives a "notice to deliver a Company Tax Return" from HMRC, and must still send a return if it makes a loss or has no Corporation Tax to pay.
scope.excluded: The single 9-months-and-1-day payment date does not apply to companies with taxable profits above £1.5 million — they must pay Corporation Tax in instalments, with separate rules for profits between £1.5 million and £20 million and for profits above £20 million. People who are self-employed as a sole trader or in a partnership do not file a Company Tax Return at all and must file a Self Assessment return instead. A company that has told HMRC it is dormant for Corporation Tax will not need to file another Company Tax Return unless HMRC asks it to or it begins trading again.
scope.from_when: Long-standing; current GOV.UK guidance as read on 14 November 2026 (pay-corporation-tax page public update date 22 November 2024; company-tax-returns public update date 8 November 2024; deadlines table page updated 23 October 2026).
scope.how_to_claim: No claim. Both deadlines run automatically from the end of the accounting period. A company with no Corporation Tax to pay must still tell HMRC that it does not owe any by the 9-months-and-1-day date, and must still file the return by the 12-month date even if it made a loss.

notes: The counter-intuitive point for clients is that the tax is payable three months BEFORE the return that calculates it is due. Note also that the Corporation Tax accounting period is not necessarily the same as the Companies House accounting reference date period, so the three deadlines (Companies House accounts at 9 months, CT payment at 9 months and 1 day, CT600 at 12 months) are measured from dates that can differ.

title: Companies House Late Filing Penalties

figures.what: private company or LLP — accounts delivered not more than 1 month after the deadline
private company or LLP — more than 1 month but not more than 3 months late
private company or LLP — more than 3 months but not more than 6 months late
private company or LLP — more than 6 months late
public company bands for the same four periods of lateness (up to 1 month; 1-3 months; 3-6 months; over 6 months)
"The late filing penalty will be doubled if accounts are filed late in 2 successive financial years"
the doubling rule applies to financial years beginning on or after this date
the same private limited company bands restated on the GOV.UK guide, with the doubling rule as "The penalty is doubled if your accounts are late 2 years in a row"

scope.who: All companies registered at Companies House, including LLPs, that deliver their annual accounts after the filing deadline. The private company bands (£150 / £375 / £750 / £1,500) apply to private companies and LLPs. The penalty is doubled where accounts are filed late in two successive financial years.
scope.excluded: The private-company bands do not apply to public companies, which are charged on a separate and higher scale (£750 / £1,500 / £3,000 / £7,500). The doubling rule does not apply unless the earlier late financial year began on or after 6 April 2008. These penalties are for late ACCOUNTS only — they are not the penalty for a late confirmation statement (failure to file accounts or a confirmation statement can instead lead to a fine and the company being struck off the register) and they are separate from HMRC's penalties for a late Company Tax Return. Dormant companies are NOT excluded: they face the same late filing penalties as other companies.
scope.from_when: Current Companies House guidance as at 14 November 2026 (page last updated 16 January 2026). The amounts derive from The Companies (Late Filing Penalties) and Limited Liability Partnerships (Filing Periods and Late Filing Penalties) Regulations 2008 and apply to financial years beginning on or after 6 April 2008. The GOV.UK page does not itself state when the current amounts took effect.
scope.how_to_claim: Not a relief to claim — a penalty imposed on the company. Companies House states that "the law imposes an automatic late filing penalty" where accounts are delivered late, so the penalty arises automatically with no discretion exercised at the point of charge. Directors, or an LLP's designated members, are personally responsible for delivering accounts on time. Penalties are paid via gov.uk/pay-penalty-companies-house.

notes: "automatic" is set false because the field asks whether the subject is automatic or must be claimed — a penalty is neither claimed nor granted; the accurate statement, quoted above, is that the law imposes it automatically on the company. ECCTA did not change these bands: the page was updated 16 January 2026 and still carries the 2008 amounts. The doubling rule bites hardest on clients who miss two years running — £1,500 becomes £3,000 for a private company more than 6 months late twice. Companies House also publishes its enforcement approach at gov.uk/government/publications/companies-house-approach-to-financial-penalties/companies-house-approach-to-financial-penalties, which was not read for this entry.

title: Annual Investment Allowance

figures.what: the AIA amount — "The AIA (annual investment allowance) amount is £1 million"

figures.value: 100% of cost, up to the limit
figures.what: AIA is claimable on "most plant and machinery" up to the AIA amount
accounting periods that are not 12 months get a proportionately reduced AIA limit
two or more limited companies controlled by the same person share a single AIA between them

scope.who: Sole traders, partnerships and limited companies investing in plant and machinery. AIA gives relief for most plant and machinery up to £1 million in the accounting period, pro-rated for periods that are not 12 months. Sole traders and partnerships with more than one business usually get one AIA per business, except where the businesses are under the same control and share either the same premises or similar activities, in which case they get only one.
scope.excluded: AIA cannot be claimed on: business cars (claim writing down allowances instead); "items you owned for another reason before you started using them in your business"; and "items given to you or your business". Mixed partnerships cannot claim at all — "AIA (annual investment allowance) is only available for partnerships where all the members are individuals", so a partnership with a corporate member is excluded. A business that is closing cannot claim AIA on items bought in its final accounting period. Sole traders and partnerships cannot claim the full value of an item also used outside the business — the claim is reduced by the private-use proportion. Two or more limited companies controlled by the same person get only one AIA between them, not one each.
scope.from_when: The £1 million limit is the permanent AIA amount (it was legislated at £1m rather than reverting to £200,000). Confirmed in force on the GOV.UK guide as read on 14 November 2026 (public update date 22 October 2024).
scope.how_to_claim: Must be claimed. GOV.UK: "Claim on your tax return." For a company, that is the Company Tax Return (CT600) for the accounting period in which the expenditure was incurred; for a sole trader or partnership, the Self Assessment return. The page links to separate guidance on how to claim capital allowances.

notes: The car exclusion is the single most common client misunderstanding: a van or a lorry is plant and machinery and qualifies, a car does not and goes into a writing down allowance pool instead. Zero-emission and electric cars sit under a separate first-year allowance regime (HMRC CA23153), not AIA — do not blur the two in copy. The common-control rule means a client with several companies has £1 million in total, not £1 million each. GOV.UK also publishes gov.uk/government/publications/legislating-the-annual-investment-allowance-at-1m/legislating-the-annual-investment-allowance-aia-at-1m, which was surfaced in search but not read for this entry.

title: Dormant Company Accounts and Dormancy for Corporation Tax

figures.value: no 'significant' transactions in the financial year
figures.what: the Companies House test — "Your company is called dormant by Companies House if it's had no 'significant' transactions in the financial year"
"Significant transactions do not include:" filing fees paid to Companies House; penalties for late filing of accounts; money paid for shares when the company was incorporated
an unincorporated association or club owing less than £100 Corporation Tax is usually dormant for Corporation Tax

figures.value: annual accounts and a confirmation statement
figures.what: what a company dormant for Corporation Tax must still file — "must still file annual accounts and a confirmation statement (previously annual return)"
"Dormant company accounts submitted to Companies House do not need to include a profit and loss account"
dormant companies have the same accounts filing deadlines as other companies and face the same late filing penalties
a company dormant for Companies House that also qualifies as small can file dormant accounts and does not need an auditor's report

scope.who: A company or association "may be 'dormant' if it's not doing business ('trading') and does not have any other income". Dormant means two different things. For COMPANIES HOUSE, a company is dormant if it has had no significant transactions in the financial year; filing fees paid to Companies House, late filing penalties, and money paid for shares on incorporation do not count as significant. A company dormant for Companies House that also qualifies as small may file dormant accounts instead of full accounts and does not need an auditor's report, and those accounts need not include a profit and loss account. For CORPORATION TAX, a company is usually dormant if it has stopped trading and has no other income (for example investments), is a new limited company that has not yet started trading, is an unincorporated association or club owing less than £100 Corporation Tax, or is a flat management company.
scope.excluded: A company that has had any significant accounting transaction in the financial year is not dormant for Companies House — only filing fees, late filing penalties and share money paid at incorporation are disregarded, so a single bank charge, a bank interest receipt or any trading transaction breaks dormancy. A company that is dormant for Companies House but does not also qualify as small cannot file dormant accounts. Dormancy does not excuse filing: a dormant company must still file annual accounts and a confirmation statement, and must still file a Company Tax Return online if it has received a notice to deliver one. Being dormant for Corporation Tax does not make a company dormant for Companies House, or vice versa — the two tests are separate. A company registered for VAT that plans to restart trading must still send nil VAT returns while dormant.
scope.from_when: Current GOV.UK guidance as at 14 November 2026 (dormant-company overview, dormant-for-companies-house and dormant-for-corporation-tax pages all updated 23 October 2026; Companies House accounts guidance updated 23 October 2026).
scope.how_to_claim: Dormancy for Corporation Tax must be notified: tell HMRC using the online service at gov.uk/tell-hmrc-your-company-is-dormant-for-corporation-tax, or by phone or post via HMRC's Corporation Tax enquiries contact page. You need the company name, its 10-digit Unique Taxpayer Reference and the date it stopped trading if it traded; tax agents need an agent code. After telling HMRC, no further Company Tax Return is needed unless HMRC asks for one or the company begins trading again. Dormant accounts are filed with Companies House in the normal way, by the normal deadline.

notes: Two separate tests, two separate bodies, and clients routinely assume one notification covers both — it does not. Telling HMRC the company is dormant does nothing about the Companies House accounts and confirmation statement, which are still due on the normal timetable and attract the normal late filing penalties. The dormancy-breaking trap is that bank charges and bank interest are significant transactions, while the three disregarded items are narrow. The gov.uk/tell-hmrc-your-company-is-dormant-for-corporation-tax page does not itself define dormancy or mention notices to deliver — those come from gov.uk/dormant-company/dormant-for-corporation-tax, which should be the citation for the definition.

title: Council Tax single person discount and the main discounts and exemptions

figures.what: single person discount off the Council Tax bill where you live alone, or where everyone else in the home is 'disregarded'
Disabled Band Reduction Scheme: the bill is charged at the next lowest Council Tax band
reduction for a Band A property under the Disabled Band Reduction Scheme (there is no lower band)
severe mental impairment discount where the person lives alone, or every other adult is also severely mentally impaired or a full-time student
severe mental impairment discount where everyone else in the household is 'disregarded'
discount where you live with someone who is severely mentally impaired and there are no other countable adults

figures.value: up to 2 times the normal bill
figures.what: second homes premium a council may charge on a furnished second home

figures.value: up to 4 times the normal bill
figures.what: empty home premium where a home has been empty for at least 10 years
period for which a second homes or empty homes premium may be waived, for example after a grant of probate or while the property is being marketed for sale or rent

scope.who: The person liable for Council Tax who is the only adult resident, or whose only other adult residents are all 'disregarded'. GOV.UK lists as disregarded: people under 18; some apprentices; 18 and 19 year olds in full-time education; full-time students; some under-25s funded by the Education and Skills Funding Agency; student nurses; some foreign language assistants; people who are severely mentally impaired; live-in carers; and diplomats. Separate reductions exist for disabled residents (band reduction) and for severe mental impairment (100%, 50% or 25%).
scope.excluded: No single person discount where two or more adults who are not 'disregarded' live in the property. The discount is not means-tested, so it is not available on income grounds to a household with two countable adults. GOV.UK's Council Tax guide signposts Scotland separately (mygov.scot) because the rules are different there, so these rules do not apply in Scotland. Second homes and long-term empty homes attract a premium rather than a discount, and the disabled band reduction is refused unless the property is larger than it would need to be if no one disabled lived there (an extra bathroom, kitchen or room needed for the disabled person, or extra internal space for wheelchair use) and is the main home of at least one disabled adult or child.
scope.from_when: Ongoing; the discount and the disregard categories are the standing rules, and bills and any second home or empty home premium are set annually by each council for the financial year starting 1 April.
scope.how_to_claim: Apply to your own billing authority (for a Birmingham or West Midlands reader, your city or borough council — Birmingham City Council, Solihull, Sandwell, Dudley, Walsall, Wolverhampton or Coventry). GOV.UK routes applications through the council finder on its 'apply for a Council Tax discount' page. Report a change (for example another adult moving in) to the council, as the discount is removed from the date the household changes.

notes: The rules are different in Scotland and GOV.UK links to mygov.scot for Scottish residents. Council Tax Reduction (formerly Council Tax Benefit) is a separate, means-tested scheme each council runs under its own local rules, so Birmingham's scheme differs from neighbouring authorities'. Valuation bands for England and Wales are checked with the Valuation Office Agency; Scotland uses a separate service. Not verified at primary source in this pass: whether Northern Ireland has Council Tax at all (it operates domestic rates), so no claim is made about Northern Ireland.

title: Business rates for retail, hospitality and leisure in England: the 40% relief has ended and been replaced by lower RHL multipliers

figures.what: small business RHL multiplier for 2026/27, for qualifying retail, hospitality or leisure property with a rateable value under £51,000
standard RHL multiplier for 2026/27, for qualifying RHL property with a rateable value from £51,000 to under £500,000
small business (non-RHL) multiplier for 2026/27, rateable value under £51,000
standard (non-RHL) national multiplier for 2026/27, rateable value £51,000 to under £500,000
high-value multiplier for 2026/27, applying to all property with a rateable value of £500,000 or more, including RHL property
the RHL multipliers carry no per-business cash cap, unlike the relief they replaced
the cash cap that applied to the old 40% RHL relief in 2025/26 — the relief it capped is now closed to new claims

figures.value: higher of £800 or the transitional relief percentage (5%, 15% or 30% depending on rateable value)
figures.what: cap on the bill increase in 2026/27 for a property that lost the 40% RHL relief

figures.value: 44.5p standard RHL and 39.5p small business RHL
figures.what: already-announced RHL multipliers for 2027/28, with eligible RHL bills also capped by CPI inflation in 2027/28 and 2028/29

scope.who: Occupied property wholly or mainly used as retail, hospitality or leisure and open to visiting members of the public, with a rateable value under £500,000. GOV.UK's examples are shops, supermarkets, hairdressers, garages, launderettes and travel agents (retail); restaurants, cafes, pubs, takeaways, hotels, B&Bs, holiday homes and campsites (hospitality); and cinemas, theatres, museums, libraries, gyms, nightclubs, live music venues and bowling alleys (leisure). Selling online as well does not disqualify a shop, and requiring membership, tickets or appointments does not disqualify a venue.
scope.excluded: Property with a rateable value of £500,000 or more, which pays the 50.8p high-value multiplier instead. The Schedule 1 excluded uses: financial services, medical and health services, professional services, warehouses used for online sales, certain business-use recording or film studios, crematoria, taxi firms, show homes, conference centres, betting shops, postal sorting offices, citizens advice bureaux, job centres, car parks and most public transport (bicycle docking stations are not excluded). Also outside it: schools, colleges, nurseries and universities; breweries not mainly open to the public; film and theatre production companies; accommodation providing significant nursing care; and unoccupied property, which reverts to the national multipliers once Empty Property Relief ends. The former 40% RHL relief itself is closed — GOV.UK states 'You cannot make a new claim for retail, hospitality and leisure relief.'
scope.from_when: The lower RHL multipliers took effect from 1 April 2026 (the 2026/27 rating year) and are permanent, replacing the temporary RHL relief that ran to 31 March 2026. The 2027/28 multipliers have already been announced.
scope.how_to_claim: The multipliers are not a discretionary relief: the billing authority must determine whether each hereditament meets the legal definition and bill accordingly, so it should appear on the bill without an application. In practice many councils (Birmingham and other West Midlands authorities included) publish a short form asking the ratepayer to confirm the property's RHL use, so check the bill and complete any confirmation the council requests.

notes: The headline for a 2026/27 client conversation is that the 40% RHL relief with its £110,000 cash cap has gone and been replaced by permanently lower multipliers with no cash cap — so a business comparing its 2026/27 bill with 2025/26 should look at transitional relief and the Supporting Small Business scheme, not at RHL relief. Claims for RHL relief for earlier years may still be made to the council. A separate Pubs and Live Music Venue Relief exists for 2026/27 in England (GOV.UK business rates information letter 3/2026); its percentage and cap were not reproduced on the letter and so are not reported here. For 2027/28 GOV.UK states vape shops and adult gaming centres lose eligibility for the RHL multipliers. Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales set their own rates reliefs.

title: Warm Home Discount

figures.what: one-off discount off the winter electricity bill; the money is not paid to the household
the qualifying date for winter 2026 to 2027 — the conditions must all have been met on that day
window in which eligible households are sent a confirmation letter
deadline to call the helpline if the letter asks you to confirm or supply further information
date by which the supplier must apply the discount
Universal Credit income thresholds used by the separate Park Homes Warm Home Discount route

scope.nation: England, Wales and Scotland (not Northern Ireland)
scope.who: England and Wales: the single 'core group' — on 23 August 2026 your electricity supplier was in the scheme, you or your partner received a qualifying means-tested benefit (Pension Credit including Savings Credit, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Housing Benefit, or Universal Credit), and your or your partner's name was on the electricity bill. Scotland keeps two routes: a core group that gets the discount automatically (Pension Credit, certain Universal Credit or ESA premiums, or a Support for Mortgage Interest loan, and certain unemployed parents or carers of a child under 5), and a broader group who must apply to their electricity supplier. Park home residents who buy electricity from the site owner apply to a separate supplier-funded Park Homes scheme run by Charis Grants.
scope.excluded: Northern Ireland — GOV.UK states 'The Warm Home Discount scheme is not available in Northern Ireland' and points residents to the Affordable Warmth scheme. Also excluded: anyone whose electricity supplier was not in the scheme on 23 August 2026; anyone receiving none of the qualifying benefits on that date; anyone whose name (or notified partner's or legal representative's) is not on the electricity bill; people living permanently in a residential or nursing home; non-domestic property and property not supplied with electricity mainly for domestic use, removed by address data analysis and AddressBase classification; caravans, which are generally excluded and are not sent letters, though a small number of permanent residences may qualify on evidence through the helpline; and park home residents who buy electricity through the site owner, who are not eligible for the main scheme and must use the separate Park Homes route, whose funding is finite and closes once spent.
scope.from_when: The 2026 to 2027 scheme year, with 23 August 2026 as the qualifying date and the discount applied by suppliers by 31 March 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: England and Wales: automatic — if the letter confirms eligibility you need do nothing and the supplier applies the discount to the electricity bill by 31 March 2027; if the letter asks for more information, call the scheme helpline by 26 February 2027, and if no letter has arrived by early January 2027, contact the scheme. Scotland core group: automatic. Scotland broader group: you must apply to your electricity supplier, which sets extra criteria, and you should apply early because the number of discounts is limited and you must stay with that supplier until the discount is paid. Prepayment meter customers are told by the supplier how they receive it, for example as a voucher to top up the meter; a supplier providing both fuels may apply it to the gas bill instead.

notes: Scotland: the same £150 and the same 23 August 2026 qualifying date, but it keeps a two-group structure, and broader group households must apply to their supplier rather than being found automatically. Northern Ireland: no Warm Home Discount; GOV.UK directs residents to the Affordable Warmth scheme. From scheme year 16 the former Core Group 1 and Core Group 2 in England and Wales were merged into a single core group, so older material referring to two core groups is out of date for England and Wales.

title: Free school meals in England, including the expanded Universal Credit entitlement

figures.value: all households on Universal Credit, regardless of earnings
figures.what: expanded free school meals entitlement, in force from the start of the 2026 to 2027 academic year (September 2026), set out in law in the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026

household earnings threshold that still defines 'targeted' free school meals, which also attract pupil premium and other disadvantage funding; households on Universal Credit above it get expanded free school meals, which carry no disadvantage funding
year groups covered by universal infant free school meals at a state-funded school, regardless of earnings or benefits

figures.value: end of the 2025 to 2026 academic year
figures.what: when the transitional protections that had run since 1 April 2018 ceased

scope.who: From the start of the 2026 to 2027 academic year, any child in a household receiving Universal Credit, whatever the household earns. Also eligible: households receiving support under Part VI of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, or the guarantee element of Pension Credit, and households meeting the separate 'no recourse to public funds' criteria. Children paid a qualifying benefit directly rather than through a parent or guardian qualify in their own right, as may a child below compulsory school age who is in full-time education. Separately, every pupil in reception, year 1 and year 2 at a state-funded school gets universal infant free school meals regardless of income. Students at DfE-funded further education institutions are entitled to free meals under separate criteria.
scope.excluded: Households receiving none of the qualifying benefits, apart from the universal infant entitlement for reception to year 2. Pupils who kept eligibility only through the transitional protections that ran from 1 April 2018: those ended at the close of the 2025 to 2026 academic year, so from the 2026 to 2027 academic year a household must actually meet the criteria to keep provision (such a pupil still counts in the 'Ever 6' cohort for school funding). Expanded free school meals cover the meal only and bring no disadvantage funding, so a Universal Credit household earning over £7,400 does not attract pupil premium. Children educated otherwise than at school (EOTAS) have no specific legal entitlement, and the local authority considers equivalent food provision case by case. The duty described in the guidance applies to maintained schools, academies, free schools, school-based and maintained nursery schools and non-maintained special schools, so independent schools are outside it. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland run their own schemes and are not covered.
scope.from_when: The expanded Universal Credit entitlement is in force now, from the start of the 2026 to 2027 academic year (September 2026). GOV.UK's application page was last updated 27 October 2026 and states it.
scope.how_to_claim: Apply through your local authority — for a Birmingham reader, Birmingham City Council; GOV.UK routes applications through the council finder on its 'apply for free school meals' page. The claim must be made and verified by the school or local authority. Universal infant free school meals in reception to year 2 need no application, but GOV.UK still asks families on a qualifying benefit to apply, because a targeted eligibility check brings extra funding to the school. Families with no recourse to public funds should ask the school or local authority, as they may still be eligible.

notes: Two tiers now sit behind one meal: 'expanded' free school meals (any Universal Credit household) and 'targeted' free school meals (Universal Credit household earning £7,400 a year or less), and only the targeted tier carries pupil premium and other disadvantage funding — the distinction matters to schools' budgets, not to the child's meal. Eligible children also qualify for the Holiday Activities and Food programme. Scotland: mygov.scot. Wales: gov.wales. Northern Ireland: nidirect.gov.uk. Not verified in this pass: the further education free meals criteria, which GOV.UK holds in a separate guide.

title: NHS Healthy Start

figures.what: payment during pregnancy, from the 10th week of pregnancy
payment for a child from birth until their first birthday
payment for a child aged 1 to 4; payments stop when the child turns 4
how often the money is loaded onto the prepaid card
family take-home pay from employment allowed on the Universal Credit route (and on the no-recourse-to-public-funds route)
the pregnancy threshold for applying

scope.nation: England, Wales and Northern Ireland (not Scotland)
scope.who: People more than 10 weeks pregnant, and parents or guardians with parental responsibility for at least one child under 4, who receive a qualifying benefit. Routes: Universal Credit with family take-home pay from employment of £408 a month or less (apply online); Pension Credit including the child addition (apply by email or phone); income-related Employment and Support Allowance, which can qualify a pregnant applicant though that route ends when the baby is born; anyone under 18 and more than 10 weeks pregnant, who qualifies with no benefit at all until the baby is born; and a non-British parent of one or more British children under 4 who has a no-recourse-to-public-funds condition or no immigration status, with family take-home pay of £408 a month or less. Children must be named and verified on the Universal Credit claim and the applicant's details must match it. The money buys certain types of milk, infant formula, and fruit and vegetables, and claimants also get free Healthy Start vitamins.
scope.excluded: People living in Scotland — GOV.UK states 'If you live in Scotland you cannot get Healthy Start'; they apply for Best Start Foods instead. Also excluded: households whose take-home pay from employment is above £408 a month on the Universal Credit or no-recourse-to-public-funds routes; applicants receiving none of the qualifying benefits (other than an under-18 who is more than 10 weeks pregnant); children aged 4 and over, and children the applicant does not have parental responsibility for; a second application or a second active claim from the same household, and a partner applying separately for the same child; an applicant whose details do not match their Universal Credit claim. An under-18 pregnant claimant who is not on a qualifying benefit after the birth stops being paid 4 weeks after the baby's due date. The pregnant-person route is not open to the non-British, no-recourse-to-public-funds extension, which covers British children only. The card cannot be used online, abroad (including the Republic of Ireland), for cash withdrawals or at fast food restaurants, and is closed after 16 weeks of ineligibility.
scope.from_when: Ongoing. Payments start from the 10th week of pregnancy; after the birth you must tell the scheme within 12 weeks of the due date to keep being paid.
scope.how_to_claim: You must apply. Online at the NHS Healthy Start website for the Universal Credit route; by email or phone for the Pension Credit route and for under-18s more than 10 weeks pregnant. Non-British parents who cannot claim public funds because of their immigration status request an application form by email. If you are under 10 weeks pregnant when you apply you can add the pregnancy later without a new application.

notes: Scotland is a genuine carve-out, not a variation: Best Start Foods is a separate Scottish Government scheme with its own amounts and rules, so Healthy Start figures must never be quoted to a Scottish reader. Free Healthy Start vitamins are arranged differently in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, so point readers at their own local arrangement. Not verified at primary source in this pass: whether Income Support and income-based Jobseeker's Allowance remain listed qualifying benefits — the current NHS application page names only Universal Credit and Pension Credit as live routes, with income-related ESA mentioned in the scheme rules, so a legacy-benefit claimant should be told to check the scheme rules page rather than be given a list.
