scope.nation: Great Britain - England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland is NOT covered by the Ofgem cap.
scope.who: Domestic customers on a standard variable (default) tariff, where the unit rate can rise or fall with the energy market. Covers Direct Debit, standard credit and prepayment meter customers; the level and the standing charge vary by where you live, how you pay, the fuel and the meter type.
scope.excluded: Households in Northern Ireland (Ofgem's cap levels and its postcode checker cover England, Scotland and Wales only, and Ofgem does not regulate the Northern Ireland retail market). Ofgem states you are NOT protected by the price cap if you have agreed a fixed tariff with your supplier, get your heat from a heat network, or use heating oil. Ofgem's fuller list also excludes anyone on a NON-DOMESTIC energy contract - 'for example businesses, charities or alternative home residents' - so it is not only businesses that fall outside the cap.
scope.from_when: 1 October 2026 (the cap level in force runs to 31 December 2026). The next level, for 1 January to 31 March 2027, is due to be announced on 25 November 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. The cap is a legal maximum Ofgem places on suppliers, applied automatically to the tariff of anyone on a default tariff.

notes: RE-CHECKED 18 November 2026. Every in-force figure confirmed unchanged. Ofgem has MOVED its cap explainer page: the old /information-consumers/energy-advice-households/ path now returns a 301 to /your-energy-supply/your-energy-bill/, and official_page has been updated accordingly. The cap for 1 January to 31 March 2027 has NOT been announced - Ofgem will announce it on 25 November 2026, seven days from today. Do not publish any January 2027 figure before then, and from 25 November this entry must be rewritten to carry both the in-force £1,723 (to 31 December 2026) and the newly announced January level with its own dates. The cap sets the maximum a supplier can charge per unit of energy and for the daily standing charge - Ofgem states it 'does not limit the cost of your total bill'. The headline £1,723 is an illustration for typical consumption, not a cap on what any household pays. Nation: Ofgem's own wording is that the cap protects people in 'Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales)' - Northern Ireland is not covered and Ofgem does not regulate the Northern Ireland retail market. VAT, corrected 18 November 2026: the temporary zero rate of VAT on domestic electricity in Great Britain is being extended to 30 JUNE 2027 (not 'July 2027'), per Budget 2026 OOTLAR section 2.20, with 0% applying from 1 April 2027 to supplies that would otherwise be reduced-rate. That extension is ANNOUNCED BUT NOT YET LEGISLATED - the government will lay secondary legislation in early 2027. Note a live inconsistency between primary sources: Revenue and Customs Brief 10 (2026) predates the Budget and still says the zero rate runs only to 31 March 2027. So do NOT write that electricity VAT returns on 1 April 2027. In Northern Ireland domestic electricity remains liable to VAT at the reduced rate of 5%. TDCV trap, confirmed: £1,663 and £1,723 sit on the July 2026 revised typical consumption values; on the old 2023 values they would be £1,862 and £1,935, so any year-on-year comparison of the headline pound figure is wrong twice over, on VAT and on consumption basis. Ofgem's press release of 21 November 2025 gave £1,758 for January to March 2026 on the OLD basis, so £1,723 today is NOT a fall from £1,758. Levels reset every 3 months.

scope.who: Anyone aged 18 or over who is resident in the UK, or who lives abroad and is a member of the armed forces, a Crown servant (diplomatic or overseas civil service) or the spouse or civil partner of one of these. For a Lifetime ISA you must also be under 40 to make your first payment, and you can keep paying in until you turn 50.
scope.excluded: Anyone under 18 (children can have a Junior ISA instead); anyone aged 40 or over cannot open a Lifetime ISA, and no one can pay in or earn the bonus after turning 50; non-UK residents, unless they fall into the armed forces or Crown servant categories; anyone wanting to hold an ISA jointly — you cannot hold an ISA with someone else.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: You must open an ISA with a provider and pay money in; the allowance is per tax year and cannot be carried forward. The Lifetime ISA bonus is added by the provider on payments made, with no separate claim by the saver.

notes: There is NO separate cash ISA limit in force for 2026/27 — the gov.uk ISA guidance gives only the single £20,000 overall figure. A reduction of the cash ISA limit to £12,000 for savers under 65 is announced and takes effect 6 April 2027; the overall £20,000 ISA limit is unchanged, and savers aged 65 and over keep the full £20,000 cash ISA limit. HMRC's policy paper (published 17 September 2026) describes the ISA Regulations as a measure that 'will be amended' and does not confirm the amending regulations have been made, so for 2026/27 content the correct line is £20,000 with no cash sub-limit, with the 2027 change flagged as coming. Accompanying anti-circumvention rules announced 23 June 2026 include restrictions on transfers from non-cash ISAs into cash ISAs and a flat 22% charge on interest on cash held in non-cash ISAs. CORRECTED 19 November 2026: this entry previously carried a £12,000 cash ISA limit taking effect 6 April 2027, from the Autumn Budget 2025 announcement. Budget 2026 dropped that measure. HMRC Tax-free savings newsletter 24 (October 2026) states the reduction of the cash ISA limit and associated anti-circumvention rules announced at Autumn Budget 2025 will not take effect, the £20,000 annual cash ISA limit will be retained from 6 April 2027, and the regulations setting the £12,000 limit will be revoked. Do not publish a cash ISA cut.

scope.who: Individuals whose other taxable income — not counting savings interest or dividends — is less than £17,570. The Personal Allowance is used first against wages, pensions and other income; every £1 of other income above the Personal Allowance then reduces the £5,000 starting rate band by £1, so the full £5,000 is available only where other income does not exceed the Personal Allowance.
scope.excluded: Anyone whose other taxable income (excluding savings interest and dividends) is £17,570 or more gets no starting rate band at all, because £17,570 less the £12,570 Personal Allowance exhausts the £5,000. Anyone with other income between £12,570 and £17,570 gets only part of the band, not the full £5,000. Dividend income and savings interest do not count as 'other income' for the test and so cannot create entitlement.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Normally applied automatically — HMRC usually works it out from information from banks, building societies and (for those in Self Assessment) the tax return, and adjusts the tax code where relevant. No separate claim is needed, though tax already deducted in error is reclaimed from HMRC.

notes: The £5,000 is a band, not an allowance in its own right: it is only ever available in full to someone whose non-savings, non-dividend income is at or below the Personal Allowance, and it tapers £1 for £1 above that. HMRC's worked example: £16,000 of wages is £3,430 above the Personal Allowance, leaving a £1,570 starting rate band. It stacks with the Personal Savings Allowance. The gov.uk page does not pin the figures to a named tax year. Forward-looking point for content: tax on savings income rises by 2 percentage points across all bands from April 2027 (basic 20% to 22%, higher 40% to 42%, additional 45% to 47%); no change to the £5,000 starting rate band was announced alongside it, and the 2026/27 savings rates are unchanged.

scope.who: Self-employed people with taxable profits. Profits of £7,105 or more a year have Class 2 treated as paid, so no Class 2 is actually charged while still protecting the National Insurance record. Class 4 is payable where profits are over £12,570 a year, at 6% up to £50,270 and 2% above. Those with profits below £7,105 can choose to pay voluntary Class 2 at £3.65 a week to protect their record.
scope.excluded: Self-employed people with profits below £7,105 are not required to pay anything (payment is voluntary only). Ministers of religion who receive no salary or stipend do not pay. People who make investments for themselves or others do not pay, provided they do not do it as a business and receive no fee or commission. Examiners, moderators, invigilators and people who set exam questions pay Class 4 where due through Special Class 4 National Insurance arranged with the National Insurance office rather than through Self Assessment.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Class 4 is not claimed — it is calculated and paid through Self Assessment with your Income Tax. Voluntary Class 2 is a choice: it is paid through the Self Assessment return, or arranged directly with HMRC where Self Assessment does not apply.

notes: The key point for content: Class 2 at the flat compulsory rate no longer bites. Anyone with profits at or above the £7,105 Small Profits Threshold is treated as having paid Class 2 without paying it, and anyone below can pay voluntarily at £3.65 a week to keep a qualifying year. The gov.uk self-employed page itself does not use the terms 'Small Profits Threshold', 'Lower Profits Limit' or 'Upper Profits Limit' — those names and the £7,105 / £12,570 / £50,270 figures are confirmed in HMRC's National Insurance rates and allowances tables. That page also does not address under-16s or people over State Pension age, so no exemption for those groups is claimed here.

title: Full Expensing And First Year Allowances

figures.what: proportion of qualifying plant and machinery cost deducted from profits before tax in the year of purchase under full expensing
first-year allowance rate on qualifying special rate expenditure, deducted in the year of purchase
date from which expenditure must be incurred to qualify

scope.who: Companies only. HMRC's guidance states 'Only companies can claim full expensing and the 50% first-year allowance', and its Capital Allowances Manual requires the expenditure to be incurred by a company within the charge to Corporation Tax. The plant or machinery must be bought from 1 April 2023, must be unused and not second-hand, and must not fall within the general exclusions from first-year allowances. Buying from a dealer rather than a manufacturer does not stop an asset being unused, and limited testing, delivery or demonstration use does not either.
scope.excluded: Sole traders, partnerships and anyone not within the charge to Corporation Tax cannot claim. Cars are excluded — General exclusion 2: 'Expenditure incurred on the provision of a car is not eligible for full expensing or the 50% first-year allowance.' Plant or machinery bought for leasing is excluded — General exclusion 6: 'Expenditure on the provision of plant or machinery for leasing is excluded from the scope of full expensing' (with an exception for background plant or machinery in a building leased under an excluded lease). Second-hand or already-used assets are excluded. Expenditure that would be long-life asset expenditure but for transitional provisions is excluded under General exclusion 5. Where new parts are combined with used parts, only the cost of the new parts qualifies. You cannot claim both full expensing and the 50% first-year allowance against the same expenditure.
scope.from_when: Expenditure incurred on or after 1 April 2023
scope.how_to_claim: Must be claimed on the Company Tax Return. HMRC also provides an eligibility checker tool on the full expensing guidance page.

notes: Companies only — this is the single most-misstated point in third-party content, and HMRC's wording is unambiguous. The asset must be new and unused: second-hand kit goes to the Annual Investment Allowance or writing-down allowances instead. gov.uk's live guidance states the qualifying window as 'bought from 1 April 2023' with no end date, consistent with full expensing having been made permanent. Two further manual points worth knowing: second-hand components broken down and reformed into a new asset are treated as unused and not second-hand, and computer software is plant but for companies falls within the intangible fixed assets regime unless they elect out. HMRC's manual lists the general exclusions by reference to CAA 2001 s.46(2) and the page read here sets out only exclusions 2, 5 and 6, so no claim is made here about cessation-period expenditure, gifts or connected persons.

scope.nation: Whole of the UK - England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The rates are set by HMRC and are the same everywhere; Scottish and Welsh income tax are collected by HMRC and carry the same interest rates.
scope.who: Anyone who pays HMRC late (individuals, sole traders, partnerships, trustees, companies) is charged late payment interest; anyone HMRC owes money to is paid repayment interest. Covers Income Tax, National Insurance contributions, Capital Gains Tax, Stamp Duty Land Tax, Stamp Duty, Stamp Duty Reserve Tax, VAT for accounting periods starting on or after 1 January 2023, Alcohol Duty from 1 September 2025 and Vaping Product Duty from 1 October 2026.
scope.excluded: The 7.75%/2.75% (and from 24 November 2026 the 8.00%/3.00%) main rates do NOT apply to Corporation Tax quarterly instalment payments: large companies in the instalment regime have their own lower rates, 6.50% on underpaid and 3.75% on overpaid instalments from 16 November 2026. VAT periods that started before 1 January 2023 are outside the harmonised rates, as is Alcohol Duty before 1 September 2025 and Vaping Product Duty before 1 October 2026. Repayment interest is not paid below the 0.5% floor, so a base rate below 1.5% would not cut it further. Corporation Tax pay and file, Inheritance Tax, Petroleum Revenue Tax and judgment debts each sit in their own separate tables on the same page. Re-read 18 November 2026: those tables carry the SAME current rates as the main rates (8.00%/3.00% from 24 November 2026; judgment debts 8.00%) - it is only their HISTORIC rates that diverge, from 2009 onwards. So the headline rate is safe for those taxes today, but the headline rate must not be quoted for a HISTORIC period on them. The same point applies to the Departmental interest rates table (default and statutory interest, covering Air Passenger Duty, Insurance Premium Tax, environmental taxes and pre-harmonisation VAT, Alcohol Duty and Vaping Product Duty): its current figures are also 8.00% default and 3.00% statutory, not different ones. Three further tables carry a late payment rate only and no repayment rate: Corporation Tax pre-pay and file / SDRT to 30 September 1999 / Petroleum Revenue Tax reg 3AA; Corporation Tax Self Assessment from the normal due date; and IT-CP and other duties attracting section 87 interest for accounting periods ending on or after 1 July 1999.
scope.from_when: 7.75% late payment / 2.75% repayment have applied since 9 January 2026 and remain in force to 23 November 2026. 8.00%/3.00% apply from 24 November 2026. The Corporation Tax quarterly instalment rates of 6.50% (underpaid) and 3.75% (overpaid) apply from 16 November 2026, so they changed on 16 November 2026. Bank Rate has been 4% since the MPC decision published 5 November 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. HMRC charges late payment interest and pays repayment interest automatically, by statute, and the rate changes follow the Bank Rate automatically without any application.

notes: RE-CHECKED 18 November 2026: every figure confirmed unchanged at primary source, including the 8.00%/3.00% row dated 24 November 2026 and the Corporation Tax instalment rates of 6.50%/3.75% from 16 November 2026. The gov.uk page is still last updated 6 November 2026. Bank Rate is 4% and the Bank of England page now shows the next MPC decision as due 17 December 2026. The one thing a reader would get wrong is the dates. Interest rate changes do not take effect on the day the MPC moves: Bank Rate went to 4% on 5 November 2026, but the main HMRC rates only change on 24 November 2026, while the Corporation Tax quarterly instalment rates changed earlier, on 16 November 2026. So for the week of 16 to 23 November 2026 the main rates are still 7.75%/2.75% while the instalment rates are already 6.50%/3.75% - a genuinely confusing week to publish into. Anything published before 24 November 2026 should say 7.75%/2.75% as the current main rates with 8.00%/3.00% flagged as coming; anything published on or after 24 November must be rewritten. Note also that 8.00% is not new ground: the main rate was already 8.00% from 27 August 2025 to 8 January 2026, so 'highest ever' or 'record' framing is wrong. Interest is not a penalty, runs from the due date, and is not reduced for a reasonable excuse. No nation differences.

title: Voluntary National Insurance Class 3

figures.what: Class 3 voluntary National Insurance rate for 2026 to 2027

deadline to fill a gap in the 2025 to 2026 tax year

scope.who: People with gaps in their National Insurance record who do not have enough qualifying years for the full new State Pension and are not eligible for National Insurance credits. Class 3 is paid at £18.40 a week; some self-employed people can pay Class 2 at £3.65 a week instead. You can pay only for gaps in the past 6 tax years, with each deadline falling on 5 April — the deadline for a 2025 to 2026 gap is 5 April 2032. People below State Pension age can ask the Future Pension Centre whether paying will benefit them.
scope.excluded: You cannot pay if you have no gaps in your record, unless you are getting Class 3 credits and are eligible to pay Class 2 contributions. Married women and widows paying reduced rate National Insurance cannot pay voluntary contributions. You cannot pay once the deadline for the period with the gap has passed, so gaps older than 6 tax years are closed. People already eligible for National Insurance credits may not need to pay, and people who have reached State Pension age should contact the Pension Service (or, if abroad or recently abroad, the International Pension Centre) first because paying may not help.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 for the £18.40 weekly rate
scope.how_to_claim: You must check your National Insurance record and State Pension forecast, confirm that paying will benefit you, and then pay. HMRC updates the record after payment — up to 5 working days through the State Pension forecast service, or up to 8 weeks by other payment methods. People who have lived or worked abroad must check what to do before paying, as a different route applies.

notes: Two warnings that belong in any copy on this. First, paying does not always help: gov.uk states plainly that 'voluntary contributions do not always increase your State Pension', for example where you were contracted out — so the forecast check comes before the payment, not after. Second, Class 2 at £3.65 a week is far cheaper than Class 3 at £18.40, so eligibility for Class 2 should be checked first. The normal limit is the past 6 tax years with a 5 April deadline; gov.uk gives 5 April 2032 for a 2025/26 gap, and no extended deadline is currently advertised. Deadline dates for individual earlier years beyond that one example were not stated at primary source, so only the 6-year rule and the 2025/26 date are reported here rather than a derived year-by-year table.

title: The 31 October paper Self Assessment deadline - and what missing it actually costs

figures.what: Paper Self Assessment return deadline for the 2025 to 2026 tax year

Deadline to file online if you want HMRC to collect the tax through your PAYE tax code

Daily late filing penalties after the return is 3 months late

figures.value: 5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is greater
figures.what: Further late filing penalty after 6 months, and again after 12 months
Late payment penalty charged at 30 days, 6 months and 12 months, plus interest on the amount owed

scope.nation: UK-wide. Self Assessment filing deadlines are set by HMRC for the whole of the UK - England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland alike. Scottish and Welsh taxpayers have different income tax rates, but identical filing and payment dates.
scope.who: Anyone HMRC has issued a notice to file to for 2025-26 who chooses to file on paper (form SA100) rather than online - typically sole traders, landlords, higher earners, people with untaxed income, partners and trustees.
scope.excluded: The 31 October date does NOT apply to: trustees of registered pension schemes, non-resident company landlords and non-UK-resident partnerships, and others who cannot file online for operational or technical reasons - they have a paper filing date of 31 January instead (SAM120510, SAM120545). Partnerships with a limited company partner whose accounting date falls between 1 February and 5 April get 9 months after the accounting date on paper, not 31 October. Anyone who registered for Self Assessment after 5 October 2026 gets a deadline three months from the date on HMRC's letter instead. And no late filing penalty arises at all for someone who simply misses 31 October but then files online by 31 January 2027 - the £100 attaches to the filing deadline that applies to them, not to the paper date as such.
scope.from_when: 31 October 2026 for the 2025 to 2026 tax year (the return being filed this season). The same pattern repeats every year: 31 October following the end of the tax year.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim - post form SA100 to HMRC by 31 October. Miss it and you switch to filing online by 31 January. Penalties are issued automatically; appeal with form SA370 if you have a reasonable excuse.

notes: The single most misunderstood point: missing 31 October is not itself a penalty event. If you miss the paper date you can still file online by 31 January 2027 with no penalty - you have simply lost the paper option. The real cliff edge is 31 January. Two genuine advantages of filing on paper by 31 October: HMRC calculates the tax for you and tells you what to pay before 31 January, and small amounts owed (under £3,000) can be collected through your tax code where possible. Nation differences: none for the deadline. Income tax administration is reserved UK-wide, so Scotland and Wales do not run separate Self Assessment schemes even though they set their own income tax rates - a Scottish or Welsh taxpayer files to the same dates. Commonly confused with: the 5 October registration deadline (a different date, for telling HMRC you need to file at all); the 30 December online deadline (only for coding the bill out through PAYE); and the Companies House accounts deadline, which is unrelated.

scope.nation: UK-wide. The amendment window is set in UK-wide Self Assessment law and applies identically in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: Anyone who has already filed a Self Assessment return for a year still inside the 12-month window and needs to change a figure - whether that increases or reduces the tax.
scope.excluded: You cannot amend in the first 3 days (72 hours) after filing - the system will not let you. You cannot use the amendment route at all once the 12-month window has passed, or for any earlier tax year: you must write to HMRC instead, and to recover tax you must make a formal overpayment relief claim within 4 years of the end of the tax year. If you filed through commercial software you cannot necessarily amend via HMRC's own service - you must contact your software provider first and only approach HMRC if the software cannot make the correction. And a tax agent is excluded from signing an overpayment relief claim: the declaration must be signed by the taxpayer personally, or a company officer for a limited company - 'No one else, including a tax agent, can sign on your behalf.'
scope.from_when: The window runs to 12 months after the 31 January filing deadline. For the 2024-25 return that is 31 January 2027; for the 2025-26 return being filed this season it will be 31 January 2028.
scope.how_to_claim: Online: sign in, go to More Self Assessment details, then At a glance, then Tax return options, pick the year, correct it and file again. On paper: send corrected SA100 pages marked 'amendment' with your name and UTR to the address on your Self Assessment paperwork. Outside the window: write to HMRC, or claim overpayment relief.

notes: Two separate things get muddled here. An amendment (inside 12 months) is you changing your own return - no explanation needed, no penalty for the amendment itself. A disclosure or overpayment relief claim (outside 12 months) is a formal letter, and for overpayment relief it must state the tax year, why you believe you overpaid, how much, and carry your own signature - HMRC says an incomplete claim will be rejected outright. The 4-year overpayment relief limit is a hard stop, not a discretion. Nation differences: none - this is UK-wide HMRC administration, not a devolved scheme. Commonly confused with: HMRC's own power to correct obvious errors in your return (a different thing, done by HMRC within 9 months); a return under HMRC enquiry, where your right to amend is restricted; and voluntary disclosure of undeclared income, which is a disclosure not an amendment and can carry penalties.

figures.what: Deadline to make the claim to reduce - for 2025-26 payments on account that is 31 January 2027
What HMRC charges if you reduce payments on account and your actual bill turns out higher

figures.value: Maximum equal to the difference between the amount that would have been paid and the amount actually paid on account
figures.what: Penalty where a taxpayer fraudulently or negligently makes an incorrect statement in a claim to reduce

scope.nation: UK-wide. Payments on account and the SA303 claim are UK-wide Self Assessment mechanics - no devolved variation.
scope.who: Taxpayers who have been asked to make payments on account and genuinely expect a lower liability for the current year - because business profits or other income has gone down, the tax relief they are entitled to has gone up, or tax deducted at source is higher than the previous tax year.
scope.excluded: You cannot claim if you have no payments on account to reduce in the first place - and you have none if last year's tax bill was under £1,000, or if more than 80% of last year's tax was already collected at source (PAYE code, bank interest taxed before you filed). Capital gains tax and student loan repayments are excluded from the payments on account computation entirely (SALF303), so an SA303 cannot touch them - they fall due with the balancing payment. A claim submitted after 31 January following the year of assessment is rejected outright because the time limit has expired (SAM1001). And no penalty is available to HMRC where a reduction turns out wrong through innocent error or where the taxpayer acted in good faith on correct information that later changed - but equally, no relief from the interest.
scope.from_when: Applies to the current payments on account cycle: for 2025-26 payments on account the claim must be made before 31 January 2027. For 2026-27 payments on account, before 31 January 2028.
scope.how_to_claim: Online through your HMRC account - open your latest return and select 'Reduce payments on account'. Or complete form SA303 on screen, print it and post it to HMRC. You need your UTR (or employer reference) and the name and address of the HMRC office shown at the top of your statement.

notes: The risk is asymmetric and that is the whole story. Reduce too far and HMRC charges interest on the shortfall - and the interest runs from the original payment on account due dates, not from the day you found out. Reduce too little and any overpayment simply comes back to you with repayment interest. So the cost of being cautious is small and the cost of being optimistic is real. Worse, SALF303 confirms HMRC can charge a penalty where the claim contains an incorrect statement made fraudulently or negligently, capped at the difference between what should have been paid and what was actually paid - so a guessed-low figure is not a free option. A claim must state what you believe the year's liability will be and the grounds for that belief; it is a reasoned estimate, not a wish. Nation differences: none - no Scottish or Welsh variant exists. Commonly confused with: Time to Pay (a payment plan for tax you accept you owe, not a reduction of the liability); the balancing payment, which is not a payment on account and cannot be reduced by SA303; and the 31 July instalment, which many people wrongly believe is optional.

title: Simple Assessment and the PA302 - the tax bill that arrives without a tax return

figures.what: The official reference for the Simple Assessment tax calculation letter
Amount owed at or above which tax generally cannot be collected through the tax code and a Simple Assessment is issued instead
Payment deadline stated on current Simple Assessment letters, unless a different date is shown
Due date where the PAYE reconciliation is completed from April up to and including 24 October

figures.value: 3 months and 7 days from the reconciliation date
figures.what: Due date where the reconciliation is completed after 24 October
Window from the issue date of the PA302 to report a query to HMRC
Window to appeal in writing following closure of the query
Period after which an unresolved query is automatically closed

scope.nation: UK-wide. Simple Assessment is a UK-wide HMRC process under PAYE and income tax law - England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland alike.
scope.who: People who owe tax for a previous tax year that cannot be collected automatically through their tax code: those owing £3,000 or more, people who have to pay tax on their State Pension (including new state pensioners whose State Pension exceeds their personal allowance), and people with untaxed income such as savings interest or dividends. It replaces the need to file a Self Assessment return for these people.
scope.excluded: If you are registered for Self Assessment you do NOT get one - gov.uk is explicit: 'You will not get a tax calculation letter or a Simple Assessment letter', because your bill is adjusted through your return instead. Customers with more complex tax affairs stay in Self Assessment and keep filing returns. An in-year reconciliation never produces a Simple Assessment - that generates a P800 instead (PAYE96301). And where HMRC holds an RLS (returned letter service - address gone away) indicator, the PA302 is suspended and not issued at all.
scope.from_when: Simple Assessment has operated for underpayments from the 2016-17 tax year onwards. Letters in circulation now carry a 31 January 2027 payment date unless a different date is shown on the letter.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim and no return to file - HMRC issues the PA302 by post or to your Personal Tax Account. Check the figures against your own records, pay by the date on the letter, and report a query to HMRC within 60 days if anything is wrong.

notes: The practical warning is that a PA302 looks like a letter and gets filed in a drawer. It is a legally enforceable assessment with a payment date, and penalties and interest follow if it is ignored. The two-stage dispute route matters: you first raise a query within 60 days of the issue date - that is not an appeal - and only once HMRC closes the query do you have 30 days to appeal in writing. An unresolved query auto-closes after 6 months, which can quietly start the appeal clock. Note also that the payment date is not always 31 January: if HMRC's reconciliation ran after 24 October, the due date is 3 months and 7 days from the reconciliation date, which is why letters carry their own date. Nation differences: none in the mechanism; Scottish and Welsh taxpayers can receive a Simple Assessment calculated at their own income tax rates. Commonly confused with: the P800 tax calculation (same look, different legal status - a P800 is not an assessment and often shows a refund); Self Assessment itself (a Simple Assessment is HMRC assessing you, not you assessing yourself); and the P2 tax code notice, which changes future deductions rather than billing for a past year.

figures.what: The payment reference you must quote, or the payment may be delayed or applied to a different tax bill
Deadline for any balancing payment for the previous tax year and your first payment on account
