scope.nation: UK-wide. HMRC payment channels and clearing times are the same across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: Anyone paying a Self Assessment balancing payment or payment on account - and the same timings apply to paying a Self Assessment penalty.
scope.excluded: You can no longer pay at the Post Office - gov.uk states this flatly, so that option is gone. Direct Debit is excluded as a last-minute option: if it is not already set up with HMRC it takes 5 working days, so setting one up in late January will not meet the deadline. Paying at a bank or building society counter is excluded unless you already hold a paying-in slip from HMRC. And the 'pay by the last working day before the deadline' rule does not apply to Faster Payments or to debit and credit card payments - those two are excluded from the weekend and bank holiday warning because they clear regardless.
scope.from_when: Current. Applies to the 31 January 2027 deadline for the 2025 to 2026 tax year and the 31 July 2027 second payment on account.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim - choose a method that clears in time. For a last-minute payment use Faster Payments, approve a payment through your online bank account, CHAPS, or a debit or corporate credit card online, and always quote the 11-character reference (UTR plus K).

notes: The trap is that the deadline is when the money reaches HMRC, not when you press send. A Bacs payment started on 30 January arrives late and triggers the late payment penalty and interest. If the deadline falls on a weekend or bank holiday, HMRC expects the payment to reach it by the last working day before - except for Faster Payments and card payments, which are exempt from that rule. The second trap is the reference: use the wrong one and HMRC may delay the payment or set it against a different tax bill you owe, which looks like non-payment on your record. Nation differences: none. Commonly confused with: Time to Pay, which is a payment plan rather than a payment method; paying a Self Assessment penalty, which uses a different gov.uk route and a different reference; and the old Post Office and personal credit card routes, both of which people still ask for and neither of which is available.

title: Cash basis is now the default for the self-employed - accruals is the thing you have to choose

figures.what: The year from which cash basis became the default method of calculating trading profits
Former turnover limit for entering the cash basis - removed entirely from 2024-25
Former turnover limit at which a business had to leave the cash basis - removed from 2024-25
Former cap on interest deductions under the cash basis - removed, so interest wholly and exclusively for the trade is now deductible
Look-back period for a business premises renovation allowance claim that bars use of the cash basis

scope.nation: UK-wide. The basis of calculating trading profits for income tax is reserved and applies across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: Sole traders and partnerships without corporate partners - gov.uk: 'You can use cash basis if you're a sole trader or partnership without corporate partners.' Since 2024-25 there is no turnover limit, so cash basis is the starting position whatever the size of the business.
scope.excluded: gov.uk lists businesses that cannot use cash basis: a limited company; a limited liability partnership; a partnership with one or more corporate partners; a Lloyd's underwriter; a farming business with a current herd basis election; a farming or creative business with a fluctuating profit averaging claim; a business that has claimed business premises renovation allowance within the previous 7 years; a business carrying on a mineral extraction trade; and a business that has ever claimed research and development allowance. Property businesses are outside this measure and unaffected. Any business that wants accruals must positively elect out - it does not happen by default.
scope.from_when: Default from the 2024 to 2025 tax year (6 April 2024) onwards, so it is the position for the 2025-26 returns being filed this season and for 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: Cash basis needs no claim - it applies automatically. To use traditional accruals accounting you must opt out: 'When you send your Self Assessment tax return you'll need to say that you've used traditional accounting.'

notes: The reform flipped the default. Before 2024-25 you elected into cash basis; now you elect out of it, and the election is made by ticking the traditional accounting box on the return. That means a business whose adviser does nothing has silently moved onto cash basis. Three restrictions people still quote that no longer exist: the £150,000 entry threshold, the £300,000 exit threshold, and the £500 cap on interest deductions - all removed. The loss position also improved: cash basis losses can now be set against general income of the same year or carried back under the usual loss relief rules, rather than only being carried forward. Accruals still earns its keep for businesses with high stock, significant debtors and creditors, or lenders who want proper accounts - gov.uk itself points complex businesses and those needing finance that way. Nation differences: none. Commonly confused with: Making Tax Digital for Income Tax, a separate reporting obligation; the property income cash basis for landlords, which is a different regime; and simplified expenses (flat rates), which is an independent choice you can make whether you use cash basis or accruals.

title: Simplified expenses flat rates - mileage jumps to 55p, and the home rates stay put

figures.what: Flat rate for cars and goods vehicles, first 10,000 business miles, for 2026-27 (up from 45p)
Flat rate for cars and goods vehicles after 10,000 business miles - unchanged
Flat rate for motorcycles

figures.value: From 45 pence per mile to 55 pence per mile
figures.what: The increase to the first-band rate, retrospective taking effect from 6 April 2026, covering self-employed simplified mileage rates as well as AMAPs
The first-band rate for 2025-26 and earlier years - still the rate for the return being filed this January
Working from home flat rate for 25 to 50 hours worked from home per month
Working from home flat rate for 51 to 100 hours per month
Working from home flat rate for 101 hours or more per month
Minimum hours worked from home before the home flat rate can be used at all

scope.nation: UK-wide. Simplified expenses are part of UK-wide income tax law and apply in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: Sole traders and business partnerships that have no companies as partners. Optional, and you can mix methods across different vehicles.
scope.excluded: gov.uk: 'Simplified expenses cannot be used by limited companies or business partnerships involving a limited company.' You cannot use the mileage rate for a vehicle you have ever claimed capital allowances on, or whose costs are already in your business profits. Once you use flat rates for a vehicle you must keep using them for as long as that vehicle is in the business - you cannot switch to actual costs until you replace it. Cars designed for commercial use, such as black cabs and dual-control driving instructor cars, are outside the mileage rate (BIM75005). Under the cash basis, if you have deducted the cost of acquiring a goods vehicle or motorcycle you cannot then use the mileage rate for it. The home flat rate is excluded entirely below 25 hours a month, and it never covers telephone or internet - those must be claimed on actual business-use cost. Tolls, congestion charges and parking are not inside the mileage rate and are claimed separately.
scope.from_when: The 55p first-band mileage rate applies from 6 April 2026 (announced retrospectively), so it is the 2026-27 rate. For the 2025-26 return being filed by 31 January 2027 the rate is still 45p. The working from home rates of £10, £18 and £26 are the current rates and were not changed.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to register - keep contemporaneous mileage and hours records and enter the flat rate figures in the expenses boxes of the self-employment pages of your Self Assessment return instead of actual costs.

notes: The live risk this season is using the wrong year's mileage rate. 55p is the 2026-27 rate; the return due by 31 January 2027 covers 2025-26 and uses 45p. Get those the wrong way round and every mileage claim is wrong. The increase was announced as retrospective to 6 April 2026 and covers both employee AMAPs and self-employed simplified mileage, so the two stay aligned. Note what the flat rate does and does not absorb: it covers running costs and the capital cost of the vehicle, which is why claiming capital allowances on the same vehicle is barred for life, but it does not cover tolls, congestion charges or parking. On the home rate, the hours test is hours actually worked from home in the month, and the bands are not pro-rated within a month. Nation differences: none. Commonly confused with: the £6 a week employee working from home allowance, which is a different relief for employees under PAYE; the business proportion method, which is the alternative to flat rates and often gives a bigger deduction for a home office; and the cash basis, which is a separate choice.

title: Appealing a Self Assessment penalty - what HMRC accepts as a reasonable excuse

figures.what: The statutory appeal period against a late filing penalty
The period HMRC actually allows - the 30-day statutory window plus 7 days for printing and despatch of the notice
Form to appeal an individual Self Assessment late filing or late payment penalty by post (SA371 for partnership penalties)
The initial late filing penalty most appeals are against
Period from the date on the penalty notice within which the penalty itself must be paid

scope.nation: UK-wide. Penalty appeals and the reasonable excuse test sit in UK-wide tax law and apply across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: An individual or partnership charged a Self Assessment penalty for late filing or late payment who does not agree the penalty is due. For a partnership penalty the appeal 'must be made by the nominated partner, or authorised agent and dealt with through the partnership record' (SAM10080). HMRC accepts as reasonable excuses: the death of a partner or another close relative shortly before the deadline; an unexpected stay in hospital that prevented you dealing with your tax affairs; a serious or life-threatening illness; computer or software failure while preparing the online return; issues with HMRC online services; a fire, flood or theft that prevented you completing the return; postal delays you could not have predicted; delays related to a disability or mental illness you have; being unaware of or misunderstanding your legal obligation; and relying on someone else to send your return who did not.
scope.excluded: gov.uk states these are NOT reasonable excuses: 'your cheque bounced or payment failed because you did not have enough money'; 'you found the HMRC online system too difficult to use'; 'you did not get a reminder from HMRC'; and 'you made a mistake on your tax return'. An appeal is also excluded once the window has gone without HMRC accepting a late appeal, and the excuse fails unless you then put matters right - 'You must send your return or payment as soon as you're able to.' Appealing does not suspend the debt: if you do not pay and the appeal is rejected you pay interest on the penalty from the date it was due to the date you paid.
scope.from_when: Current. The appeal window runs from the issue of the penalty notice - statutorily 30 days, with HMRC allowing 37 days from issue.
scope.how_to_claim: Appeal online through HMRC's appeal service, or download and post form SA370 (SA371 for partnerships). Have ready the date the penalty was issued, the date you filed, the date you paid, and the details of your reasonable excuse. If HMRC refuses, ask for a review of the decision.

notes: Two things decide most appeals. First, the excuse has to explain the whole period of lateness, not just the deadline week - and HMRC expects you to have filed or paid as soon as you were able once the obstacle passed. Second, several of the accepted excuses are narrower than they sound: 'computer or software failure' means failure while you were preparing the return, not a laptop that died in November; 'relying on someone else' is accepted on the gov.uk list but HMRC still looks at whether you took reasonable care in choosing and chasing them. Pay the penalty while you appeal if you can - if the appeal fails, interest runs from the original due date, and if it succeeds HMRC repays you with interest. A separate and often better route: if you never needed to file at all, ask HMRC to cancel the penalty and withdraw the return requirement rather than appealing on excuse grounds. Nation differences: none. Commonly confused with: Time to Pay, which deals with inability to pay rather than cancelling a penalty (and note that having no money is expressly not a reasonable excuse); special reduction, a separate HMRC discretion; and the First-tier Tribunal, which is the next stage only after HMRC's own review.

title: Shared Parental Leave and Statutory Shared Parental Pay

figures.what: Statutory Shared Parental Pay weekly rate 2026-27, or 90% of average weekly earnings, whichever is lower
Lower earnings limit per week 2026-27 - average weekly earnings must be at least this in the relevant period (usually the 8 weeks to the qualifying week) to get ShPP
Continuity of employment test - continuous employment with the same employer up to and including the 15th week before the expected week of birth (or the week of matching for adoption)

figures.value: £30 a week in 13 of 66 weeks (£390 total)
figures.what: Employment and earnings test applied to the OTHER parent - 26 weeks' work (not necessarily consecutive) in the 66 weeks before the expected week of birth, averaging at least £30 a week in 13 of them
Maximum SPL and ShPP available, because the mother must take 2 weeks of maternity leave and 2 weeks of maternity pay; rises to 52/39 weeks if the mother dies

scope.nation: Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales). The employment and earnings test requires the other parent to have worked in Great Britain. Northern Ireland has its own separate Shared Parental Leave legislation - do not quote these rules to a Northern Ireland employer without checking NI guidance.
scope.who: An employee who passes the continuity of employment test (26 weeks' continuous service up to the 15th week before the due date, or the matching week for adoption), is still employed in the week before SPL starts, shares main responsibility for the child with the other parent, and whose partner passes the employment and earnings test. For ShPP the employee must also qualify for SMP or SAP, or qualify for SPP where the partner qualifies for SMP, SAP or Maternity Allowance. The mother must curtail her maternity leave or pay for any SPL/ShPP to exist.
scope.excluded: Self-employed parents cannot get SPL or ShPP at all (their employed partner may still qualify if the self-employed parent passes the employment and earnings test). Agency workers cannot get SPL, though they may get ShPP if they qualify for SMP, SAP or SPP. If BOTH parents are self-employed neither gets SPL or ShPP - the mother may get Maternity Allowance instead. Employees who fail the 26-week continuity test are excluded. Employees whose partner fails the employment and earnings test are excluded. A mother who qualified only for Maternity Allowance and not SMP cannot get ShPP herself, although her partner may. People not working or not employed are excluded. Employees earning below £129 a week on average are excluded from ShPP.
scope.from_when: Current rates apply from 6 April 2026 for tax year 2026-27. SPL/ShPP must be taken within one year of the birth or placement.
scope.how_to_claim: Employee gives the employer at least 8 weeks' written notice of entitlement plus a declaration that the partner meets the employment and earnings test, then books leave in up to 3 separate blocks. Employer pays ShPP through payroll and reclaims it from HMRC.

notes: Commonly confused with Statutory Parental Leave (the separate 18 weeks of unpaid parental leave) and with the old Additional Paternity Leave that SPL replaced. SPL is not an extra entitlement on top of maternity leave - it converts the mother's untaken maternity leave and pay, so the pot is 52 weeks minus leave already taken and 39 weeks minus SMP/Maternity Allowance already taken. The employer is not required to verify the other parent's declaration. Nation difference: the scheme sits in Great Britain employment legislation; Northern Ireland runs a parallel scheme under its own rules, so a Birmingham employer with a Belfast-based employee must check NI guidance separately.

title: Statutory Adoption Pay and Leave

figures.what: Statutory Adoption Pay for the first 6 weeks, with no cap
Statutory Adoption Pay weekly rate for the remaining weeks 2026-27, or 90% of average weekly earnings, whichever is lower
Minimum average weekly earnings over the 8-week relevant period to qualify for Statutory Adoption Pay (the 2026-27 lower earnings limit)
Continuous employment required with the same employer, up to any day in the week the employee was matched with a child, to qualify for Statutory Adoption Pay

scope.nation: Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales). The gov.uk employer guide does not extend these rules to Northern Ireland, which operates its own adoption leave and pay legislation.
scope.who: An employee (employment status required) who has been matched with a child by a UK adoption agency or local authority, or is adopting from overseas, or is a parent of a child born to a surrogate. Adoption LEAVE is available regardless of length of service. Statutory Adoption PAY additionally requires 26 weeks' continuous employment up to any day in the matching week, being on the payroll, average weekly earnings of at least £129 over the 8-week relevant period, correct notice and proof of adoption. For overseas adoptions the 26 weeks must be complete by the start of the week pay begins; for surrogacy the 26 weeks run to any day in the 15th week before the baby is due.
scope.excluded: Special guardians and kinship carers get neither adoption leave nor adoption pay. Anyone adopting a stepchild or another family member is excluded. Anyone adopting privately - for example without permission from a UK authority or adoption agency - is excluded. Anyone not classed as an employee is excluded from adoption leave. Employees with under 26 weeks' continuous service at the matching week are excluded from Statutory Adoption Pay (though leave is still available). Employees averaging under £129 a week are excluded from the pay. Employees who do not give correct notice or supply proof of adoption when asked are excluded. Agency workers, directors and educational workers are subject to different entitlement rules on gov.uk rather than a clean exclusion, so check those separately.
scope.from_when: Current rates apply from 6 April 2026 for tax year 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: Employee gives the employer notice within 7 days of being matched and supplies a matching certificate (or form SC6 for an overseas adoption with a partner). Employer pays SAP through payroll and reclaims 92% from HMRC, or 103% with Small Employers' Relief.

notes: Statutory Adoption Leave runs up to 52 weeks (26 weeks Ordinary plus 26 weeks Additional) and Statutory Adoption Pay runs up to 39 weeks; those durations are stated in the gov.uk employer guide but are structural rather than annually uprated figures, so they sit here in notes rather than in the verified figures list. Only ONE member of an adopting couple can take adoption leave - the other may qualify for paternity leave and pay instead, which is why form SC6 exists. Commonly confused with foster care: fostering alone carries no adoption leave, although 'fostering for adoption' and concurrent planning placements can qualify. Also commonly confused with Statutory Maternity Pay - the first 6 weeks at 90% with no cap mirrors SMP, which is why payroll staff often mis-key the two. WARNING for the content bank: a stale HMRC mirror of this guide at hmrc.gov.uk/employers-adoption-pay-leave/print is still serving the 2024-25 rate of £184.03. Do not use that page; the current rate is £194.32.

title: Parental Bereavement Leave and Pay (Jack's Law)

figures.what: Statutory Parental Bereavement Pay weekly rate 2026-27, or 90% of average weekly earnings, whichever is lower
Parental Bereavement Leave per child who died or was stillborn - can be taken as 2 consecutive weeks, 2 separate single weeks, or just one week
Window from the date of death or stillbirth within which the leave must be finished
Continuous employment required up to the end of the relevant week (the Saturday-ending week before the week of death or stillbirth) to qualify for Statutory Parental Bereavement Pay
Minimum average gross weekly earnings to qualify for Statutory Parental Bereavement Pay (the 2026-27 lower earnings limit)

scope.nation: Now effectively UK-wide, but by two different routes and on two different dates. Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales): already in force. Northern Ireland: eligibility applies to bereavements on or after 6 April 2026, and the Northern Ireland rules are explicitly different - they also cover MISCARRIAGE, which the Great Britain scheme does not.
scope.who: An employee who had a child die under the age of 18, or a stillbirth after 24 weeks of pregnancy. Covers biological, adoptive and surrogacy parents and their partners. Also covers non-parents with day-to-day care responsibility where the child lived with them for 4 continuous weeks ending on the date of death. Adoptive parents qualify after the adoption order, or before it where the child was placed and the placement was not disrupted. Surrogacy parents qualify after a parental order, or before it where they applied or intended to apply within 6 months of birth. LEAVE is available from day one with no service requirement; PAY needs 26 weeks' continuous service, still being employed on the day the child died, and average earnings of at least £129 gross a week.
scope.excluded: Biological parents are excluded after an adoption order or parental order has transferred parenthood, unless a contact order was in place after the adoption. Non-parents are excluded if the child did not live with them for 4 continuous weeks ending on the date of death, or if they lacked day-to-day care responsibility. Paid carers are excluded, unless they were a foster parent paid a fee or allowance by a local council, were reimbursed care-related expenses, or received payments under a will or trust for the child's care. Anyone is excluded where a parent or a person with parental responsibility was also living in the household. Anyone not classed as an employee is excluded from the leave. Employees with under 26 weeks' continuous employment are excluded from the pay (leave still applies). Employees who leave before the day of the death are excluded from the pay. Employees averaging under £129 gross a week are excluded from the pay. Anyone who does not give correct notice is excluded from both. Bereavements before 6 April 2026 in Northern Ireland are excluded.
scope.from_when: Great Britain: already in force for current bereavements. Northern Ireland: bereavements on or after 6 April 2026. Current pay rate applies from 6 April 2026 for 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: Employee notifies the employer (notice can be informal and the window is generous given the 56-week period). Employer pays SPBP through payroll and reclaims it from HMRC like other statutory parental payments.

notes: The Great Britain commencement date usually quoted for Jack's Law is 6 April 2020, but gov.uk did not state that date on the pages read, so it is NOT treated as verified here - the verified date is the Northern Ireland start of 6 April 2026. The biggest nation trap: Northern Ireland's version covers miscarriage as well as stillbirth after 24 weeks and death of a child under 18, so a post written for a Great Britain audience understates the Northern Ireland right. The leave is unusually flexible compared with other statutory leave - two non-consecutive single weeks are allowed, and a separate 2 weeks applies for EACH child in a multiple bereavement. Commonly confused with the ordinary right to time off for dependants (unpaid, emergency, no fixed length) and with compassionate leave, which is contractual and has no statutory floor. Note also the separate Statutory Bereaved Partner's Paternity Leave, which is a different entitlement.

title: Neonatal Care Leave and Pay

figures.what: Statutory Neonatal Care Pay weekly rate 2026-27, or 90% of average weekly earnings, whichever is lower
Maximum Neonatal Care Leave and Statutory Neonatal Care Pay (one week for each week the baby spends in neonatal care, after the first 7 days)

figures.value: 7 days or more in a row
figures.what: Minimum unbroken period the baby must spend in neonatal care before the entitlement is triggered
Continuous employment required up to the end of the relevant qualifying week to get Statutory Neonatal Care Pay
Minimum average weekly earnings before tax over the 8-week relevant period to qualify for Statutory Neonatal Care Pay (the 2026-27 lower earnings limit)

scope.nation: Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales). The gov.uk employer guidance covers England, Scotland and Wales and does not mention Northern Ireland. The Neonatal Care (Leave and Pay) Act 2023 section 3(2) formally extends to Northern Ireland, but section 3(1) gives each amendment in the Schedule the same extent as the provision it amends, and those are Great Britain employment and social security provisions - so treat the operative right as Great Britain and check Northern Ireland guidance separately.
scope.who: An employee who is a parent with caring responsibility for the baby - biological parents, adoptive parents, parents of a child born to a surrogate, and the partner of the baby's mother where caring responsibility is shared. The baby must have been born on or after 6 April 2025 and have spent 7 or more consecutive days in neonatal care. Neonatal Care LEAVE is available from the first day of employment with no service requirement. Statutory Neonatal Care PAY needs 26 weeks' continuous employment to the end of the qualifying week, continued employment up to the week before the claim, and average earnings of at least £129 a week over an 8-week period. The qualifying week is the 15th week before the due date if the employee already qualifies for maternity or paternity pay, the matching week if they qualify for adoption pay, and otherwise the week immediately before the baby enters neonatal care.
scope.excluded: Babies born before 6 April 2025 are excluded entirely - this is the single most common error. Babies who spend fewer than 7 consecutive days in neonatal care are excluded. Anyone who is not an employee, such as a worker or someone with no employment contract, is excluded from the leave. Parents who do not meet the parental or caring-responsibility criteria are excluded. Employees with under 26 weeks' service are excluded from the pay, although the leave is still available from day one. Employees averaging under £129 a week are excluded from the pay. Employees who do not remain employed up to the week before they claim are excluded from the pay. For overseas adoptions, an employee without official notification that they may adopt is excluded. For surrogacy, an employee who does not apply for a parental order within 6 months of birth is excluded.
scope.from_when: Babies born on or after 6 April 2025. Current pay rate applies from 6 April 2026 for 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: Employee gives the employer notice; notice requirements are relaxed for leave taken while the baby is still in neonatal care (Tier 1) and stricter for leave taken afterwards (Tier 2). Employer pays SNCP through payroll and reclaims it from HMRC.

notes: This is the newest of the family leave entitlements and the one clients get wrong most often. It sits ON TOP of maternity, paternity, adoption and shared parental leave - it does not replace or reduce them, and it is the only family leave that can be taken at the very end of a 52-week maternity period. The 7-day trigger is 7 days IN A ROW, and the entitlement is one week of leave per week in care, capped at 12 weeks. Leave is a day-one right but pay is not, so a short-service employee can be entitled to 12 weeks off with no statutory pay - a cashflow point worth flagging to employers. Northern Ireland position is the gap to watch: do not assert a Northern Ireland entitlement from the Great Britain guidance. There is also a detailed employers' technical guide published on gov.uk for complex cases.

title: Unpaid Carer's Leave

figures.what: Unpaid Carer's Leave entitlement - a 'week' means the number of hours the employee usually works over 7 days, so a 3-day-a-week employee gets 3 days
Carer's Leave carries no statutory pay - it is wholly unpaid unless the employer chooses to pay contractually
The dependant's expected care need - a physical or mental illness or injury expected to require care for more than 3 months, or a disability under the Equality Act 2010, or care needs due to old age

figures.value: 3 days' notice, or twice the leave length
figures.what: Notice required - at least 3 days for a half day or one day, and at least twice the length of the leave where more than one day is taken
Date the Carer's Leave Regulations 2024 came into force

scope.nation: Great Britain only - England, Wales and Scotland. Verified at legislation.gov.uk: the Carer's Leave Regulations 2024 extend to England, Wales and Scotland and do NOT extend to Northern Ireland. The Carer's Leave Act 2023 section 3(2) formally extends to Northern Ireland, but section 3(1) gives each amendment the same extent as the provision it amends, and the Schedule amends the Employment Rights Act 1996, which is Great Britain legislation. Northern Ireland employees have NO statutory carer's leave right under these Regulations.
scope.who: Employees in England, Wales and Scotland, from their first day of work - there is no minimum service requirement. The employee must be providing or arranging care for a dependant with a long-term care need. The dependant does not have to be a family member. Leave can be taken as a whole week, individual days, or half days, and the one week per 12 months can be spread across more than one dependant.
scope.excluded: Northern Ireland employees are excluded entirely - the Regulations do not extend there. Anyone who is not an employee is excluded: the right is given to employees only, so workers, agency workers who are not employees, and the self-employed have no entitlement. Carers of someone whose care need is expected to last 3 months or less are excluded, unless the dependant has an Equality Act 2010 disability or care needs due to old age. Employees who do not give the required notice (3 days, or twice the length of the leave) are excluded for that request. Employees who have already used their one week in the current 12-month period are excluded until it resets.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2024 (Carer's Leave Regulations 2024). Still the current position for 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: Employee requests the leave from the employer with the required notice. The request does not have to be in writing and NO evidence of the care need may be required. The employer cannot refuse the request outright but may postpone it where the absence would cause serious disruption, in which case the employer must agree a new date within one month of the date requested and give the reason and the new date in writing within 7 days of the original request and before the leave was due to start.

notes: The two things clients get wrong: it is UNPAID, and it is a day-one right with no service qualification. Employers cannot demand proof of the dependant's condition and cannot refuse outright - only postpone, and only on the serious-disruption test with a written reason inside 7 days. Commonly confused with the separate statutory right to reasonable unpaid time off for DEPENDANTS, which covers emergencies and unexpected disruption, needs no notice and has no annual cap - an employee can use both. Also commonly confused with Carer's Allowance, which is a DWP benefit paid to the carer and has nothing to do with the employer or payroll. Nation difference is the sharpest of all eight subjects: a Birmingham employer with staff in Northern Ireland must not assume the right travels, because it does not. For irregular-hours employees, calculate the 'week' by adding up hours worked in the previous 12 months and dividing by 52 (or by the weeks since they started, if under a year), and use expected weekly hours in the first week.

title: Statutory Annual Leave and Holiday Pay for Irregular-Hours Workers

figures.what: Statutory paid annual leave for a full-year worker - 4 weeks paid at normal rate of pay plus 1.6 weeks paid at basic rate of pay
Statutory cap on paid holiday entitlement - someone working 6 days a week gets 28 days, not 33.6
Accrual rate for irregular-hours and part-year workers - 12.07% of hours actually worked in each pay period, rounded to the nearest hour; reflects 5.6 weeks against 46.4 working weeks
The accrual method, accrual during maternity, family-related and sick leave, and rolled-up holiday pay apply to leave years beginning on or after this date
The alternative reference period an employer may use to calculate holiday pay instead of rolled-up pay

scope.nation: Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales) under the Working Time Regulations 1998. Northern Ireland is NOT covered: the Working Time Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2016 consolidated and replaced the Northern Ireland 1998 Regulations and govern annual leave there, and the 2024 Great Britain reforms (12.07% accrual and rolled-up holiday pay) were made by amending the Great Britain Regulations, so they do not apply in Northern Ireland.
scope.who: All workers, not just employees - this is wider than every other subject in this set. A full-year worker gets 5.6 weeks' paid leave. An 'irregular hours worker' is one whose paid hours per pay period are, under the contract, wholly or mostly variable, which captures casual and zero-hours contracts. A 'part-year worker' is one who, under the contract, works only part of the year with at least one period of a week or more when they are neither required to work nor paid - fixed hours do not rule this out. Those two groups accrue at 12.07% of hours worked and may be paid rolled-up holiday pay.
scope.excluded: Genuinely self-employed people have NO statutory holiday entitlement at all and are excluded completely. Workers with regular, fixed hours all year round are excluded from the irregular-hours and part-year rules and must use the standard 5.6-weeks method - the 12.07% shortcut is unlawful for them. A rotating shift pattern with fixed hours in each week is expressly NOT irregular hours, so it is excluded from the 12.07% method. Agency workers who are neither irregular-hours nor part-year workers are excluded from the new rules and keep the standard method. Northern Ireland workers are excluded from these Great Britain reforms. Leave years beginning before 1 April 2024 are excluded from the accrual and rolled-up pay rules and use the previous calculation. Entitlement above 28 days is excluded from the statutory cap - anything more is contractual only.
scope.from_when: Leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024 for the accrual method and rolled-up holiday pay. From 1 January 2024 for the other changes, including the definition of normal pay and the carryover rules. Still the current position for 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: Entitlement accrues automatically and does not need claiming, but the worker must request and take the leave. Rolled-up holiday pay must be shown as a separate itemised line on the payslip and paid with wages.

notes: The 12.07% figure is the single most misapplied number in UK payroll. It is lawful ONLY for irregular-hours and part-year workers, and only for leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2024. Applying it to a regular part-time worker under-pays them and is a common tribunal claim. Rolled-up holiday pay is OPTIONAL, not mandatory - the employer may instead use a 52-week reference period - and before switching to it the employer should check the contract for a variation requirement and tell the workers. The 4 weeks at 'normal' pay versus 1.6 weeks at 'basic' pay split matters where a worker gets commission, regular overtime or allowances, because those feed the normal-rate 4 weeks but not necessarily the basic-rate 1.6. Where hours are fixed but unevenly spread, apply the 28-day cap as 28 days of the AVERAGE working day. Nation difference: a West Midlands employer running payroll for Northern Ireland staff cannot use the 12.07% accrual or rolled-up pay rules there.

title: Statutory Redundancy Pay - Weekly Cap and Maximum Award

figures.what: Maximum amount of a week's pay for calculating statutory redundancy pay from 6 April 2026, under section 227(1) Employment Rights Act 1996 - up from £719
Maximum compensatory award for unfair dismissal from 6 April 2026, under section 124(1ZA)(a) Employment Rights Act 1996 - up from £118,223
Maximum statutory redundancy payment from 6 April 2026 - derived arithmetic, being the 30-week statutory maximum multiplied by the £751 capped week's pay
Date the Employment Rights (Increase of Limits) Order 2026 comes into force, per article 1(2)

scope.nation: England and Wales and Scotland only. Verified from article 1(3) of the Order: 'This Order extends to England and Wales and Scotland.' The Order does not mention Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland sets its own limits separately through the Department for the Economy, so the £751 cap must NOT be quoted to a Northern Ireland employer.
scope.who: Employees being made redundant in England, Wales and Scotland. Statutory redundancy pay is calculated from the employee's age, length of service and weekly pay, with each week's pay capped at £751 for dismissals where the appropriate date falls on or after 6 April 2026.
scope.excluded: Dismissals where the 'appropriate date' falls before 6 April 2026 are excluded from the new limits and keep the previous £719 cap - this is expressly provided by article 4 of the Order. Northern Ireland is excluded from this Order entirely, as article 1(3) limits the extent to England and Wales and Scotland. Pay above £751 a week is excluded from the calculation, so a high earner's statutory entitlement is capped regardless of actual salary. Service beyond the statutory 20-year maximum is excluded from the reckonable calculation.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026, per article 1(2) of the Employment Rights (Increase of Limits) Order 2026 (SI 2026/310).
scope.how_to_claim: The employer must calculate and pay statutory redundancy pay as part of the dismissal. If the employer fails to pay, or is insolvent, the employee claims from the Redundancy Payments Service or an employment tribunal.

notes: Two figures get mixed up constantly: £751 is the capped WEEK'S PAY for redundancy, while £123,543 is the maximum COMPENSATORY AWARD for unfair dismissal - a different claim with a different basis. Statutory redundancy pay is tax-free, and so is the first £30,000 of any wider termination package, which is a separate rule from these caps. The maximum statutory redundancy payment of £22,530 shown above is arithmetic: the 30-week maximum (1.5 weeks for each of a maximum 20 reckonable years) comes from section 162 Employment Rights Act 1996 and was NOT separately re-verified at primary source in this pass, so treat the £751 and £123,543 as the hard verified figures and the £22,530 as derived. The two-year qualifying service requirement for statutory redundancy pay, and the exclusion of employees who unreasonably refuse suitable alternative employment, are long-standing rules in the Employment Rights Act 1996 but were also not re-verified at primary source here, so they are flagged rather than asserted in the excluded field. Nation difference: Northern Ireland uprates its own limits on a separate instrument and the figures have historically differed.

title: Employer Class 1 Secondary National Insurance - Threshold and Rate

figures.what: Employer (secondary) Class 1 National Insurance rate on earnings above the relevant threshold for 2026-27

figures.value: £96 a week / £417 a month / £5,000 a year
figures.what: Class 1 secondary threshold for 2026-27 - the point at which employer National Insurance starts for category letters A, B, C and J

figures.value: £967 a week / £4,189 a month / £50,270 a year
figures.what: Upper secondary threshold for 2026-27 - applies to under-21s, apprentices under 25 and veterans; employer pays 0% up to this point and 15% above it

figures.value: £481 a week / £2,083 a month / £25,000 a year
figures.what: Freeport and Investment Zone upper secondary threshold for 2026-27 - employer pays 0% up to this point and 15% above it

figures.value: £129 a week / £559 a month / £6,708 a year
figures.what: Lower earnings limit for 2026-27 - not an employer NI trigger, but the earnings floor that preserves benefit entitlement and gates statutory payments

scope.nation: United Kingdom - genuinely UK-wide. National Insurance is a reserved matter, so the same secondary threshold and 15% rate apply in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. This is the only subject in this set with no nation variation, which is itself worth saying, because Scottish income tax divergence leads clients to assume NI diverges too.
scope.who: Every employer with employees whose earnings exceed the relevant secondary threshold. For the main category letters A, B, C and J the employer pays 15% on all earnings above £96 a week / £417 a month / £5,000 a year. There is no upper limit on employer secondary contributions - unlike employee contributions, they do not drop to a lower rate at the upper earnings limit.
scope.excluded: Employees aged under 21 (category letters M and Z) are excluded from employer NI on earnings up to £967 a week, the upper secondary threshold - the employer pays 0% below that and 15% only above it. Apprentices under 25 on an approved scheme (category H) are excluded on the same basis up to £967 a week. Qualifying veterans in their first 12 months of civilian employment (category V) are excluded up to £967 a week. Employees working in a Freeport or Investment Zone (categories D, E, F, I, K, L, N and S) are excluded up to £481 a week / £25,000 a year. Earnings below the £96 weekly secondary threshold are excluded for every category. Category C (employees over State Pension age) is NOT excluded - the employer still pays 15% throughout, even though the employee pays nothing, which is the most frequently missed point. Category K, a state pensioner category, is 0% only up to the Investment Zone threshold and 15% above it, not 0% throughout.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 for tax year 2026-27. The secondary threshold remains at the level set from April 2025 (£96 a week / £5,000 a year) and the rate remains 15%.
scope.how_to_claim: Employer NI is calculated and paid automatically through payroll under RTI. The zero-rate reliefs are not claimed separately - they are applied by using the correct National Insurance category letter for the employee, so the category letter is the control point. Employment Allowance is claimed separately through the Employer Payment Summary.

notes: The secondary threshold of £5,000 a year is far lower than people remember - it was cut from £9,100 in April 2025 and has not moved, so employer NI now bites from roughly £96 a week. Paired with the 15% rate, the cost of a low-paid or part-time hire rose sharply and has stayed there. The reliefs are delivered entirely through the category letter, so a payroll running an under-21 or an under-25 apprentice on category A silently overpays 15% from £96 a week instead of from £967 - a very common and very recoverable error worth auditing. Do not confuse the secondary threshold (employer, £96 a week) with the primary threshold (employee) or the lower earnings limit (£129 a week, which gates statutory payments and benefit entitlement but triggers no contributions). Also note there is no upper cap on employer contributions, unlike the employee side. Employment Allowance, which offsets employer NI for eligible employers, is already in the content bank and is deliberately not covered here.

title: Companies House identity verification for directors and PSCs

figures.what: Date voluntary identity verification opened - individuals could verify with Companies House via GOV.UK One Login or an Authorised Corporate Service Provider (ACSP) from this date

Date identity verification became a legal requirement for directors (and equivalents) and PSCs, and the start of the 12-month transition period. The Companies House campaign site still states in terms, checked again today: 'This date is not a deadline. It marks the start of a 12-month transition period'

Transition period for people already registered as directors or PSCs before 18 November 2025 - so it closes on 18 November 2026, tomorrow. It is a window, not a single deadline: within it each person's own due date is set by their company's confirmation statement date (directors, and PSCs who are also directors) or their birth month (PSCs who are not directors)

figures.value: next confirmation statement on or after 18 November 2025
figures.what: The actual deadline rule for an existing director: give your Companies House personal code in the company's next confirmation statement. A director of more than one company must do it for each. Overseas companies must confirm all directors have verified by the anniversary of registration of the UK establishment

Window in which a PSC must give their personal code via the 'Provide identity verification details for a PSC' service. For a PSC who is also a director of the same company the 14 days start the day AFTER the company's confirmation statement date. For a PSC who is not a director the window is the first 14 days of their birth month (a 22 January birthday gives 1-14 January). A PSC added after 18 November 2025 can give the code when first added or within 14 days of being added. Filing an early confirmation statement does not move these dates. Companies House says the dates of your 14-day period can be checked on the public register

Extension the registrar may grant to a PSC's identity verification due date, requested online before the deadline passes. A PSC granted an extension stays compliant. After 2 digital extensions a further request goes to an examiner with supporting evidence

How long Companies House says it will pause enforcement if it accepts a written representation about extenuating circumstances. Representations received outside the timeframe Companies House gives are not considered, and its decision is final

Length of the Companies House personal code given to a person once they have verified. It belongs to the individual, not the company; the same code covers all their appointments; it can be shared with someone trusted to file on their behalf
Companies House press-release estimate of the number of individuals who will need to verify their identity by mid-November 2026

The figure used on the Companies House outline transition plan (policy paper, still last updated 23 October 2026 when read today) for individuals on the register requiring identity verification - higher than the '6 to 7 million' press-release estimate. Quote whichever source you cite

First Insolvency Service prosecutions for identity verification offences, at City of London Magistrates' Court: fines of £166, £307 and £80, each plus £85 costs and a victim surcharge. One director had verified herself but was fined for not stopping a co-director acting while unverified. Proof that enforcement is already live for people who missed their own due dates, well before general compliance activity starts

Cost of verifying directly with Companies House using GOV.UK One Login - 'It is free of charge'. Verifying through an ACSP instead is not free: the ACSP 'may charge a fee for their services' and Companies House does not set or publish that fee

figures.value: no earlier than the end of 2026
figures.what: When Companies House still expects, as at today, to complete the transition period for all individuals on the register requiring identity verification and 'start compliance activity against those who have failed to verify their identity'. No firmer date has been announced

The offence an unverified director commits by continuing to act. Companies House: 'It is unlawful for a director to act as a director without completing identity verification.' The company may also be in breach for failing to rectify it, and Companies House may refer the case to The Insolvency Service

The point at which Companies House says non-compliance is likely to be treated as serious. Prosecution may lead to a criminal conviction, director disqualification and fines. Companies House calls this a guideline for its decision making, not a rule

The registrar's published fixed financial penalty scale - minor £250/500/750/1,000, serious £500/750/1,000/1,500, very serious £750/1,000/1,500/2,000 for a first, second, third and fourth-or-later penalty. IMPORTANT: this document does not mention identity verification and the identity-verification non-compliance guidance does not cross-refer to it, so do not state this as the fine for not verifying
The statutory transitional period for existing directors and PSCs - SI 2025/1118 reg. 4, so it ended at the end of 17 November 2026
The last existing non-director PSC appointed day, for November birthdays - with the 14-day window, the final existing-PSC deadline closed on 14 November 2026 (SI 2025/1118 reg. 5)
Date by which Companies House says all companies must have met the identity verification requirement or be on a compliance or enforcement pathway

Verified appointments as at 11 November 2026 - 7.32m directors, 4.54m PSCs, 135,000 LLP members, being 85.55% of those due; 88.1% of companies had met the confirmation-statement-linked requirement and 11.4% were on a compliance or enforcement pathway

scope.nation: UK-wide (England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland). Companies House is a UK-wide registrar and the requirement comes from the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 amending the Companies Act 2006; there is no separate devolved rule. Guidance is also published in Welsh.
scope.who: Individual directors of UK companies and their equivalents - LLP members, general partners and managing officers; directors of overseas companies registered in the UK; individual people with significant control (PSCs); and Authorised Corporate Service Providers (ACSPs). Applies both to people appointed or registered on or after 18 November 2025 and to everyone already on the register before that date. Verification is normally needed only once per person - Companies House says 'you must not verify again unless we tell you to' - but the personal code must then be linked to each company role separately.
scope.excluded: Shareholders who are not PSCs, employees, and company secretaries do not have to verify - Companies House lists only directors (and equivalents), PSCs and ACSPs as the people who must verify by law. Specifically outside the requirement as at 17 November 2026: sole traders (not registered at Companies House); corporate or legal-entity PSCs, including relevant legal entities (RLEs); a PSC who has died (Companies House confirms no verification is needed and the PSC stays on the register until a grant of probate or letters of administration is received). Deferred to a later date, so not yet required: people who file at Companies House on a company's behalf (expected no earlier than November 2027, with at least 6 months' notice - this group was removed from the 'who needs to verify' guidance on 1 June 2026), limited partnerships, corporate directors, corporate LLP members, and officers of corporate PSCs.
scope.from_when: Voluntary from 8 April 2025. A legal requirement from 18 November 2025 for new incorporations and new appointments (SI 2025/1118 reg. 2(1)). For people already on the register before 18 November 2025: during the transitional period of 12 months beginning with 18 November 2025 (SI 2025/1118 reg. 4), which ENDED at the end of 17 November 2026. Within that period each person's own due date was set individually - for directors, by the company's next confirmation statement falling in the period (and if the company delivered none in the period, with the next one after); for a PSC who is also a director, within 14 days of the confirmation statement date; for a PSC who is not a director, within the first 14 days of their birth month, by appointed day running from December 2025 (December birthdays) through to 1 November 2026 (November birthdays). A company with an overdue confirmation statement at 18 November 2025 had its s.167M deferral end at the earlier of compliance or the end of 2 December 2025. Companies House says all companies must have met the requirement or be on a compliance or enforcement pathway by the end of March 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: The individual must act. Verify once, either free with Companies House using GOV.UK One Login (online, or in person at a participating Post Office with the right documents) or through an Authorised Corporate Service Provider, which may charge. You are then given your 11-character personal code. You must then actively link it to each role: a director gives the code in the company's confirmation statement; a PSC gives it through the 'Provide identity verification details for a PSC' service within their own 14-day window. Someone who is both a director and a PSC of the same company must do both separately. Nothing happens automatically and no one does it for you - an accountant can file using your code but cannot verify your identity on your behalf, and Companies House says it cannot verify identities for people either.

notes: RE-CHECKED 18 November 2026, the first day AFTER the transition period. CORRECTION to the previous entry: the transitional period is '12 months beginning with 18th November 2025' (SI 2025/1118 reg. 4), so it ended at the end of 17 November 2026 - NOT on 18 November 2026. Today is the first day after it, not its last day. Companies House's own prose nowhere states an end date: the campaign site says only 'a 12-month transition period' and still carries the words 'This date is not a deadline.' The position today: the transitional period is over; every existing non-director PSC window closed by 14 November 2026 at the latest (the last birth-month appointed day was 1 November 2026, with a 14-day window); but existing DIRECTORS' individual due dates still trail into late November 2026, because a confirmation statement dated as late as 17 November 2026 carries a 14-day filing window. Companies House published a news story on 18 November 2026 marking one year of mandatory verification, with register-wide figures. Enforcement is live against people whose own due dates have passed - three directors were fined on 16 September 2026 - but no wave of penalties landed today, and Companies House's transition plan still says general compliance activity starts 'no earlier than the end of 2026'. The single most misreported point therefore stands: 18 November 2026 was not a cliff-edge on which non-verifiers were fined. The next real milestone is the end of March 2027, by which Companies House says all companies must have met the requirement or be on a compliance or enforcement pathway. On penalties: a published fixed-penalty scale does exist (£250 to £2,000 depending on seriousness and how many times), but that document does NOT mention identity verification and the identity-verification non-compliance document does NOT cross-refer to it. So the honest line is 'the registrar's published fixed-penalty scale runs £250 to £2,000', never 'the fine for not verifying is £250'. Whether that scale is in fact applied to identity verification offences is NOT VERIFIED. The campaign site's wider line ('you will not be able to make any filings for your company or start a new company') is broader than the guidance - do not quote it as a mechanism. Verification is free via GOV.UK One Login; an ACSP may charge a fee that Companies House does not publish.

title: Companies House filing fees

figures.what: incorporating a company - digital (online) or by software
incorporating a company - paper
same-day incorporation (software filing only)
confirmation statement - digital or software (first statement in the 12-month payment period)
confirmation statement - paper
change of company name - digital or software
change of company name - paper
same-day change of company name (online and software)
same-day reduction of capital by solvency statement (paper, upload service only)
date the current round of Companies House fee increases took effect

scope.who: Anyone incorporating or running a UK company, LLP or other registrable entity: the fee is payable by whoever makes the filing, so by the company, its directors, or its accountant or formation agent acting for it.
scope.excluded: Fees are not charged on every filing. There is no fee for filing annual accounts, for appointing or removing a director or secretary, for changing a registered office address, for changing a company's accounting reference date, or for the second and later confirmation statements filed within the same 12-month payment period - the £50 covers only the first statement in that period. Companies House fees are also not refundable where a filing is rejected for error, and they are not the same as, and are not reduced by, any agent or software charge. Late filing penalties are a separate charge and are not fees.
scope.from_when: Current fees took effect on 1 February 2026; the fees publication was last updated 25 September 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Pay the fee at the point of filing: by card or Companies House payment account when filing online or by software, or by cheque or postal order with a paper form. Digital filing is cheaper than paper for every one of these transactions, so filing online is the cost saving. Companies House publishes any fee changes in its fees guidance.

notes: UK-wide, with identical fees across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Companies House is a cost-recovery body and does not make a profit on fees. Commonly confused: the £50 confirmation statement fee is an annual payment period fee, not a per-filing fee, so a company that files several confirmation statements in a 12-month payment period pays once; the confirmation statement fee is entirely separate from the duty to file it on time; and Companies House fees are not tax, so they are not paid to HMRC. Also commonly confused: 'same day' services are priced separately and are only available on some channels (same-day incorporation is software-only). Register of Overseas Entities fees also rose on 1 February 2026 and are covered in the Register of Overseas Entities entry.

title: Changes to small and micro company accounts filing

figures.what: date from which all UK registered companies must file accounts in iXBRL format using commercial software
date after which smaller companies keep the option to remove profit and loss information from the accounts they file (filleting)
extra preparation time given by moving software-only accounts filing from April 2027 to April 2028
date the earlier announcement was withdrawn and replaced, confirming the profit and loss requirement is paused

scope.who: All UK registered companies, for the move to software-only accounts filing from April 2028 - this applies equally to companies that file their own accounts and to those whose accountant or agent files for them. The audit exemption eligibility statement applies to directors of any company claiming an audit exemption, including the dormant company exemption. The limit on shortening the accounting reference period applies to any company changing its period.
scope.excluded: Small companies and micro-entities are NOT, as matters stand, required to file a profit and loss account: that requirement has been paused and has no start date. Companies filing abridged accounts are not losing that option - the government will continue to allow abridged accounts. Smaller companies are not losing the ability to fillet. Non-accounts filings are also out of scope: web filing stays open for the confirmation statement and other non-accounts forms, so only accounts filing moves to software. Entities that are not UK registered companies are outside this.
scope.from_when: April 2028 for software-only iXBRL accounts filing, the stronger audit exemption eligibility statement, filing the component parts of accounts and reports together, and the limit on shortening the accounting reference period. The profit and loss filing requirement for small companies and micro-entities is paused with no date; the filleting option continues after 1 April 2028.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim - this is a compliance change. Before April 2028 a company (or its accountant) must have commercial accounts filing software capable of iXBRL, because the Companies House web and paper accounts filing routes close for accounts. Companies claiming audit exemption will need to file a directors' eligibility statement identifying the exemption and confirming the company qualifies.

notes: UK-wide, identical in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. This is the subject with the biggest gap between what was legislated and what is actually happening, so it is worth being precise. The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 as enacted splits the small and micro filing rules into new sections 443A and 444 of the Companies Act 2006, requires small companies to file a profit and loss account and directors' report, requires micro-entities to file a profit and loss account, and removes the option to file abridged accounts. But those provisions need secondary legislation to commence, and following the Small Business Regulatory Taskforce the government paused the profit and loss requirement and confirmed it will continue to allow abridged accounts. So as at 15 November 2026: abridged accounts are NOT abolished, filleting is NOT abolished, and profit and loss filing is NOT mandatory. What is firmly scheduled is software-only iXBRL accounts filing from April 2028. Commonly confused: the ECCTA company accounts factsheet on gov.uk still describes the removal of abridged accounts and mandatory profit and loss as if they were going ahead, and still quotes the pre-April-2025 small and micro size thresholds, so it should not be used as the current position. Also commonly confused: filleting (leaving the profit and loss out of the public filing) and abridging (preparing a reduced set of accounts with shareholder consent) are two different things, and neither is the same as the small company accounts exemption or audit exemption.

title: The PSC register: duties and the 25% tests

figures.what: condition 1 - an individual who holds more than 25% of the shares in the company
condition 2 - an individual who holds more than 25% of the voting rights in the company

figures.value: over 25% up to 50%, over 50% up to 75%, 75% or more
figures.what: the three bands in which shareholdings and voting rights must be reported
deadline to report new or changed PSC information to Companies House after confirming it
maximum period before a company must confirm its PSC register is accurate if it has not been updated
maximum prison sentence for PSC offences, which can also carry a fine, or both

scope.who: UK companies limited by shares, limited by guarantee and unlimited companies (including dormant companies); unregistered companies; UK Societas; limited liability partnerships; and eligible Scottish partnerships (Scottish limited partnerships and Scottish qualifying partnerships). Each must identify its PSCs, confirm their details and report them to Companies House. An individual who is a PSC must give the company the information it asks for, as must anyone who knows who the PSCs are.
scope.excluded: The PSC requirements do not apply to: companies with voting shares admitted to trading on a UK or EEA regulated market, or on the specified markets in Switzerland, the USA, Japan and Israel listed in Schedule 1 to the Register of People with Significant Control Regulations 2016 (they are covered instead by FCA DTR 5); overseas companies operating in the UK through a UK establishment (they may be caught by home-country beneficial ownership rules instead); mutuals registered by the FCA, such as building societies and co-operative societies; investment vehicles registered by the FCA, such as open-ended investment companies; and Charitable Incorporated Organisations registered with the Charity Commission. Condition 4 (significant influence or control) does not apply where conditions 1 to 3 are already met.
scope.from_when: The PSC regime has applied since 2016 under the Register of People with Significant Control Regulations 2016. From 18 November 2025 the separate local PSC register kept at the company was abolished and Companies House holds the register.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim - this is a duty. The company must take reasonable steps to identify its PSCs, serve notices on people it believes are PSCs or who know who they are, confirm the details (name, date of birth, nationality, country of residence, addresses and the date they became a PSC), and file with Companies House within 14 days of confirming the information or a change. The register must never be left blank: if PSC details cannot be given, the company files a notice explaining why. Where a PSC is at serious risk of violence or intimidation they can apply for their details to be protected.

notes: UK-wide, with eligible Scottish partnerships being the one Scotland-specific feature (SLPs and SQPs are in scope even though they are partnerships, not companies). The five conditions in order: more than 25% of shares; more than 25% of voting rights; the right to appoint or remove a majority of the board; otherwise having or actually exercising significant influence or control; and the trust or firm condition, which catches a trustee or firm member who meets any of the first four (or would if they were an individual) plus anyone with significant influence or control over that trust or firm. Commonly confused: the tests are 'more than 25%', not '25% or more', so an exact 25% holding does not by itself make someone a PSC; shareholdings and voting rights are reported in bands, not as exact percentages; a PSC is not the same thing as a shareholder or a director, and a company can have a director who is not a PSC and a PSC who is not a director; where the company is owned by another entity the rules on registrable relevant legal entities apply instead, and an exempt listed company or building society may still have to be reported as an RLE by a company it controls. Separately, PSCs now also have to verify their identity with Companies House - see the identity verification entry - which is a different duty from being entered on the register.

scope.who: Overseas entities - legal entities governed by the law of a country or territory outside the UK, including the Republic of Ireland, that are a legal person under that law (bodies corporate, partnerships or other entities). They must register, and give Companies House their registrable beneficial owners or managing officers, if they own or want to buy, sell or transfer UK property or land within the scope dates for each nation. Governments and public authorities of other states must register too, even where the land is used officially, such as an embassy.
scope.excluded: Out of scope: UK-incorporated entities, because they are not governed by the law of a country outside the UK; overseas entities that do not own UK land within the scope dates (on or since 1 January 1999 in England and Wales, 8 December 2014 in Scotland, 5 September 2022 in Northern Ireland); and an entity that is not, or is no longer, a registered owner of UK property or land, which can apply to be removed from the register. Dispositions made by statute, by court order or by operation of law do not need to be registered. Separately, certain beneficial owners are exempt from being disclosed - broadly where the interest is held through a legal entity subject to its own disclosure requirements (a PSC-regime entity, an entity with voting shares on a specified market, an eligible Scottish partnership, an entity already on the Register of Overseas Entities, or a regulated foreign trust services provider) - and the Secretary of State may exempt a person from the disclosure duties where necessary for national security or to prevent or detect serious crime. Pension scheme trusts providing benefits for more than 250 people are exempt from the transitional verification requirement and from some update and removal information duties. Governments and public authorities cannot claim an exemption.
scope.from_when: The register opened on 1 August 2022 under the Economic Crime (Transparency and Enforcement) Act 2022, with a registration deadline of 31 January 2023 for entities already holding qualifying property. The update statement duty runs from one year after registration and every year after that. Current fees took effect on 1 February 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Register online with Companies House, paying £250, and give details of the entity and its registrable beneficial owners or managing officers; the information must be verified by a UK-regulated agent. You then receive an overseas entity ID, which the land registries require before the entity can be registered as owner or make a disposition. Every year the entity files an update statement - online, £134, within 14 days of its statement date - reviewing everything on the register and updating anything that has changed, with any changes verified by a UK-regulated agent no more than 3 months before the statement date. The online update service is not currently available where any beneficial owner or managing officer has protected personal information at Companies House, or is awaiting the result of such an application.

notes: UK-wide but with three different start dates, which is the main national difference: England and Wales reach back to 1 January 1999, Scotland to 8 December 2014, and Northern Ireland only to 5 September 2022, so the same entity can be in scope for one nation's land and not another's. Scotland also has its own 'qualifying registrable deeds'. The update statement must be filed even if nothing has changed - it is a confirmation that the register is correct, not a change filing, and this is the single most commonly missed point. Missing it is a criminal offence that can be prosecuted or fined, the overseas entity ID becomes invalid so the entity cannot buy, sell, transfer, lease or charge UK property or land, and a note that the statement has not been filed is added to the public record. Not complying with the Act generally can mean a fine, a prison sentence, or both. Commonly confused: the Register of Overseas Entities is a separate register from the Companies House register of companies, and an overseas company with a UK establishment registered at Companies House is a different thing again; the overseas entity update statement is not the company confirmation statement and has its own date and its own fee; and the beneficial owner test borrows the PSC conditions but the two registers are not interchangeable - an overseas entity does not keep a PSC register.
