scope.who: Any employee or director who has a car made available to them, or to a member of their family or household, by reason of their employment and available for private use. The employer reports the benefit and pays Class 1A National Insurance on it; the employee or director pays income tax on it.
scope.excluded: No car benefit charge arises where: the car is a pool car meeting the pool car conditions; the car is genuinely not available for private use; or the car is made available for reasons unrelated to the employment. The charge is also reduced or removed by periods of unavailability of 30 or more consecutive days (shorter gaps give no reduction, and a replacement car that is not materially better is not separately charged) and by payments the employee is required to make specifically for private use, which can reduce the charge to nil - but payments for services such as petrol or insurance do not count. Certain accessories are left out of the price: those necessary for the job, gas-conversion equipment, disability equipment, mobile phones, accessories added before 1 August 1993, and later accessories costing £100 or less. The new car registration fee is excluded from the list price. Diesel cars certified to Euro standard 6d (RDE2) are exempt from the diesel supplement, as are all non-diesels. Vans and commercial vehicles are outside this charge and have their own van benefit rules.
scope.from_when: The 2026-27 appropriate percentages apply for the tax year 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027. The 4% diesel supplement has applied since 2018-19, and the RDE2 exemption since April 2018.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim - the charge arises automatically once a car is made available for private use. The employer reports it, either by payrolling the benefit (reporting it through PAYE in real time) or on form P11D after the tax year, and pays Class 1A NICs. The calculation is: take the list price published by the manufacturer, importer or distributor on the day before first registration (including standard accessories, VAT and delivery, but excluding the new car registration fee); add qualifying accessories (later accessories over £100); deduct the employee's capital contributions up to £5,000; multiply by the appropriate percentage for the car's CO2 emissions and, for 1-50g/km hybrids, its electric range, adding the 4% diesel supplement if it applies and capping at 37%; then reduce for any days of unavailability and for required private use payments. Where a car is 15 years old or more and worth £15,000 or more, market value less capital contributions replaces the list price. Where two or more chargeable employees share a car concurrently, each benefit is calculated and then reduced on a just and reasonable basis.

notes: UK-wide rules, but the tax paid on the benefit differs by nation because Scotland sets its own income tax rates and bands on non-savings income, so a Scottish taxpayer with the same company car pays a different amount of income tax from an employee in England, Wales or Northern Ireland; the benefit value itself and the employer's Class 1A NICs are identical across the UK. Electric cars are no longer a zero-rated perk: the appropriate percentage for a 0g/km car is 4% in 2026-27 and rises again in later years, so this is worth re-checking each April. For cars first registered on or after 6 April 2020 use the WLTP CO2 figure. Commonly confused: the appropriate percentage is applied to the list price, not to what the employer actually paid, so a discounted or second-hand purchase does not reduce the benefit; capital contributions are capped at £5,000 while private use payments are uncapped but must be required and specifically for private use; the car benefit and the car fuel benefit are two separate charges, and providing electricity for an electric company car is not a fuel benefit; and the electric range bands only matter for cars emitting 1 to 50g/km. Caution for content: chapter 12 of booklet 480 still carries engine-size percentage tables for cars with no CO2 figure that were last updated in April 2021, so those particular figures should not be quoted as current.

title: Trivial benefits exemption for employees and directors

figures.what: maximum cost of providing a single benefit for the trivial benefits exemption to apply
annual cap on exempt trivial benefits where the employer is a close company and the recipient is a director or other office holder, or a member of their family or household
date from which the statutory trivial benefits exemption applies
number of conditions that must all be met for the exemption to apply

scope.who: All employees and directors, and members of their family or household where the benefit is provided to them by reason of the employment. It also covers a benefit provided by a third party, such as a group management services company, on the employer's behalf, provided the employer ultimately bears the cost. Where the exact cost per person cannot practicably be worked out for a benefit provided to a group, the average cost per employee is used against the £50 limit.
scope.excluded: The exemption does not apply to: cash or a cash voucher; anything the employee is entitled to under a contractual obligation, including under a salary sacrifice arrangement; anything provided in recognition of particular services the employee performs as part of their duties, or in anticipation of such services; and any benefit costing more than £50 to provide. If any of the four conditions fails, the whole benefit is taxed in the normal way (subject to any other exemption or deduction) - it is not just the excess that is taxed. For a close company, exempt trivial benefits to a director or other office holder, or to their family or household, stop at £300 of total cost in the tax year, and benefits above that cap are taxable. Rank-and-file employees of a close company are not subject to the £300 cap.
scope.from_when: Benefits provided from 6 April 2016, under section 323A ITEPA 2003. HMRC's earlier non-statutory approach for 2015-16 and before is in EIM21860.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim and nothing to report. Where the four conditions are met the benefit is exempt automatically, so it does not go on a P11D, is not payrolled, and carries no Class 1 or Class 1A National Insurance. Employers should keep a record of trivial benefits given, and close companies in particular need a running total per director and per family or household member so the £300 annual cap is not breached.

notes: UK-wide, identical in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland - and because the benefit is exempt there is no Scottish income tax difference to worry about here. For most owner-managed companies, which are close companies, the practical position is £50 per benefit and £300 per director per tax year, and the £300 cap applies separately to the director's family or household members where benefits are provided to them. Commonly confused: the £50 is a cap on the cost of providing each individual benefit, not an annual allowance, so an employee of a non-close company can receive any number of £50 benefits; a benefit costing £51 is wholly taxable, not taxable on £1; the £300 cap is not a fifth condition but a separate restriction for close companies; and trivial benefits are completely separate from the annual staff entertaining exemption for an annual function (the separate £150 per head limit), from long service awards, and from the rules on gift vouchers - a non-cash gift voucher can qualify as a trivial benefit, but a cash voucher cannot. Also note that providing a trivial benefit does not stop the £150 per head annual function exemption being used as well, as they are different exemptions.

title: Associated companies and the marginal relief thresholds

figures.what: lower profit limit - the small profits rate applies at or below this and marginal relief starts above it
upper profit limit - the main rate applies above this and marginal relief stops at it

figures.value: number of associated companies plus one
figures.what: the divisor applied to both the £50,000 and £250,000 limits
the divided limits where a company has three other associated companies (limits divided by four)
corporation tax main rate, applying to profits over £250,000
corporation tax small profits rate, applying to profits of £50,000 or less
date from which marginal relief and the two profit limits apply

scope.who: UK resident companies with taxable profits between the lower and upper limits. Two companies are associated if one has control of the other, or if both are under the control of the same person or persons (section 18E CTA 2010), with 'control' having the same meaning as for close companies under sections 450 and 451 CTA 2010. A company counts as associated even if it was associated for only part of the accounting period, and it counts regardless of where it is tax resident - so an overseas company controlled by the same person still divides the limits. Where a person controls more than one company, every one of those companies has its limits divided by the total number of associated companies plus one.
scope.excluded: Marginal relief cannot be claimed by: non-UK resident companies; close investment holding companies; and companies whose profits exceed the upper limit of £250,000, including where that is reached by adding distributions received from unrelated, unassociated companies. Companies with profits of £50,000 or less do not need marginal relief because they pay the 19% small profits rate. When counting associated companies, a company that has not carried on any trade or business at any time in the accounting period is disregarded, and a company associated for only part of the period that carried on no trade or business in that part is also disregarded.
scope.from_when: 1 April 2023, when the 25% main rate, the 19% small profits rate and the £50,000 and £250,000 limits were introduced.
scope.how_to_claim: The company works out its associated companies for the accounting period, divides both the £50,000 and £250,000 limits by the number of associated companies plus one, reduces the limits proportionately again if the accounting period is shorter than 12 months, and then calculates marginal relief on profits falling between the adjusted limits. The result is reflected in the Company Tax Return; HMRC publishes a Marginal Relief calculator on its marginal relief guidance page. Where an accounting period straddles two financial years with different limits or fractions, or where the number of associated companies changes during the period, HMRC's worked examples are at CTM03955, CTM03956 and CTM03957.

notes: UK-wide: corporation tax is not devolved, so the rates, limits and associated company rules are the same in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. This is the single biggest trap for a client who owns more than one company: a person with four companies does not get £50,000 of small profits band four times - each company's lower limit becomes £12,500 and its upper limit £62,500, so a company making £70,000 pays the full 25% main rate even though £70,000 would attract marginal relief if it stood alone. Commonly confused: the associated companies test from 1 April 2023 is a control test under section 18E CTA 2010, not the 51% group companies test that applied for the quarterly instalment payments and for the 2015-2023 single-rate period - the two are different and the 51% test still matters elsewhere; associated companies are counted even if associated for only part of the period, so incorporating or acquiring a second company mid-year still divides the limits for that period; non-trading and genuinely dormant companies are disregarded in the count, so a dormant holding or shelf company is not automatically a problem; and a non-UK resident company can be an associated company that divides your limits even though it cannot itself claim marginal relief. The lower and upper limits are also reduced for short accounting periods, which stacks with the associated companies division.

title: VAT bad debt relief: the 6-month rule

figures.what: VAT Notice 700/18 sections 2.2 (condition 5) and 2.3 - the debt must have remained unpaid for 6 months after the later of the date payment was due and payable and the date of supply
VAT Notice 700/18 section 2.3 - time limit to make the claim, running from the later of the payment due date and the date of supply (supplies made after 30 April 1997)

VAT Notice 700/18 sections 2.4 and 5.3 - the claim is made by including the VAT in box 4 of the VAT Return for the period in which the conditions are met; it cannot be claimed on a return for an earlier period (section 2.3)
VAT Notice 700/18 section 2.8 - records (copy VAT invoices and the separate bad debt account) must be kept for 4 years from the date the claim is made

VAT Notice 700/18 sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.6 - the mirror obligation on the customer: a business that has not paid its supplier within 6 months of the relevant date must repay the input tax by a negative entry reducing box 4

scope.who: A VAT-registered business that has accounted for and paid VAT on a supply, has written the debt off in its day-to-day VAT accounts and transferred it to a separate bad debt account, and where the debt has gone unpaid for 6 months after the later of the due date and the date of supply (VAT Notice 700/18 section 2.2).
scope.excluded: Businesses on the Cash Accounting Scheme and certain retail schemes do not need the relief, because they only account for VAT on amounts actually received (section 2.2). Also excluded: debts factored or sold under an absolute/valid legal assignment, and any debt still assigned to a factor (sections 2.2 condition 4 and 3.12); debts paid in full by a guarantor or other third party, with partial payment reducing the claim (section 3.10); supplies made before a business transfer unless the purchaser also took over the VAT registration on form VAT68 (section 5.1); any amount by which the value of the supply exceeded the customary selling price (section 2.2 condition 3); and claims made outside the 4 year 6 month window (section 2.3). Where a Margin Scheme was used, relief is capped at the VAT on the margin (section 5.7). A credit note cannot be used instead, simply because the customer has not paid (section 5.6).
scope.from_when: Current rules apply to supplies made after 30 April 1997. Older supplies carry extra conditions: for goods supplied before 19 March 1997 ownership must have passed to the customer or through them to a third party, and for supplies to a VAT-registered customer between 26 November 1996 and 30 April 1997 a notice must have been sent to the customer and a copy kept (VAT Notice 700/18 sections 2.2 conditions 6 and 7, and 2.6 to 2.7).
scope.how_to_claim: Write the debt off in the VAT accounts and move it to a separate bad debt account, then include the VAT in box 4 of the VAT Return for the period in which all the conditions are first met (sections 2.4 and 5.3). Keep copies of the VAT invoices and the bad debt account, showing the amount written off, the VAT claimed and the customer's name, for 4 years from the claim (sections 2.5 and 2.8).

notes: Commonly confused with simply issuing a credit note, which section 5.6 says cannot be done merely because a customer has not paid. Also commonly confused with the writing-off of a debt for corporation tax or income tax purposes, which is a separate matter on a different timetable. The customer-side rule is the point most often missed: section 4.1 obliges a business that has not paid a supplier within 6 months to repay the input tax it already claimed, whether or not the supplier ever claims the relief. Businesses on cash accounting have no need of the relief at all. No nation differences - VAT is UK-wide, and bad debt relief is unaffected by the Northern Ireland Protocol/Windsor Framework, which bears on goods rather than on debt relief.

title: Zero rate VAT on energy-saving materials

figures.what: VAT Notice 708/6 sections 1.1 and 2.1 - zero rate on the installation of certain specified energy-saving materials, from 1 May 2023 to 31 March 2027
VAT Notice 708/6 sections 1.1 and 2.1 - the period of the time-limited zero rate
VAT Notice 708/6 section 2.1 - from 1 April 2027 onwards these installations revert to the reduced rate of VAT of 5%

VAT Notice 708/6 sections 2.7, 2.14, 2.18, 2.19, 2.20 and 2.22 - date water source heat pumps, electricity-storage batteries, smart diverters and the groundworks/dredging needed to install ground or water source heat pumps were added, and the date the relief was extended to buildings used solely for a relevant charitable purpose
VAT Notice 708/6 section 2.21 - an institution counts as residential accommodation where it is the sole or main residence of at least 90% of its residents

scope.nation: UK-wide, including Northern Ireland from 1 May 2023. VAT Notice 708/6 section 2.2 records that Northern Ireland applied the 5% reduced rate to residential installations from 1 October 2019 to 30 April 2023; the zero rate applies there from 1 May 2023.
scope.who: The installer makes a zero-rated supply when installing specified energy-saving materials in residential accommodation, and from 1 February 2024 also in a building used solely for a relevant charitable purpose (VAT Notice 708/6 sections 2.1, 2.21 and 2.22). Residential accommodation covers houses, blocks of flats and other dwellings, armed forces residential accommodation, children's homes, care homes for elderly, disabled or dependent people, hospices, monasteries, nunneries and similar religious communities, student or pupil accommodation, self-catering holiday accommodation, caravans used as permanent habitation, houseboats designed for permanent habitation, and institutions that are the sole or main residence of at least 90% of their residents (section 2.21).
scope.excluded: Supplying the materials without installing them is standard-rated (VAT Notice 708/6 section 2.3) - this is the single most common trap. Hospitals, prisons, hotels and inns are standard-rated (section 2.21). Standard-rated items include other energy-efficient products such as boilers (unless grant-funded under section 3), double glazing and fridge freezers (section 2.23); multi-fuel and dual-fuel boilers, stand-alone wood-burning stoves and log stores (section 2.17); portable (not permanently fixed) air source heat pumps (section 2.15); and curtains and carpets (section 2.10). Unrelated work carried out in the same job, such as building an extension, is standard-rated (section 2.5.2).
scope.from_when: 1 May 2023 for the zero rate (UK-wide, including Northern Ireland). Water source heat pumps, electricity-storage batteries, smart diverters, the associated groundworks/dredging, and the extension to relevant charitable purpose buildings all apply from 1 February 2024. The zero rate ends 31 March 2027 and the rate reverts to 5% from 1 April 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. The installer applies the zero rate to its own invoice for the qualifying installation, so the customer simply pays no VAT on it. The customer makes no application to HMRC. Where a job mixes qualifying installation with unrelated work, the installer must apportion and standard-rate the unrelated element (section 2.5.2).

notes: The qualifying list in section 2.7 and following is: controls for central heating and hot water systems (2.8), draught stripping (2.9), insulation (2.10), solar panels (2.11), wind turbines (2.12), water turbines (2.13), ground source heat pumps (2.14), permanently fixed air source heat pumps (2.15), micro combined heat and power units (2.16), wood-fuelled boilers (2.17), and from 1 February 2024 water source heat pumps (2.18), batteries storing electricity (2.19) and smart diverters (2.20). Most commonly confused with the separate grant-funded heating supplies relief in section 3 of the same notice, and with the general 5% reduced rate on domestic fuel and power in VAT Notice 701/19, which is a different thing entirely. Also note that installing energy-saving materials during the construction of a new dwelling is zero-rated anyway under section 2.6, through the new-build rules rather than through this relief. Nation point: the relief now runs the same across all four nations, but Northern Ireland reached the zero rate only on 1 May 2023 after a period at 5%, so pre-May-2023 Northern Ireland jobs follow the old treatment.

title: VAT margin scheme for second-hand goods

figures.what: Rate of VAT applied to the margin (the difference between what you paid for the item and what you sold it for) rather than to the full selling price
The VAT due figure that must be recorded against each sale in the stock book
Retention period for margin scheme VAT records; where stock bought more than 6 years ago is still to be sold under the scheme, the records must be kept until the item is sold

scope.who: A VAT-registered business selling eligible second-hand goods, works of art, antiques or collectors' items on which it was not charged VAT when it bought them, and which keeps the required stock book and purchase and sales invoices.
scope.excluded: Any item bought on which VAT was charged cannot go into the scheme, nor can precious metals, investment gold or precious stones. A business that does not meet all the scheme's requirements - in particular the stock book and invoicing conditions - must account for VAT on the full selling price of each item rather than on the margin. Separate rules apply to, and so are out of scope of the general scheme, second-hand vehicles, horses and ponies, houseboats and caravans, unredeemed pawns, auctioneers, agents, hire purchase and part-exchange goods, joint purchases and shares, imports and exports, and goods bought and sold between Northern Ireland and the EU; high volume low value stock may instead use the Global Accounting Scheme.
scope.from_when: Available now, with no start date to wait for - the scheme can be adopted at any time simply by keeping the correct records and reporting the sales on the VAT Return.
scope.how_to_claim: Optional, and self-applied: choose to use it, keep a stock book recording for each purchase a stock number in numerical sequence, the purchase date, the purchase invoice number, the purchase price, the seller's name and an item description, and for each sale the sale date, sales invoice number, selling price or method of disposal, buyer's name, the margin and the VAT due at one-sixth. Obtain a purchase invoice and issue a sales invoice showing the total price without VAT shown separately, the stock book number and one of the margin scheme phrases - 'margin scheme - second hand goods', 'margin scheme - works of art' or 'margin scheme - collectors' items and antiques'. Report the sales on the VAT Return. Keep the records for 6 years.
scope.notes_on_source: VAT Notices 718 and 718/1 are marked [Withdrawn] on GOV.UK as at 2026-11-15; the live primary guidance is the GOV.UK margin schemes guide and its sub-pages, supported by HMRC manual VATMARG.

notes: The two points most often got wrong: VAT is one-sixth of the margin, not one-sixth of the selling price, and the sales invoice must not show VAT separately - showing it defeats the scheme. An item bought with VAT charged on it can never be sold under the margin scheme, which catches businesses buying from other VAT-registered traders outside the scheme. Commonly confused with the Flat Rate Scheme and with the Global Accounting Scheme: Global Accounting is a variant of the margin scheme for high volume, low price items where individual stock-book tracking is impractical. Second-hand vehicles are the biggest carve-out and have their own dedicated guidance, so motor traders should not be pointed at the general scheme. Nation point: VAT is UK-wide, but the Northern Ireland Protocol/Windsor Framework affects goods, and HMRC publishes separate guidance for using a margin scheme when buying and selling goods between Northern Ireland and the EU - a Northern Ireland trader dealing with the EU must read that page, not just the general one. Note also that bad debt relief interacts with this scheme: relief is capped at the VAT on the margin (VAT Notice 700/18 section 5.7).

Only one claim can be made under the scheme; further invoices or information can be sent in support of that existing claim
The postal claim form for new houses; claims can alternatively be made through the HMRC online service

scope.who: A private individual building a new home for their own or their relatives' residential or holiday use - either constructing a new dwelling or buying a shell from a developer and fitting it out - where planning permission is in place and the building meets the definition of a dwelling (self-contained accommodation, no direct internal access to another dwelling, and planning consent). Also a person constructing a new charity building for a charitable or relevant residential purpose.
scope.excluded: Anyone whose planning permission prohibits the property from being sold or used separately from another building cannot claim. Anyone who intends to sell or let the property, or use it for another business purpose, cannot claim - and a home built because the claimant needs to live where they work counts as a business purpose. Buildings that do not meet the dwelling definition are out, including a loft conversion into a flat. Conversions of existing buildings are outside this guidance and run on separate rules and a separate form (VAT431C). Property developers are effectively outside the scheme, since their sales of new houses are zero-rated and the scheme exists for people building their own homes. Contractor services cannot be reclaimed, because a contractor building a qualifying new dwelling must zero-rate its services, so there is no VAT on them to recover. Non-reclaimable items are fitted furniture other than fitted kitchen furniture and the materials to build it (with narrow exceptions for basic wardrobes and storage built into the fabric of the building); most electrical and gas appliances such as washing machines, dryers, fridges, freezers, doorbells and electric doors or gates (though some heating, ventilation, alarm and lift equipment does qualify); carpets, underlay and carpet tiles; garden ornaments, sheds and greenhouses; plant, tools and equipment, which covers tool hire; consumables not incorporated into the building; and building land. Late claims are excluded by the time limit.
scope.from_when: The scheme is long-standing; the current 6-month time limit applies to buildings completed on or after 5 December 2023, with 3 months applying to earlier completions.
scope.how_to_claim: Make a single claim within 6 months of completion (3 months if completed before 5 December 2023), either through the HMRC online service or by posting form VAT431NB to BT&C VAT, HM Revenue and Customs, BX9 1WR. The claim must include the building regulation completion certificate (copies accepted), evidence of planning permission, and plans of the building. HMRC does not accept hand-delivered or dropped-off claims and does not return original documents, so originals should not be sent.

notes: The scheme exists to put the self-builder in the same position as a buyer of a new house from a developer, which is why only materials are recoverable: a contractor's services on a qualifying new build should already be zero-rated, and if a contractor has charged 20% the answer is to go back to the contractor, not to claim it here. The single-claim rule and the time limit together are where most claims fail - the 6-month clock runs from completion, so the claim is prepared, not started, at completion. Commonly confused with the conversion version of the scheme (form VAT431C, different rules), with the 5% reduced rate for residential conversions and renovations in VAT Notice 708, and with the energy-saving materials relief. The 'no separate use or disposal' planning condition catches annexes and granny flats more often than people expect. No nation differences in the VAT treatment - it runs UK-wide - although building regulations and planning regimes differ by nation, which affects the completion certificate and planning evidence a claimant supplies rather than the VAT entitlement itself.

title: Zero rate VAT on young children's clothing and footwear

figures.what: VAT Notice 714 section 1.3 - all four must be met: it must be an article of clothing or footwear, not made of fur, designed for young children, and suitable only for young children

figures.value: under 14 (up to the eve of the 14th birthday)
figures.what: VAT Notice 714 sections 4.2, 4.2.2, 4.3.2 and 4.4.1 - the age the article must be designed for; the measurements are based on children up to the eve of their 14th birthday
VAT Notice 714 section 4.2 - maximum measurement for shirts and knitwear; chest measured 2.5cm below the armhole and doubled, garment flat with buttons fastened
VAT Notice 714 section 4.2 - maximum measurement for trousers and shorts

figures.value: Boys chest 109cm / girls 110cm (jackets and waistcoats); boys 114cm / girls 115cm (top coats and outerwear)
figures.what: VAT Notice 714 section 4.2 - maximum chest measurements for outer garments

figures.value: Boys up to and including shoe size 6.5; girls up to and including size 3; true unisex up to and including size 5.5
figures.what: VAT Notice 714 sections 4.3 and 4.3.3 - footwear size limits. Other girls' shoes also qualify in sizes 3.5 to 5.5 where the heel height does not exceed the sole depth by more than 4cm; girls' court shoes (low cut, no straps or fastenings) are limited to size 3

figures.value: Height boys 163cm / girls 161cm; chest boys 84cm / girls 85cm; waist boys 70cm / girls 69cm; hips boys 85cm / girls 90cm
figures.what: VAT Notice 714 section 4.2.2 - the body measurements of the under-14 child the garment must be designed for, which can allow zero rating regardless of garment size

figures.value: Lifejackets 52kg maximum body weight; teen bras size 34B; leotards/body stockings shoulder to crotch 70cm; tights 51cm lightweight and 56cm heavyweight
figures.what: VAT Notice 714 section 4.2 table - maximum limits for specific named items
VAT Notice 714 section 3 - fur trim is disregarded unless it covers more than one-fifth of the surface area (or, for new garments, costs more than the material)

scope.who: Any supplier selling an article of clothing or footwear that meets all four conditions in VAT Notice 714 section 1.3 - clothing or footwear, not made of fur skin, designed for young children (under 14), and suitable only for young children. Suitability is normally shown by the article being 'held out for sale' for young children, which section 5.2 says covers labelling, packaging, display, invoicing and advertising.
scope.excluded: Articles wholly or partly of fur skin are standard-rated, though artificial fur can be zero-rated (section 3). Items that are not clothing at all are standard-rated whatever their size: reflective armbands, buoyancy aids, fastenings, badges, patches, hand muffs and ear muffs (section 2.2), and alice bands, hair ribbons and slides, scrunchies, sports headbands and sun visors (section 4.4.2). Novelty, party and play hats are standard-rated as toys (section 4.4.2). Garments sold in one size to fit both children and adults cannot be zero-rated (section 4.2.3). Anything exceeding the section 4.2 measurements needs HMRC's prior written agreement before it can be zero-rated (section 4.2.1), and goods labelled to fit sizes above the section 4.2.2 body-measurement table fail the suitability test (section 5.2). Alteration, repair and embroidery are not zero-rated (section 9.2). Face masks qualify only if specifically designed and held out for young children, and not where design and packaging are unclear (section 4.4.2). Goods that were zero-rated when bought are not automatically zero-rated when sold on (section 5.2).
scope.from_when: Long-standing relief, in force now. No pending change identified at primary source as at 2026-11-15.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. The retailer applies the zero rate at the till, so the customer pays no VAT. The onus is on the supplier to satisfy the four conditions and to be able to evidence the size and 'held out for sale' tests; larger-than-standard sizes require HMRC's written agreement in advance under section 4.2.1.

notes: The test is the design and marketing of the garment, not the age of the actual wearer - an adult can buy a zero-rated child-size garment, and a large 13-year-old buying an adult-size garment pays VAT. Sections 5.1 and 5.2 frame it as suitability plus 'held out for sale', and the notice does not make the wearer's real age relevant. Protective equipment is often wrongly assumed to be excluded: cycle helmets are zero-rated irrespective of size, other helmets such as skateboarding or ice hockey qualify up to 59cm if designed and marketed exclusively for children, and riding hats qualify up to size 6 3/4 (sections 2.2, 4.2, 4.4.1). Sports footwear such as ice and roller skating boots, studded football boots and ballet shoes counts as footwear and simply has to meet the size test in section 4.3 (section 2.3). Hire is often missed: hire of a zero-rated item can be zero-rated, including nappy hire, and skate and bowling shoe hire follows the footwear size criteria, but where a single admission price includes footwear a single-or-multiple-supply analysis is needed (section 9.3). School uniforms need an agreement with a school that is exclusively for pupils under 14 (section 6.1). Elasticated waistbands are measured at full stretch, and garments with no fastening can be zero-rated up to a stretched waist of 85cm for boys or 90cm for girls (section 4.2 footnote). Commonly confused with VAT on children's car seats (reduced rate, separate rules) and with children's food. No nation differences.

title: VAT partial exemption and the de minimis limits

figures.what: VAT Notice 706 section 11.2 - the de minimis monetary limit for exempt input tax, applied as a monthly average over the tax period or longer period

figures.value: half (50%) of total input tax in the relevant period
figures.what: VAT Notice 706 section 11.2 - the second limb of the de minimis test; section 11.6 confirms both conditions must be met to pass the de minimis test

figures.value: Simplified test one: total input tax no more than £625 per month on average AND exempt supplies no more than 50% of all supplies
figures.what: VAT Notice 706 section 11.7 - the first simplified de minimis test

figures.value: Simplified test two: total input tax less input tax directly attributable to taxable supplies no more than £625 per month on average AND exempt supplies no more than 50% of all supplies
figures.what: VAT Notice 706 section 11.7 - the second simplified de minimis test
HMRC Partial Exemption Manual PE24500 - the legal basis for the de minimis limit, with regulation 106 providing for the de minimis limit itself

figures.value: Value of taxable supplies in the period excluding VAT / total value of supplies in the period excluding VAT x 100
figures.what: VAT Notice 706 section 4.3 - the standard method formula giving the recoverable percentage of residual input tax

VAT Notice 706 section 12.2 - the length of the tax year, which is the normal longer period for the annual adjustment; section 12.1 confirms the input tax claimed in each tax period is provisional and is reviewed at the end of the longer period

scope.who: A business that makes, or intends to make, both taxable and exempt supplies and incurs input tax relating to both - such a business is classified as partly exempt (VAT Notice 706 section 2.1). A partly exempt business that passes a de minimis test may recover all of its exempt input tax as well as its taxable input tax.
scope.excluded: A business whose exempt input tax exceeds either limb of the test fails de minimis, and section 11.3 then says that normally it cannot claim any of its exempt input tax - exempt input tax above the limit is generally irrecoverable, though it is still used in the standard method calculation (section 4.9 step 7). Both conditions must be met: passing the £625 monthly average but failing the 50% test, or vice versa, is a fail (section 11.6). A business making only taxable supplies, or only exempt supplies, is not partly exempt and the de minimis rules do not apply to it. In-year recovery is provisional only: under the annual test in section 11.11 a business that fails the test at year-end must repay the exempt input tax it provisionally recovered in-year, and under section 12.1 the input tax claimed in each tax period is provisional and is reviewed at the end of the longer period.
scope.from_when: Long-standing. The £625 monthly average and 50% limits are in force now, under regulations 105 and 106 of the VAT Regulations 1995. No pending change identified at primary source as at 2026-11-15.
scope.how_to_claim: Self-assessed on the VAT Return. Attribute input tax to taxable and to exempt supplies, apportion the residual input tax - under the standard method, taxable supplies excluding VAT divided by total supplies excluding VAT, times 100 (section 4.3) - then test the exempt input tax against the £625 monthly average and the 50% of total input tax limits, or use one of the simplified tests in section 11.7. If de minimis is passed, recover the exempt input tax as well. Recovery in each period is provisional: carry out the annual adjustment at the end of the longer period, normally the 12-month tax year (sections 12.1 to 12.3), and repay provisionally recovered exempt input tax if the annual test is failed (section 11.11).

notes: An annual figure is widely quoted for this limit, but GOV.UK Notice 706 section 11.2 and HMRC manual PE24500 both express the limit only as £625 per month on average, and neither page carries an annual or quarterly equivalent - I checked both and the figures £7,500 and £1,875 do not appear, so no annual figure is reported here. Naming differs between sources and is a common source of confusion: PE24500 sets out three tests, the first being the standard de minimis test in Notice 706 section 11.2 and the second and third corresponding to the two simplified tests in section 11.7. Notice 706 section 11.7 itself describes only test one and test two, with no test three. Separately, section 11.11 provides an annual de minimis test, which allows a business that was de minimis in its previous partial exemption year to treat itself as de minimis in the current year. Commonly confused with exemption itself (which is about the supply, not about input tax recovery) and with the registration threshold, and distinct from the Capital Goods Scheme in Notice 706/2, which runs alongside partial exemption for large capital items. See also PE63500 on the interaction with road fuel scale charges. No nation differences.

title: VAT on business and staff entertainment: what is recoverable

figures.what: VAT Notice 700/65 paragraph 1.2 - 'You cannot recover input tax incurred on the provision of business entertainment expenses'; input tax on entertaining UK business contacts, and non-UK contacts who are not customers, is blocked from recovery under a special legal provision
VAT Notice 700/65 paragraph 3.1 - VAT on staff entertainment such as staff parties, team building and outings is input tax and is not blocked from recovery under the business entertainment rules

VAT Notice 700/65 paragraph 2.1 - entertainment is business entertainment only where all three conditions are met: entertainment is provided, it goes to people who are not employees, and it is provided free. Paragraph 2.2 defines entertainment as 'hospitality of any kind', such as food, drink, accommodation and event tickets

VAT Notice 700/65 paragraph 3.2 - where entertainment is provided only for directors or partners, the VAT incurred is not input tax, so cannot be recovered; but where directors and partners attend staff events alongside other employees, HMRC accepts the tax is input tax and is not blocked

VAT Notice 700/65 paragraph 2.8 table - recovery is allowed and the spending is not treated as business entertainment for recognised sporting bodies providing free accommodation and meals to amateur sports people and officials attending an event, and for airlines providing catering and accommodation to delayed passengers

scope.who: Any VAT-registered business incurring entertainment costs. Input tax on entertaining employees is recoverable (paragraph 3.1). Employees for this purpose include people employed by the business, directors and anyone managing the business including partners, self-employed people for subsistence only, and helpers and stewards essential to sporting events (paragraph 2.3). Input tax on entertaining overseas customers may be recoverable where it is reasonable in scale and character; an overseas customer is any customer not ordinarily resident or carrying on a business in the UK, including the Isle of Man (paragraph 2.6).
scope.excluded: Input tax on business entertainment is blocked and cannot be recovered (paragraph 1.2), which covers entertaining UK business contacts and non-UK contacts who are not customers. Entertainment provided only for directors, partners or sole proprietors is not input tax at all and cannot be recovered (paragraph 3.2). Where an employee hosts non-employees, that is not staff entertainment (paragraph 3.3), and where an event entertains both employees and non-employees only the employee portion is recoverable (paragraph 3.4). Pensioners, former employees, job applicants, and shareholders who are not also employees are not treated as employees, so entertaining them is not staff entertainment (paragraph 2.4). For overseas customers, a private benefit to the person enjoying the entertainment can trigger an output tax charge that cancels out the recovery, and hospitality given out of politeness, out of expectation, or to improve relationships is not for strict business purposes (paragraph 2.6). Where a cost is partly entertainment and partly other business use, only the entertainment part is blocked and the remainder may be recoverable subject to partial exemption (paragraph 2.7).
scope.from_when: Long-standing blocking provision, in force now. No pending change identified at primary source as at 2026-11-15.
scope.how_to_claim: Recover the input tax on qualifying staff entertainment through box 4 of the VAT Return in the normal way, holding a valid VAT invoice. Do not recover input tax on business entertainment. Where an event covers both employees and non-employees, apportion and recover only the employee portion (paragraph 3.4), and where a cost is partly entertainment and partly other business use, apportion under paragraph 2.7.

notes: The line that decides most cases is in paragraph 2.1: it is only business entertainment if the recipients are not employees and it is provided free, which is why a staff Christmas party is recoverable and a client lunch is not. Subsistence is the point most often confused with entertainment - paragraph 2.5 says subsistence for employees working away from their normal base is not business entertainment and is not covered by these rules, with the relevant rules in VAT Notice 700, and paragraph 3.1 repeats that employee and director subsistence is not employee entertainment. The directors-only rule in paragraph 3.2 catches owner-managed companies in particular: a meal out for the directors alone is not input tax, but the same directors at the staff party are fine. The overseas customer rule is often oversold: recovery is available in principle, but the private benefit output tax charge in paragraph 2.6 frequently cancels it out, so it is rarely a clean win. Commonly confused with the separate income tax and NIC treatment of staff entertaining, including the annual function exemption, which is a different regime on different figures, and with VAT Notice 700/7 on business promotions and gifts. No nation differences.

title: Stamp Duty Land Tax: residential rates and First Time Buyers' Relief

figures.what: SDLT on the portion of the price up to £125,000 (standard residential rates, single main home)
SDLT on the portion from £125,001 to £250,000
SDLT on the portion from £250,001 to £925,000
SDLT on the portion from £925,001 to £1.5 million
SDLT on the portion above £1.5 million
First Time Buyers' Relief: nil-rate threshold - no SDLT on the first £300,000
First Time Buyers' Relief: rate on the portion from £300,001 to £500,000
First Time Buyers' Relief: maximum purchase price - no relief at all above this
Deadline after completion to file the SDLT return and pay the tax
Non-UK resident surcharge added on top of the rates above (fewer than 183 days in the UK in the 12 months before purchase)

scope.who: Anyone buying a freehold or leasehold residential property, or land, in England or Northern Ireland. First Time Buyers' Relief is for individuals who have never owned an interest in a residential property in the UK or anywhere else in the world and who intend to occupy the property as their main residence, where the price is £500,000 or less.
scope.excluded: Buyers in Scotland (they pay Land and Buildings Transaction Tax) and in Wales (Land Transaction Tax). First Time Buyers' Relief is not available where the price is over £500,000; where the buyer, or any person buying with them, has ever owned a residential property interest anywhere in the world; where the buyer is not an individual (companies and most trusts cannot claim); or where the buyer does not intend to occupy it as their main residence.
scope.from_when: Current standard bands and the £300,000/£500,000 First Time Buyers' Relief thresholds apply to transactions with an effective date on or after 1 April 2025, and are unchanged for 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: An SDLT return must be filed and the tax paid within 14 days of completion - usually done by the conveyancer or solicitor. First Time Buyers' Relief is not given automatically: it must be claimed on the SDLT return.

notes: Scotland charges Land and Buildings Transaction Tax and Wales charges Land Transaction Tax instead, with their own bands and their own first-time-buyer rules - never state these figures as UK-wide. Commonly confused: on 1 April 2025 the nil-rate band dropped back from £250,000 to £125,000 and the First Time Buyers' Relief price cap dropped back from £625,000 to £500,000, so pre-April-2025 figures still circulating are wrong. Relief is all-or-nothing at £500,000, not tapered. The 2% non-UK resident surcharge and the 5% additional-dwellings surcharge stack on top of the standard rates. Separately, from 1 May 2026 no SDLT is payable on the net present value of rent under an assured tenancy.

title: SDLT higher rates for additional dwellings (second homes and buy-to-let)

figures.what: The higher-rate surcharge added to each standard residential SDLT band when the purchase means you will own more than one dwelling
The resulting higher rates band by band (up to £125,000; £125,001-£250,000; £250,001-£925,000; £925,001-£1.5m; above £1.5m)
Effective date from which the surcharge rose from 3% to 5%
Single flat rate on purchases of dwellings over £500,000 by companies and other non-natural persons (up from 15% on 31 October 2024)
Consideration threshold - purchases below £40,000 are outside the higher rates, and an interest worth under £40,000 in another dwelling is ignored
Window for selling the former only or main residence to avoid, or reclaim, the higher rates

scope.who: Individuals who, at the end of the day of the transaction, own or are treated as owning a major interest in two or more dwellings and are not replacing their only or main residence; and companies and other non-natural persons buying residential property, including on their first purchase.
scope.excluded: Buyers in Scotland (Land and Buildings Transaction Tax, with its own Additional Dwelling Supplement) and Wales (Land Transaction Tax higher rates). Also outside the higher rates: purchases where the chargeable consideration is under £40,000; caravans, mobile homes and houseboats; buyers replacing their only or main residence where the previous one is disposed of before or on the day of completion; and buyers who hold only a small share in a recently inherited property.
scope.from_when: The 5% surcharge applies to transactions with an effective date on or after 31 October 2024 (it was 3% before that) and is unchanged for 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: There is nothing to claim to pay the surcharge - it is reported and paid on the SDLT return within 14 days of completion. Where the higher rates were paid because the former main residence had not yet sold, a refund can be applied for from HMRC once that property is sold within the 36-month window.

notes: Scotland and Wales have their own equivalents, at their own rates - never state this as UK-wide. Commonly confused: the test is applied to a spouse or civil partner as well as to the buyer, so one spouse buying alone is caught if the other would be caught, unless the couple are legally or permanently separated; transfers of interests between spouses or civil partners living together are disregarded. Also often misstated: the surcharge is 5 percentage points on top of the whole standard rate ladder, not a flat 5% of the price, and it applies even where the buyer's other property is abroad. Companies pay the 17% flat rate on dwellings over £500,000 unless a relief applies.

title: Business Asset Disposal Relief: lifetime limit and CGT rate

figures.what: Lifetime limit on qualifying gains for 2026-27 (cumulative over a lifetime, not annual)
Capital Gains Tax rate on gains qualifying for BADR, for disposals on or after 6 April 2026
The BADR rate that applied to disposals from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026 (the previous year's rate)
Reduced lifetime limit for qualifying disposals made on or after 6 April 2027
Qualifying period over which the conditions must be met, ending on the date of disposal (or on cessation if the business ended earlier)
Minimum holding of ordinary share capital, voting rights, and entitlement to profits, distributable assets and sale proceeds, for a 'personal company' share disposal

scope.who: Individuals disposing of all or part of a business, of assets of a business that has ceased (sold within 3 years of cessation), or of shares or securities in their personal company where they hold at least 5% of ordinary share capital and voting rights and are an officer or employee of a trading company or the holding company of a trading group; also associated disposals, and trustees where a qualifying beneficiary has a life or absolute interest in possession. Spouses and civil partners are assessed separately and each has their own lifetime limit.
scope.excluded: Companies. Trusts that are wholly discretionary settlements. Personal representatives, unless the disposal happened while the deceased was alive. Property letting businesses, which do not count as a business for BADR. Shares held as investments, holdings below 5%, non-trading companies, and holders who are not an officer or employee. Goodwill sold to a close company in which the seller and connected persons hold 5% or more (subject to a 28-day share-disposal exception). Anyone who has already used up their lifetime limit. Gains above the lifetime limit, which are taxed at normal CGT rates.
scope.from_when: The 18% rate applies to qualifying disposals made on or after 6 April 2026. The £1 million lifetime limit has applied since 11 March 2020 and still applies for 2026-27; it falls to £500,000 for disposals on or after 6 April 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Claim on the Self Assessment tax return, or in writing to HMRC / on the Claim for Business Asset Disposal Relief form. Trustees claim jointly with the qualifying beneficiary. The deadline is the first anniversary of the 31 January following the end of the tax year of disposal - for 2025-26 disposals, 31 January 2028.

notes: UK-wide: Capital Gains Tax is not devolved, so the rate is the same for Scottish and Welsh taxpayers even though their income tax bands differ. Two dates matter and are easy to get wrong: the rate was 10% to 5 April 2025, 14% for 2025-26 and is 18% from 6 April 2026; and the lifetime limit is still £1 million for 2026-27 but halves to £500,000 from 6 April 2027, so timing a disposal before 6 April 2027 is material. Commonly confused with Investors' Relief and with the now-announced founders' relief, and with the former name 'Entrepreneurs' Relief' - the gov.uk helpsheet is still filed under that name. Anti-forestalling rules apply to unconditional contracts entered into before a rate change (HMRC manual CG64174).

title: Inheritance Tax: nil rate band, residence nil rate band and the taper

figures.what: Inheritance Tax nil-rate band for 2026-27
Residence nil-rate band for 2026-27
Taper threshold: the net estate value above which the residence nil-rate band starts to be withdrawn
Rate at which the residence nil-rate band is reduced for estate value above the £2 million taper threshold
End of the period for which all three thresholds are frozen rather than rising with CPI

scope.who: The nil-rate band applies to every estate and to chargeable lifetime transfers. The residence nil-rate band is for estates where a home the deceased owned and lived in is closely inherited by direct descendants - children, grandchildren and other lineal descendants, stepchildren, adopted children, fostered children, children for whom the deceased was appointed guardian or special guardian while under 18, and the spouses or civil partners (including widows, widowers and surviving civil partners) of those descendants.
scope.excluded: The residence nil-rate band is not available where no qualifying residential interest passes on death; where the home passes to anyone outside the direct-descendant list, such as nephews, nieces or siblings; where the home is left in a trust under which descendants do not become entitled at death (for example they must first reach a stated age); or on lifetime gifts and transfers into trust, which never attract it. It is withdrawn entirely once the net estate is large enough for the £1-for-£2 taper to exhaust it.
scope.from_when: £325,000 has applied since 6 April 2009 and £175,000 since 6 April 2020; the £2 million taper threshold has applied since the residence nil-rate band was introduced. All three are frozen at these levels for 2026-27 and 2027-28, and the freeze then runs on to the end of 2029-30.
scope.how_to_claim: The nil-rate band is applied automatically in the Inheritance Tax calculation. The residence nil-rate band must be claimed by the personal representatives - form IHT435 alongside the IHT400, with form IHT436 to claim any unused residence nil-rate band transferred from a late spouse or civil partner.

notes: UK-wide: Inheritance Tax is not devolved, so the same thresholds apply in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Commonly confused: the residence nil-rate band is not automatic - it is lost if nobody claims it, and a claim is needed even where the estate owes no tax so that the unused amount can be transferred later. Estate value for the taper is total assets less debts, before deducting spouse exemption or business and agricultural property relief, so a large estate can lose the residence nil-rate band even though it pays no tax. Also commonly confused: unused nil-rate band and unused residence nil-rate band are both transferable between spouses and civil partners as percentages, which is where the often-quoted '£1 million for a couple' comes from - that figure is not itself a threshold. Separately, a £2.5 million allowance applies to 100% agricultural and business property relief - a different £2m-plus figure that is easy to mix up with the taper threshold.

title: Inheritance Tax on gifts: the 7-year rule, taper relief and the annual exemption

figures.what: Period you must survive a gift for it to fall out of account for Inheritance Tax
Rate of tax on a gift made less than 3 years before death
Taper relief: rate of tax on a gift made 3-4, 4-5, 5-6 and 6-7 years before death respectively (0% at 7 years or more)
Annual exemption: value of gifts each tax year that is not added to the estate; unused exemption can be carried forward one tax year only
Small gifts exemption: per person, any number of people, each tax year, provided no other allowance has been used on that same person
Wedding or civil partnership gift exemption: to a child / to a grandchild or great-grandchild / to any other person
Threshold that total gifts in the 7 years before death must exceed before tax arises on the gifts and before taper relief has any effect

scope.who: Any individual making lifetime gifts, and the executors and gift recipients of someone who dies within 7 years of making them.
scope.excluded: Gifts that are already exempt never engage the 7-year rule: gifts to a spouse or civil partner who lives permanently in the UK (no limit), gifts to charities and to political parties, and gifts within the annual, small gifts, wedding and normal-expenditure-out-of-income exemptions. Taper relief does not apply at all unless total gifts in the 7 years before death exceed the £325,000 threshold. The small gifts exemption cannot be combined with another allowance to the same person, and wedding gifts cannot be combined with the small gifts exemption. Unused annual exemption cannot be carried forward more than one tax year.
scope.from_when: Long-standing rules, unchanged for 2026-27; the £325,000 threshold is frozen to the end of 2029-30.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim in the donor's lifetime - the exemptions apply automatically. Keep records of gifts and of the exemptions used. On death the personal representatives report gifts made in the 7 years before death on form IHT403 with the IHT400, and taper relief is applied in the calculation.

notes: UK-wide: Inheritance Tax is not devolved. The single most common error: taper relief reduces the tax on the gift, not the value of the gift, and it only bites where the gifts exceed the nil-rate band - so a gift of £100,000 made 5 years before death with no other gifts is fully covered by the nil-rate band and taper relief is irrelevant. Second: the nil-rate band is set against gifts in date order before the rest of the estate, which is why early gifts shelter later ones. Third: the recipient, not the estate, becomes liable for the tax on their gift where gifts in the 7 years exceed £325,000, although in practice the estate usually pays. Gifts with reservation of benefit (for example giving away a house but continuing to live in it) are treated as still in the estate and the 7-year clock does not help.

title: Lifetime ISA: the 25% bonus and the withdrawal charge

figures.what: Maximum you can pay into a Lifetime ISA each tax year
Government bonus added to what you pay in
Maximum government bonus per year
Overall ISA allowance for 2026-27, which the £4,000 Lifetime ISA payment counts towards
Withdrawal charge on cash or assets taken out for any non-qualifying reason, including transfer to another type of ISA before age 60 - charged on the whole amount withdrawn, bonus included
Reduced withdrawal charge where the funds are used to buy a first home costing more than the £450,000 price cap
Date from which the charge on withdrawals for a first home above the price cap was reduced from 25% to 20%
First home property price cap - no withdrawal charge at or below this price
Age range in which you can open a Lifetime ISA (18 or over but under 40)
Age after which you can no longer pay in or earn the bonus, although the account stays open and keeps growing
Minimum period from the first payment into the account before a charge-free first-home withdrawal can be made
Age from which you can withdraw for any reason with no charge

scope.who: Individuals aged 18 or over but under 40 who are resident in the UK, or who are members of the armed forces or Crown servants serving overseas, or the spouse or civil partner of one. Funds can be used charge-free for a first home at or below £450,000 bought with a mortgage through a conveyancer or solicitor at least 12 months after the first payment, or for any purpose from age 60.
scope.excluded: Anyone under 18, and anyone aged 40 or over, cannot open one. Non-UK residents cannot open or continue paying in, unless they are armed forces, a Crown servant, or the spouse or civil partner of one. Nobody can pay in or earn the bonus after age 50. The charge-free first-home route is not available to anyone who owns or has ever owned a home, nor to a cash purchase without a mortgage, nor within 12 months of the first payment. Buy-to-let and second properties do not qualify.
scope.from_when: The Lifetime ISA, the £4,000 limit, the 25% bonus and the 25% withdrawal charge have applied since 6 April 2017. The reduced 20% charge for first homes above the £450,000 cap has effect from 29 October 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Open an account with an ISA manager (bank, building society or investment provider) and make the first payment before age 40. The provider claims the 25% bonus from HMRC and adds it to the account - there is no separate claim by the saver. A first-home withdrawal is made by the provider to the conveyancer or solicitor.

notes: UK-wide: ISAs are not devolved, so the limits and charges are identical across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Commonly confused: the 25% withdrawal charge is not just the bonus being taken back - it is 25% of the whole amount withdrawn, bonus and growth included, so an unauthorised withdrawal leaves you with less than you paid in. From 29 October 2026 that penalty is softened to 20% only where the money is used to buy a first home above the £450,000 cap, which returns the bonus without a further loss; the 25% charge still applies to every other non-qualifying withdrawal. No charge arises on withdrawal from age 60, on terminal illness with less than 12 months to live, or on death. The £450,000 cap is a single UK-wide figure, not a regional one, and it is the purchase price, not the mortgage amount. The £4,000 sits inside the £20,000 overall ISA allowance, it is not on top of it.

title: Junior ISA: the allowance and who controls the money

figures.what: Junior ISA savings limit for the 2026-27 tax year, across all of a child's Junior ISAs
Junior ISA subscription limit confirmed as unchanged for 2027-28
Age at which the child can take over management of the account
Age at which the child can withdraw the money; the account then becomes an adult ISA

scope.who: Children under 18 who live in the UK, or who live outside the UK as a dependant of a Crown servant such as armed forces, diplomatic service or overseas civil service. The account is opened and managed by a person with parental responsibility, but the money belongs to the child. Anyone - parents, grandparents, friends - can pay in, up to the single £9,000 limit for the child.
scope.excluded: Anyone aged 18 or over. Children who do not live in the UK, unless they are a Crown servant's dependant as above. A child cannot hold a Junior ISA and a Child Trust Fund at the same time, so a child with a Child Trust Fund is excluded until the fund is transferred into a Junior ISA. The person with parental responsibility cannot take the money out for themselves, and nobody can withdraw before the child is 18 (other than in the limited circumstances allowed by the ISA rules).
scope.from_when: The £9,000 limit has applied since 6 April 2020 and is unchanged for 2026-27 and 2027-28.
scope.how_to_claim: A person with parental responsibility opens a cash and/or stocks and shares Junior ISA with a provider. No claim to HMRC is needed - interest, dividends and capital growth are tax-free. At 16 the child can ask the provider to transfer management to them; at 18 they can withdraw or let it roll into an adult ISA.

notes: UK-wide: ISAs are not devolved, so the £9,000 limit and the age rules are the same across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The point clients most often get wrong: the money is the child's absolutely and irrevocably - a parent who funds it cannot get it back, and at 18 the child can spend it on whatever they like. Control and access are different ages: management passes at 16, withdrawal at 18. The £9,000 is per child, shared across their cash and stocks and shares Junior ISAs, and it is entirely separate from the adult £20,000 ISA allowance, so a parent's own allowance is unaffected. Commonly confused with the Child Trust Fund, which the Junior ISA replaced for children born on or after 3 January 2011 - a child cannot hold both, and an existing Child Trust Fund must be transferred rather than run alongside.

title: Landlords: the restriction on mortgage interest relief (the 20% tax reducer)

figures.what: Basic rate at which residential finance costs are relieved, as a reduction against the income tax liability rather than a deduction from rental profit
Proportion of residential finance costs still deductible from rental income - none, with 100% given as the basic rate reduction, from 2020-21 onwards
Date the restriction started, phased in at 75% deductible / 25% reducer in 2017-18, 50/50 in 2018-19, 25/75 in 2019-20
Date from which the restriction has been fully in force
The reducer is 20% of the lowest of: finance costs including any brought forward; property business profits after brought-forward losses; and adjusted total income above the personal allowance
Date from which the furnished holiday lettings rules ceased to apply for Income Tax, so furnished holiday lets are no longer outside the restriction

scope.who: Individuals with residential rental income, whether letting alone or in partnership; trustees and personal representatives of deceased estates; beneficiaries of estates chargeable to income tax on estate income that includes property income; trustees of accumulation or discretionary trusts carrying on a property business; and individuals with loans taken out to invest in a partnership carrying on a residential property business. It covers interest on mortgages and on loans to buy furnishings, and fees for taking out or repaying those loans.
scope.excluded: Companies carrying on a property business are not affected and continue to deduct finance costs in full. Also outside the restriction: loans wholly for commercial or non-residential property; residential mobile home parks, which are generally treated as a trade; and capital repayments of a mortgage, which get no relief at all under either rule. Overseas property businesses of a person claiming relief under the Foreign Income and Gains regime from 6 April 2025 cannot claim residential finance cost relief for that year. Furnished holiday lettings used to be excluded, but that exclusion ended for Income Tax from 6 April 2025.
scope.from_when: Introduced for finance costs incurred on or after 6 April 2017, phased in over four years and fully in force since 6 April 2020. Unchanged for 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: Enter the residential finance costs in the residential finance costs box on the Self Assessment property pages (SA105) rather than as an expense. HMRC's calculation then applies the 20% reducer automatically; any amount unrelieved because profits or adjusted total income were the lowest figure is carried forward to later years.

notes: UK-wide: this is an income tax rule that applies to Scottish and Welsh taxpayers on the same basis, and the reducer is set at the basic rate - do not assume it follows Scotland's different income tax bands. Commonly confused: this is still widely called 'section 24', after section 24 of the Finance (No. 2) Act 2015; the legislation now sits at ITTOIA 2005 sections 272A, 272B and 274A to 274C. The effect clients miss is that gross rents now enter total income, so the restriction can push a landlord into the higher rate band, reduce child benefit, or taper the personal allowance even where real profit is unchanged, and the reducer can never create a repayment. Note also that the property income allowance is not available in a year the reducer is applied, so landlords with restricted finance costs must choose between the allowance and claiming expenses plus the reducer. Looking ahead: from April 2027 the property rates of income tax are separated from the main rates (24% basic, 44% higher, 49% additional), so recheck how the reducer interacts with those rates before April 2027.

title: Bereavement Support Payment: two rates and the claim clock

figures.what: Higher rate first (one-off) payment
Higher rate monthly payment, for up to 18 months
Standard (lower) rate first (one-off) payment
Standard (lower) rate monthly payment, for up to 18 months
Same 2026-27 rates confirmed in the DWP benefit and pension rates table (higher rate lump sum 3500.00, monthly 350.00; standard rate lump sum 2500.00, monthly 100.00)
Claim within this of the death to get the one-off payment and all 18 monthly payments
Claim 3-12 months after death: one-off payment plus only some monthly payments; after 12 months the one-off payment is lost
Outer limit - claims more than 21 months after the death usually get nothing

scope.who: You were under State Pension age when your partner died, were living in the UK (or a country that pays UK bereavement benefits), and were married to them, in a civil partnership with them, or living with them as if married. Your partner must have paid Class 1 or Class 2 National Insurance in any one tax year since 6 April 1975, or have died because of a work accident or a work-caused disease. Higher rate if you were getting Child Benefit for a child living with you, had been told you were entitled to it, or were pregnant when they died; unmarried cohabiting partners qualify only on one of those three grounds, and at the higher rate.
scope.excluded: Anyone over State Pension age when their partner died; anyone in prison; unmarried cohabiting partners who were not getting (or entitled to) Child Benefit for a child living with them and were not pregnant; people living in a country that does not pay UK bereavement benefits; claims made more than 21 months after the death (unless the cause of death was only recently confirmed); deaths before 6 April 2017 (Widowed Parent's Allowance may apply instead).
scope.from_when: Rates shown are the 2026-27 rates. Payments start from the date of claim, with the amount cut by how late the claim is (see the 3 / 12 / 21 month figures).
scope.how_to_claim: You must claim it - contact the DWP Bereavement Service (in Northern Ireland, the Department for Communities Bereavement Service), or claim online or by post using form BSP1.

notes: Not means-tested - earnings and savings do not affect it. The two rates have inconsistent names across official pages: gov.uk's 'What you'll get' page calls the £2,500 rate the 'lower rate', while the DWP rates table and nidirect both call it the 'standard rate'. Nations: this is a reserved benefit and the rates are identical across the UK - nidirect confirms the same £3,500/£350 and £2,500/£100 for Northern Ireland, administered by the Department for Communities rather than DWP. It has NOT been devolved to Social Security Scotland, so Scottish claimants use the DWP scheme. Commonly confused with: Widowed Parent's Allowance (for deaths before 6 April 2017), the old Bereavement Allowance and Bereavement Payment (both abolished), and Funeral Expenses Payment, which is a separate means-tested payment towards funeral costs. If you reach State Pension age within 18 months of the death you may get fewer monthly payments.

title: Sure Start Maternity Grant: £500 for a first baby

figures.what: One-off Sure Start Maternity Grant, does not have to be repaid and does not affect other benefits
Earliest you can claim - from 11 weeks before the baby's due date
Latest you can claim - within 6 months after the baby's birth
You must usually have no other children under 16 in your household

scope.who: You (or your partner) get income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Pension Credit or Universal Credit (a Support for Mortgage Interest loan may also qualify you), and you usually have no other children under 16. You can still qualify with other children under 16 if you are expecting a multiple birth; if you are caring for someone else's child who was over 12 months old when the arrangement started; if you have refugee status or humanitarian protection or came to the UK from Afghanistan or Ukraine (first UK-born child); or if you are claiming for a family member under 16 (or 16-19 in approved education or training) who is having their first child and lives with you. Adopters, surrogacy parental-order holders and some carers can claim if the baby is under 1 on the claim date.
scope.excluded: Anyone living in Scotland cannot get it at all - they claim the Pregnancy and Baby Payment from Social Security Scotland instead. Also excluded: people who already have a child under 16 and do not meet one of the listed exceptions; anyone not receiving one of the qualifying benefits; claims made outside the window (earlier than 11 weeks before the due date, or more than 6 months after birth); and, for the education-based route, people on employer-paid courses, on courses that form part of a job contract, or on 'advanced' courses such as university degrees or BTEC Higher National Certificates.
scope.from_when: Claim window opens 11 weeks before the due date and closes 6 months after the birth (or after adoption / the parental, residence or guardianship order, or the date you took responsibility for the baby).
scope.how_to_claim: Not automatic - you must apply on claim form SF100, signed by a health professional (for example using your MATB1), and post it to the address on the form. If you are on Universal Credit the grant decision waits until that claim is processed.

notes: Nations - this one is a genuine trap. The gov.uk £500 grant does not cover Scotland: Scotland replaced it with the Pregnancy and Baby Payment (part of Best Start Grant) from Social Security Scotland. Northern Ireland runs its own version, the Social Fund Sure Start Maternity Grant administered by the Department for Communities on form SF100 - same £500 headline, but nidirect sets out multiple-birth uplifts not stated on the gov.uk page (£500 for twins, £1,000 for triplets or more, for a first multiple birth only, with reduced or no payment if you have had multiples before). So the gov.uk scheme as written is England and Wales. Commonly confused with: Maternity Allowance and Statutory Maternity Pay (earnings replacement, nothing to do with this), Healthy Start vouchers, and Scotland's Best Start Grant / Best Start Foods.

title: Funeral Expenses Payment: what it covers and the 6-month clock

figures.what: Cap on 'other funeral expenses' - funeral director's fees, flowers, the coffin
Cap where the deceased had a pre-paid funeral plan - maximum for items the plan does not cover
Deadline - you must apply within 6 months of the funeral, even if still waiting for a decision on a qualifying benefit
Moving the body within the UK is covered where the distance is over 50 miles

scope.who: You (or your partner) get Universal Credit, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Pension Credit or Housing Benefit (a Support for Mortgage Interest loan may also qualify you), you are arranging a funeral in the UK, EEA or Switzerland, and you meet the relationship rules: you were the deceased's partner; the parent of a baby stillborn after 24 weeks; or the parent or person responsible for a deceased child under 16 (or under 20 and in approved education or training). A close relative or friend can claim only if the deceased had no partner, or the partner (or the parent of a deceased child) cannot claim - for example because they live abroad or are in prison.
scope.excluded: Anyone in Scotland - the Funeral Support Payment from Social Security Scotland has replaced Funeral Expenses Payment there. Also excluded: anyone not on one of the four qualifying benefits; close relatives or friends where the deceased had a partner who could claim; a close relative (sibling, parent) who is in work or not on a qualifying benefit; anyone arranging the funeral outside the UK, EEA or Switzerland; and claims made more than 6 months after the funeral.
scope.from_when: Claimable from the date of death - you can claim before the funeral if you already hold an invoice or signed contract from the funeral director (an estimate is not enough) - and up to 6 months after the funeral.
scope.how_to_claim: Not automatic - claim by phone to the DWP Bereavement Service (a Welsh-language line and Relay UK / BSL video relay are available), or by post on form SF200 (SF200 Child for a child's funeral) to the address printed on the form. Northern Ireland has a different claim process via nidirect.

notes: The payment is clawed back from the estate: gov.uk says it 'will be deducted from any money you get from the deceased's estate', though the estate for this purpose excludes a house or personal possessions left to a surviving spouse or civil partner. Burial and cremation fees (including the doctor's certificate), travel to arrange or attend the funeral, moving the body over 50 miles within the UK, and death certificates are covered without the £1,000 cap - the cap bites only on 'other' expenses such as the funeral director's fees, flowers and the coffin, which is why most awards fall well short of the real bill. Nations: Scotland is out (Funeral Support Payment); Northern Ireland runs its own Funeral Expenses Payment through the Department for Communities with a separate claim route, so the gov.uk scheme as written is England and Wales. If the claimant is on Universal Credit, no decision is issued until after their next UC payment. Commonly confused with: the Bereavement Support Payment (not means-tested, nothing to do with funeral costs), the abolished Bereavement Payment, and local council public health (paupers') funerals.

title: Blind Person's Allowance: £3,250 of extra tax-free income

figures.what: Blind Person's Allowance for the 2026 to 2027 tax year, added on top of the Personal Allowance

scope.who: In England and Wales: you are registered with your local council as blind or severely sight impaired AND you hold a certificate confirming blindness or severe sight impairment, or a similar document from your doctor. In Scotland and Northern Ireland: you cannot do work for which eyesight is essential. The allowance is an Income Tax allowance, so it is worth something only where there is tax to relieve - but it can be transferred where there is not.
scope.excluded: In England and Wales, anyone not registered with their local council as blind or severely sight impaired, or without the certifying document - being sight impaired / partially sighted but not registered as severely sight impaired does not qualify. In Scotland and Northern Ireland, anyone who can still do work for which eyesight is essential. It is not a disability benefit, so people with other disabilities do not qualify. Anyone who neither pays Income Tax nor has an eligible spouse or civil partner to transfer it to gets no cash benefit from it.
scope.from_when: £3,250 applies for the 2026-27 tax year (6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027).
scope.how_to_claim: Not automatic - you must contact HMRC to claim it (HMRC Income Tax helpline, Monday to Friday 8am to 6pm except bank holidays).
