If you do not pay tax, or do not earn enough to use all of it, you can transfer the unused allowance to your spouse or civil partner, who must also be eligible for an allowance to receive it (HMRC form 575(T)).

notes: Nations: the allowance itself is UK-wide at the same £3,250, but the eligibility TEST differs - England and Wales turn on local-council registration as blind / severely sight impaired, while Scotland and Northern Ireland turn on being unable to do work for which eyesight is essential. Do not state a single test UK-wide. Because it is an allowance and not a benefit, it is not means-tested and does not affect benefit entitlement. Commonly confused with: Personal Independence Payment / Adult Disability Payment, Attendance Allowance, the Marriage Allowance and the Married Couple's Allowance (a separate figure uprated by the same statutory instrument), and the Severe Sight Impairment register itself, which is a local-authority list and not a tax claim. Worth flagging to clients: HMRC does not apply it unless asked, so long-registered clients are often years out of pocket.

title: Local Housing Allowance: the cap on help with private rent

figures.what: Birmingham broad rental market area (BRMA) shared accommodation rate, UC LHA monthly rate 2026 to 2027
Birmingham BRMA 1 bedroom rate, UC LHA monthly rate 2026 to 2027
Birmingham BRMA 2 bedroom rate, UC LHA monthly rate 2026 to 2027
Birmingham BRMA 3 bedroom rate, UC LHA monthly rate 2026 to 2027
Birmingham BRMA 4 bedroom rate, UC LHA monthly rate 2026 to 2027 (there is no 5-bedroom rate - 4 is the maximum)
Age below which a single person living alone is normally restricted to the shared accommodation rate
Deduction from the housing element for each non-dependant aged 21 or over (not your partner) living with you

scope.who: Universal Credit claimants who rent from a private landlord. The housing element covers rent and some service charges, is paid inside the UC payment, and is capped at the Local Housing Allowance rate for the broad rental market area and the number of bedrooms the household is treated as needing. Aged 35 or over and living alone: the 1 bedroom rate. Under 35 and living alone: the shared accommodation rate. Couples and families: the rate for the bedrooms the household needs, where an adult couple share, two children under 16 of the same sex share, and two children under 10 share. Extra bedrooms are allowed for a single adult aged 16 or over, a child who cannot share because shared rooms are full, a couple or child who cannot share for disability or medical reasons, and a non-resident overnight carer.
scope.excluded: Social housing tenants (council and housing association) are not on LHA - their help is worked out on eligible rent with the under-occupancy 'bedroom tax' reduction instead. Single under-35s living alone are excluded from the 1 bedroom rate and held to the shared accommodation rate, UNLESS they are a care leaver under 25, have spent 3 months or more in a homeless hostel, are an ex-offender managed under MAPPA, are a victim of domestic abuse or modern slavery, or receive certain disability or care benefits (PIP daily living, DLA care at the middle or highest rate, or Attendance Allowance). Also excluded: any rent above the LHA cap (the shortfall is never met by UC); a reduction of £96.55 a month for each non-dependant aged 21+, subject to exemptions; and rent on two homes, allowed only where you have fled violence or abuse and intend to return, or have moved in with a disabled family member before the new home is adapted.
scope.from_when: LHA rates are set for the year 2026 to 2027; the England rates table was last updated 8 April 2026. LHA rates run on the April-to-March cycle, not the tax year.
scope.how_to_claim: Not claimed separately - the housing element is part of a Universal Credit claim, and you report your rent and tenancy in your UC account. Check your own cap on the Valuation Office Agency's LHA Direct tool, selecting 'shared accommodation' under bedrooms for the shared rate. Rent can be paid straight to the landlord through a managed payment to landlord (an alternative payment arrangement), applied for via your work coach or by the landlord - if the landlord applies you have 7 days to respond.

notes: The single most misunderstood point: LHA is a CAP, not a payment. It is based on area rents, not your actual rent, so any excess is yours to find from the rest of your UC or other income. Nations: DWP publishes separate LHA tables for England, Wales and Scotland, and the help with a shortfall differs by nation - gov.uk names the Crisis and Resilience Fund in England and Discretionary Housing Payments in Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland runs UC housing costs separately through nidirect, so this is a Great Britain row, not UK-wide. The figures quoted here are the Birmingham BRMA only; every BRMA has its own rates and 'Birmingham' as a BRMA is not the same footprint as the city council area, so always check LHA Direct by postcode. Commonly confused with: Housing Benefit for private tenants (same LHA caps, but weekly figures rather than the monthly UC figures above - do not mix the two), the social-sector 'bedroom tax', the benefit cap, and Discretionary Housing Payments.

title: PIP rates 2026-27: daily living and mobility

figures.what: Daily living component, standard (lower) rate
Daily living component, enhanced (higher) rate
Mobility component, standard (lower) rate
Mobility component, enhanced (higher) rate
Same four 2026-27 rates confirmed in the DWP benefit and pension rates table
Your difficulties must be expected to last at least 12 months from when they started
Residence test - you normally need to have lived in England, Scotland or Wales for at least 2 of the last 3 years

scope.who: You are 16 or over, you have a long-term physical or mental health condition or disability, you have difficulty with everyday tasks or with getting around, you expect those difficulties to last at least 12 months from when they started, you have normally lived in England, Scotland or Wales for at least 2 of the last 3 years, and you are living in England or Wales when you apply. Not means-tested: income, savings and whether you work make no difference. Awarded as two separate components, each at a standard or enhanced rate depending on your points score.
scope.excluded: Anyone living in Scotland cannot make a new PIP claim - they apply for Adult Disability Payment from Social Security Scotland instead. Northern Ireland residents claim through nidirect, not gov.uk. Also excluded: anyone under 16; people over State Pension age making a NEW claim (they apply for Attendance Allowance instead, though you can still claim PIP if you received PIP or ADP in the previous 12 months); anyone subject to immigration control, unless a sponsored immigrant; EU, Swiss, Norwegian, Icelandic and Liechtenstein nationals and their family members without settled or pre-settled status; people who have recently returned from abroad and fail the 2-in-3-years residence test (special rules may let those returning from certain EU/EEA states or Switzerland qualify sooner). Anyone getting Armed Forces Independence Payment cannot also get PIP; War Pensioners' Mobility Supplement rules out the mobility component; and Constant Attendance Allowance reduces the daily living component. Living abroad in the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland or Liechtenstein can give entitlement to the daily living part only.
scope.from_when: These are the 2026-27 weekly rates, in payment from April 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Not automatic - you must claim. Start the PIP claim with DWP (phone or online), then complete the 'How your disability affects you' form and usually attend an assessment. In Scotland apply for Adult Disability Payment through Social Security Scotland - online via its portal, by phone or on paper.

notes: This is the big nation trap on the list: PIP has been replaced in Scotland by Adult Disability Payment, and gov.uk's own eligibility page says so in terms - 'If you live in Scotland, you need to apply for Adult Disability Payment (ADP) instead' - and requires you to be living in England or Wales when you apply. Never write PIP as UK-wide. The ADP amounts currently match PIP exactly (mygov.scot lists daily living £76.70 standard / £114.60 enhanced and mobility £30.30 standard / £80.00 enhanced), and ADP also awards the enhanced daily living rate automatically to people who are terminally ill, and enhanced mobility unlocks a leased accessible vehicle. Note that the mygov.scot ADP rates page itself carries a caution that an annual increase has gone out and the listed amounts may not be the latest, so confirm with Social Security Scotland before quoting ADP figures as of today. gov.uk uses 'lower weekly rate' and 'higher weekly rate' on the amounts page while the legislation and the DWP rates table use 'standard' and 'enhanced' - same thing. Commonly confused with: Attendance Allowance (State Pension age and over), Disability Living Allowance (children, and Scottish Adult DLA), Employment and Support Allowance and the UC health element (these are about capability for work, PIP is not), and the Blue Badge / Motability schemes, which follow from an enhanced mobility award but are not the benefit itself.

title: Scottish income tax: the six bands for 2026-27

figures.what: Personal Allowance - set by the UK Government, not Holyrood; reduced by £1 for every £2 of income over £100,000
Starter rate
Scottish basic rate
Intermediate rate
Higher rate
Advanced rate
Top rate
Same six rates and bands confirmed on gov.scot, set out by the Cabinet Secretary for Finance at the Scottish Budget on 13 January 2026

scope.who: Scottish taxpayers - you pay Scottish income tax if you live in Scotland. You may also pay it if you move to or from Scotland during the year, or have homes both in Scotland and elsewhere in the UK, in which case your main home is usually where you live and spend most of your time; if you move to Scotland you are a Scottish taxpayer for a tax year in which you live there longer than anywhere else in the UK. People with no home who stay in Scotland regularly, for example offshore workers or those living in hotels, can also be Scottish taxpayers. It applies to wages, pensions and most other taxable income, including self-employed profits, rental income and taxable benefits such as the State Pension and Carer's Allowance.
scope.excluded: These rates and bands do NOT apply to savings income or dividend income - those stay on the UK-wide rates wherever you live. They do not apply to anyone whose main home is in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. They do not change the Personal Allowance, which is reserved to the UK Government. They do not apply to National Insurance, which is UK-wide. Nor do they apply to Corporation Tax or Capital Gains Tax, which are not devolved.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim - HMRC collects and administers Scottish income tax and applies it through an 'S' prefix PAYE tax code once your address is recorded as Scottish. Keep your address up to date with HMRC, since the Scottish taxpayer status follows your main residence, and tick the Scottish taxpayer box on a Self Assessment return.

notes: Scotland has six bands against the rest of the UK's three, and the thresholds diverge sharply: the Scottish higher rate bites at £43,663 while the UK higher rate starts at £50,270, so Scottish taxpayers in the £43,663-£50,270 band pay 42% where their English, Welsh and Northern Irish counterparts pay 20%. Responsibility is split - Holyrood sets the rates and bands on non-savings, non-dividend income, the UK Government sets the Personal Allowance, and HMRC does the collecting. gov.scot's rates-and-bands page is still worded as 'proposed' from the 13 January 2026 Budget; mygov.scot publishes the identical figures under 'Current rates - 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027', which is why that page is cited as the official page here. Commonly confused with: the Welsh rates of income tax (devolved in name but currently set to match England and Northern Ireland, so no divergence); National Insurance, Capital Gains Tax and dividend tax, none of which are devolved; and the effective 'marginal rate' spike between £100,000 and £125,140 caused by Personal Allowance taper, which is a UK-wide effect and not a Scottish band.

title: Priority Services Register: free extra help from your energy supplier

figures.what: Cost of joining - Ofgem describes the Priority Services Register as 'free extra help and support'
Your energy supplier and your network operator (pipes and wires) each keep a separate Priority Services Register

scope.nation: Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales) for the energy Priority Services Register
scope.who: Energy customers in any of the circumstances Ofgem lists: you have reached State Pension age; you are pregnant or have young children; you struggle with speaking or reading English; you have a disability or long-term medical condition, including mental health conditions, conditions affecting sight, hearing or sense of smell, or a condition needing medical equipment with a power supply; or your circumstances have recently changed, for example after an injury or hospital stay, a bereavement or losing your job. Support includes priority help in an emergency, advance notice of planned power cuts where possible, an identification and password scheme so you can check a caller or doorstep visitor is genuine, nominating a family member, carer or trusted person to receive your bills and communications, help moving a prepayment meter you cannot safely reach to top up, regular meter readings, bills and account information in large print or braille, and help getting your gas supply reconnected.
scope.excluded: It is not open to people in none of the listed circumstances - Ofgem sets out who can join rather than a formal exclusion list, so there is no automatic entitlement. Critically, it does NOT cross over: membership does not transfer when you switch supplier, so you are excluded from the new supplier's register until you ask to join it; if different companies supply your gas and electricity you must contact each separately and are not on the other's register; and your supplier's register does not put you on your network operator's register. It gives no money off your bill - it is a service register, not a discount or grant. Water is not covered by it: water customers need their water company's own scheme.
scope.from_when: Support starts once your supplier or network operator has recorded your needs; there is no fixed date or annual cycle. Some entries are long-term, others are intended to cover a short period after a change in your life.
scope.how_to_claim: Not automatic - contact your energy supplier and your network operator directly, online, in writing or by phone, giving as much detail as you can about your needs; contact details are on their websites and on your energy bills. Repeat the request with each new supplier after a switch, and with each company if gas and electricity come from different suppliers. For water, contact your water company separately.

notes: Two traps worth leading with: it is per-company, so switching supplier silently drops you off and dual-fuel-from-two-suppliers means two phone calls; and the gas and electricity NETWORK operator register (the one that actually matters in a power cut) is separate from the supplier's. Water is a genuinely different scheme, not part of this one: Ofgem's PSR page does not mention water at all. Ofwat's own 'Priority Services' page confirms water companies in England and Wales offer special assistance to customers who need extra help because of age, health or disability, covering bills and literature in large print, disc or braille or read aloud over the phone, advance warning of planned supply interruptions for people with special medical needs such as home kidney dialysis, a doorstep password scheme, moving a hard-to-reach meter and help with meter readings - but that page sets out no formal eligibility criteria, does not state that the scheme is free and does not confirm a mandatory register, so do not quote water eligibility rules as settled. Nations: Ofgem regulates the Great Britain energy market, so England, Scotland and Wales. I could not confirm the Northern Ireland arrangement at primary source within the deadline - nidirect's 'Care registers' page would not load (302 redirect loop) - so do not state this as UK-wide, and check NI separately before any 'ola' or UK-wide use. Commonly confused with: the Warm Home Discount and Winter Fuel Payment (money off, means-tested or age-based, nothing to do with the PSR), WaterSure and water company social tariffs (bill caps, separate application), and the Medical Equipment Register some network operators run for life-supporting equipment.

title: New higher Income Tax rates on rental and savings income from April 2027

figures.what: Basic rate on property (rental) income from 6 April 2027
Higher rate on property (rental) income from 6 April 2027
Additional rate on property (rental) income from 6 April 2027
Basic, higher and additional rates on savings income from 6 April 2027
Personal Allowance for 2027-28, unchanged by this measure
Starting rate for savings, unchanged by this measure
Dividend allowance, unchanged by this measure

scope.nation: Savings income rates are UK-wide. Property income rates apply in England, Wales and Northern Ireland; Scotland can set its own property income rates under its existing Income Tax powers, and the UK government is engaging with the Scottish and Welsh governments on this.
scope.who: Anyone with taxable rental (property) income or taxable savings interest above their allowances - landlords, people letting a second property, and savers with interest outside an ISA.
scope.excluded: Nobody pays the new rates on income covered by an unchanged allowance: the Personal Allowance (£12,570), the £1,000 property allowance and Rent a Room relief, the starting rate for savings (£5,000) and the Personal Savings Allowance all stay as they are, so a saver or small landlord inside those limits pays nothing extra. Interest and dividends inside an ISA are not taxable income at all and are unaffected. Dividend income is not covered by this measure (dividends have their own separate rates). Employment, self-employment and pension income are not affected. National Insurance treatment of property, savings and dividend income does not change. Scottish taxpayers are outside the new property income rates pending Scotland setting its own.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2027 (tax year 2027-28). Announced at Budget 2026 on 28 October 2026; to be legislated in Finance Bill 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. For people taxed through a PAYE tax code HMRC will apply the new rates automatically, and will keep using bank and building society interest data to adjust tax codes. Anyone who meets the Self Assessment criteria must still register and file a return as usual.

notes: Two separate changes are easily confused. Budget 2025 had already set property and savings rates at 22%/42%/47% from 6 April 2027; Budget 2026 raised them again to 24%/44%/49% for the same year. Always quote 24/44/49 for 2027-28. The second trap is that these are rates on a type of income, not a new tax: a landlord's rental profit is still reduced by allowable expenses and the mortgage interest tax reducer first, and only the taxable profit above allowances meets these rates. Third, dividends are NOT in this measure - dividend rates moved separately (10.75%/35.75%/39.35% from 6 April 2026). Scotland already sets its own rates and bands on non-savings, non-dividend income, so Scottish landlords should not assume the 24/44/49 figures apply to them; savings interest, by contrast, is reserved and UK-wide, so a Scottish saver IS affected. Wales has Welsh rates of Income Tax but is listed as in scope for the new property rates. Because this is still only a Budget announcement awaiting Finance Bill 2026-27, the figures must be rechecked after Royal Assent.

title: Capital allowances: main pool writing-down allowance cut to 12%, first-year allowance raised to 50%

figures.what: Main rate writing-down allowance, reduced
Main rate first-year allowance, increased
Special rate pool writing-down allowance, unchanged
Date from which the 50% first-year allowance applies to expenditure incurred
Businesses HMRC estimates claim main rate writing-down allowance or first-year allowance

scope.nation: UK-wide. Capital allowances are a reserved tax matter, so the same rules apply in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: Businesses that buy plant and machinery going into the main capital allowances pool - sole traders, partnerships and companies. HMRC says the measure is aimed particularly at unincorporated businesses and at businesses buying plant or machinery for leasing, who cannot use full expensing.
scope.excluded: Businesses whose plant and machinery spending is already fully covered by the Annual Investment Allowance or by full expensing get no benefit and see no loss, because they never reach the main rate percentages - HMRC says many businesses will not see main rate writing-down allowance on future spending for exactly this reason. Special rate pool expenditure (long-life assets, integral features, most cars) is excluded: it stays on 6% and is untouched by both changes. The 50% first-year allowance does not apply to expenditure incurred before 1 January 2027. Anyone not carrying on a business, and anyone whose assets do not qualify as plant and machinery, is outside this entirely.
scope.from_when: The 50% first-year allowance applies to expenditure incurred from 1 January 2027. The 12% writing-down allowance applies for chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 April 2027 for Corporation Tax and 6 April 2027 for Income Tax. A chargeable period straddling those dates gets a hybrid rate, apportioned by the part of the period falling before and after the change. Announced at Budget 2026 on 28 October 2026; to be legislated in Finance Bill 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: Capital allowances are claimed on the tax return - the Company Tax Return (CT600) for a company, or the self-employment or property pages of the Self Assessment return for an unincorporated business. A claim is not made for you, and the first-year allowance in particular has to be claimed in the period the expenditure is incurred.

notes: The headline reads worse than it is for most small businesses, and better than it looks for some. Nearly all small businesses never touch these percentages because the Annual Investment Allowance gives 100% relief on qualifying plant and machinery up to its limit, so for them nothing changes at all. The two changes pull in opposite directions: a lower 12% writing-down allowance slows relief on spending carried in the pool, while a higher 50% first-year allowance speeds up relief on new qualifying spending. The timing mismatch is the real trap for planning - the 50% first-year allowance starts on 1 January 2027 by date of expenditure, but the 12% writing-down allowance starts by accounting period (1 April 2027 for companies, 6 April 2027 for the self-employed), and a period spanning the change gets an apportioned hybrid rate rather than one rate or the other. Cars are normally special rate or have their own rules, so do not assume a van and a car are treated alike. These figures are a Budget announcement awaiting Finance Bill 2026-27 and must be rechecked after Royal Assent.

title: VAT on household electricity cut to zero in Great Britain

figures.what: VAT rate on qualifying domestic electricity in Great Britain during the relief period
The reduced rate that applied before, and that qualifying electricity reverts to when the zero rate ends
VAT rate on qualifying domestic electricity in Northern Ireland, which keeps the reduced rate and does not get the zero rate
Date the zero rate started
End date of the zero rate as set out in the published tax information and impact note, with electricity returning to 5% on 1 April 2027
Extended end date announced at Budget 2026 in the government's energy bills factsheet
Average household saving from the VAT cut, per the Budget 2026 energy bills factsheet
Electricity suppliers affected

scope.nation: Great Britain only - England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland is excluded and keeps the 5% reduced rate on qualifying domestic electricity.
scope.who: Households in Great Britain taking a supply of electricity for domestic use, and charities in Great Britain taking electricity for their non-business use. The qualifying-use rules are unchanged, so whoever qualified for the 5% reduced rate before now gets 0%.
scope.excluded: Households and charities in Northern Ireland get nothing from this - their qualifying electricity stays at 5%. Business and other non-domestic electricity supply is excluded and stays at the standard rate; where a supply is mixed, the business portion must be separated out and does not get the zero rate. Gas and all other domestic fuels are excluded and stay at 5% across the whole UK. Public electric vehicle charging is not domestic use and is excluded. A household also gets no benefit to the extent a supplier does not pass the VAT cut through - HMRC says the saving depends on how far suppliers pass it on.
scope.from_when: 1 October 2026. The published impact note runs the relief to 31 March 2027; the Budget 2026 factsheet of 28 October 2026 says the cut has been extended to July 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. Electricity suppliers apply the rate on the bill. For a billing period spanning 1 October 2026 a supplier may set the rate by when the energy was consumed, and HMRC recommends using meter readings to split the bill between the two rates.

notes: The nation split is the thing readers get wrong: this is a Great Britain measure, and a household in Northern Ireland still pays 5% on electricity because Northern Ireland's VAT position on energy is governed differently. Northern Ireland also has domestic rates rather than council tax, so none of the council-tax-banded energy support maps across either. The second trap is scope - only ELECTRICITY is zero-rated, not gas, so a dual-fuel bill will show two different VAT rates and a household on mains gas sees far less benefit than an all-electric one. Third, this is domestic use only: a sole trader working from home cannot zero-rate the business share of their electricity, and a landlord supplying a commercial unit is outside it. Fourth, there is a live discrepancy on the end date - the HMRC impact note and Revenue and Customs Brief 10 (2026) both say the relief ends 31 March 2027, while the government's Budget 2026 energy factsheet of 28 October 2026 says it has been extended to July 2027; HMRC's technical pages had not been updated to reflect the extension when read on 16 November 2026, so the end date must be rechecked before this is used.

title: Employers must report company cars, vans, fuel and medical benefits through payroll from April 2027

figures.what: Date mandatory real-time payroll reporting begins for medical benefits, company cars, vans, and car and van fuel
Date most remaining benefits in kind must be reported through payroll
Date HMRC's voluntary payrolling registration service re-opened, now also allowing Class 1A NICs, employer-provided loans and accommodation to be payrolled voluntarily
Employers currently reporting benefits in kind through end-of-year processes
P11D forms HMRC currently receives each year
The single tax year for which penalties can be waived for non-deliberate inaccuracies, under a modification to Schedule 24 Finance Act 2007
Estimated one-off cost to businesses across the UK of making the change

scope.nation: UK-wide. PAYE and benefits in kind are reserved, so the same rules apply in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: Employers who provide benefits in kind to employees or directors, including owner-managed companies that provide a director's company car or private medical cover. From 6 April 2027 they must report the benefit and deduct the tax through payroll software in real time.
scope.excluded: Employer-provided loans and accommodation are excluded from mandatory payrolling at both the 2027 and 2028 dates - HMRC says these are particularly burdensome for payroll and further work continues, so they stay on end-of-year reporting. Benefits provided to globally mobile employees are also out of scope (HMRC estimates around 235,000 such employees and up to around 21,000 employers affected). Transitional arrangements mean some benefits stay outside mandation at both dates, so the start date does not apply uniformly to every employer and every benefit. Employers who provide no benefits in kind at all have nothing to do. Benefits already covered by an exemption (for example trivial benefits) are not reportable and so are unaffected.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2027 for medical benefits, company cars, vans, and car and van fuel. 6 April 2028 for most remaining benefits. Budget 2026 on 28 October 2026 delayed the first phase from 6 April 2026 to 6 April 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim - a duty on the employer. Employers need payroll software that can report benefits in kind through Real Time Information, and must be ready for 6 April 2027. Employers wanting to start early, or to payroll benefits that are not being mandated, can register for voluntary payrolling through HMRC's registration service, which re-opened on 5 November 2026.

notes: This is a change of plumbing with a real cash-flow effect, and three things get misread. First, the start date has moved: it was 6 April 2026, Budget 2026 pushed the first phase to 6 April 2027, so any adviser working from older notes will be a year out. Second, it is phased, not a single switch - only medical benefits, company cars, vans and car and van fuel are caught in 2027, most of the rest follow in 2028, and employer-provided loans and living accommodation are not being mandated at either date and stay on the old end-of-year route. Third, P11D does not simply vanish: HMRC says existing end-of-year reporting continues for benefits not yet in scope or until alternative arrangements are confirmed, so many employers will run both processes side by side. Employees should expect a bigger PAYE deduction from April 2027 because tax on the benefit is collected in the year rather than later through a tax code, and in the first two years some people will be paying current-year benefits through payroll while still settling earlier years the old way - HMRC says it will remove the mandated current-year benefit from tax codes to prevent double taxation. There is a one-year softening: penalties can be waived for non-deliberate inaccuracies for 2027-28 only. Secondary legislation on exactly how benefits and the associated Class 1A National Insurance are reported and paid is still to come, so recheck before relying on the detail.

title: High Value Council Tax Surcharge on homes worth £2 million or more in England

figures.what: Value a residential property in England must reach to be in scope of the surcharge
The year in which property values are assessed for the surcharge
Date the surcharge takes effect
Premium applied to homes left empty for 12 months or more, confirmed at Budget 2026
Estimated revenue from 2028-29, to support local services

scope.who: Owners of residential property in England valued at £2 million or more, with values assessed in 2026. The surcharge is additional to the existing Council Tax bill on the property.
scope.excluded: Every residential property in England valued below £2 million in the 2026 assessment is outside the surcharge, which is the overwhelming majority of homes - an ordinary Birmingham or West Midlands household is not affected. All property outside England is excluded: Scotland and Wales run their own council tax and property tax policy and are not covered, and Northern Ireland has domestic rates rather than council tax so the surcharge has no application there at all. Non-residential and commercial property is excluded, as that pays business rates rather than Council Tax. The government confirmed at Budget 2026 that there will also be a set of discounts and exemptions and a deferral scheme, but the published factsheet does not yet specify who they cover - these are to be legislated in Finance Bill 2026-27.
scope.from_when: April 2028. Announced at Budget 2026 on 28 October 2026 and to be legislated in Finance Bill 2026-27.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim to be charged - local authorities will collect the surcharge on behalf of central government and are fully compensated for their administration costs. A deferral scheme, discounts and exemptions were confirmed at Budget 2026 but the detail, including how to apply, has not yet been published.

notes: Three things to get right. First, this is England only - it is not a UK property tax. Scotland and Wales set their own council tax policy and are not in scope, and Northern Ireland does not have council tax at all (it has domestic rates), so the surcharge cannot apply there. Second, it is a surcharge on top of existing Council Tax, not a replacement for it and not a reband: a property stays in its existing Council Tax band and the surcharge is added. Third, the valuation date matters more than the charge date - values are assessed in 2026 but the charge starts in April 2028, so an owner whose home is near the £2 million line should care about the 2026 assessment, not the 2028 market. The amounts actually payable, the value bands above £2 million, the deferral scheme and the list of discounts and exemptions are NOT yet in the published factsheet; only the £2 million entry threshold, the England-only scope, the April 2028 start, the 100% empty-homes premium and the £400 million revenue estimate are confirmed at primary source. Do not quote a surcharge amount until Finance Bill 2026-27 detail is published. Separately, the £100 Household Energy Payment for Council Tax bands A to D is a different England-only measure and should not be conflated with this.

title: Asking HMRC to collect your Self Assessment bill through your tax code: 30 December deadline

figures.what: the maximum Self Assessment balance that can be collected through your PAYE tax code
deadline to file the online tax return if you want the tax collected through your tax code (30 December 2026 for the 2025-26 return)
deadline to file a paper tax return if you want the tax collected through your tax code (31 October 2026 for the 2025-26 return)
HMRC will not use your tax code if doing so would mean you pay more than 50% of your PAYE income in tax
HMRC will not use your tax code if you would end up paying more than twice as much tax as you normally do

scope.nation: UK-wide. The route works the same for taxpayers in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, because it is a PAYE and Self Assessment mechanism, not a devolved scheme.
scope.who: People who owe less than £3,000 on their Self Assessment bill AND already pay tax through PAYE (for example as an employee or on a company pension), AND who filed on paper by 31 October 2026 or file online by 30 December 2026 for the 2025-26 return.
scope.excluded: You cannot use it if you owe £3,000 or more (you cannot make a part payment to get under the threshold — HMRC will refuse it); if you do not have enough PAYE income for HMRC to collect the amount; if it would mean paying more than 50% of your PAYE income in tax; or if you would end up paying more than twice as much tax as normal. Self-employed people generally cannot pay Class 2 National Insurance this way unless it has been due since before 6 April 2015. People with no PAYE income at all (for example a sole trader with no employment or pension) are outside it entirely.
scope.from_when: For the 2025-26 tax return: file online by 30 December 2026. Tax is then collected through the PAYE code in a later tax year, not on 31 January 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: There is no separate form. File the 2025-26 Self Assessment return online by 30 December 2026 (or the paper return by 31 October 2026) and meet all the conditions on the GOV.UK page; HMRC then adjusts your tax code instead of asking for a lump sum.

notes: The thing readers get wrong: 30 December is NOT an extension of the 31 January filing deadline — it is only the cut-off for this one payment route. Miss 30 December and the return is still due by 31 January 2027 and the bill is still payable in full on 31 January 2027. Also, the £3,000 test is on what you owe, not on your income, and you cannot part-pay your way under it. Nation makes no difference here.

title: Paying employers' PAYE, National Insurance and CIS deductions: the 22nd (electronic) and the 19th (post)

figures.what: deadline for electronic payment of PAYE, NICs and CIS deductions if you pay monthly — 22 December 2026 for the 6 November to 5 December tax month, and 22 January 2027 for the 6 December to 5 January tax month
deadline if you pay by cheque through the post — the cheque must reach HMRC by the 19th

figures.value: 22nd after the end of the quarter
figures.what: deadline for quarterly payers, for example 22 July for the 6 April to 5 July quarter; the 6 October to 5 January quarter is therefore due 22 January 2027
employers paying more than £1,500 per month (or £18,000 or more a year) must pay monthly; below that average they may pay quarterly
what HMRC counts as electronic payment on time and in full — HMRC must have received cleared funds for the full amount by the 22nd

scope.nation: UK-wide. PAYE and the Construction Industry Scheme are reserved, so the dates are identical in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: Employers operating a PAYE scheme, and CIS contractors paying over deductions made from subcontractors.
scope.excluded: Employers whose average monthly payment is below £1,500 (under £18,000 a year) are not bound by the monthly 22nd date — they pay quarterly by the 22nd after the quarter end instead. Businesses with no PAYE scheme and subcontractors (who have deductions taken from them rather than paying them over) are outside this altogether.
scope.from_when: Continuing monthly and quarterly obligation. The two dates in this window are 22 December 2026 and 22 January 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. Pay HMRC by the due date using your 13-character accounts office reference plus the 4-digit period number, electronically by the 22nd or by posted cheque reaching HMRC by the 19th.

notes: Two traps in this window. First, 19 December 2026 is a Saturday, so an employer still paying by posted cheque has in practice to get it to HMRC by Friday 18 December. Second, HMRC's own manual measures the electronic deadline as CLEARED FUNDS in its account by the 22nd, not as the day you press send — Faster Payments usually land same or next day, but Bacs and cheques need several working days, and the bank holidays on 25 and 28 December 2026 and 1 January 2027 cut the number of banking days available. 22 December 2026 is a Tuesday and 22 January 2027 is a Friday, so neither date itself falls on a weekend.

title: CIS monthly return: the 19th deadline and the late filing penalty scale

figures.what: deadline to send the CIS monthly return, following the last tax month — so 19 December 2026 for the month to 5 December 2026 and 19 January 2027 for the month to 5 January 2027
penalty once the CIS return is 1 day late
further penalty once the return is 2 months late

figures.value: £300 or 5% of the CIS deductions, whichever is higher
figures.what: further penalty once the return is 6 months late

figures.value: £300 or 5% of the CIS deductions, whichever is higher
figures.what: further penalty once the return is 12 months late

figures.value: up to £3,000 or 100% of the CIS deductions
figures.what: additional penalty that may be charged for returns more than 12 months late

scope.nation: UK-wide. The Construction Industry Scheme runs identically in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: CIS contractors — anyone who pays subcontractors for construction work. A return is due every month, including a nil return showing payments of 0 if you paid no subcontractors that month.
scope.excluded: Subcontractors do not file monthly CIS returns and are not exposed to these penalties. A contractor who has told HMRC they have temporarily stopped using subcontractors (an inactivity request) does not need to file nil returns for the months that request covers, so no penalty arises for them.
scope.from_when: Continuing monthly obligation. Returns in this window: due 19 December 2026 and 19 January 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. File the monthly return online by the 19th, or make an inactivity request if you have temporarily stopped using subcontractors.

notes: The penalty that catches people out is on the NIL return: if you used no subcontractors in the month you must still file showing 0, or ask HMRC for an inactivity period — forgetting it costs £100 even though no tax was due. The penalties stack rather than replace each other, and the 6 and 12 month charges are the higher of £300 or 5% of the deductions on the return, so a big month can produce a penalty far above £300. Note the CIS return date is the 19th even for contractors who pay HMRC electronically by the 22nd — filing and paying have different dates.

title: Capital Gains Tax on UK residential property: report and pay within 60 days

figures.what: time limit to report and pay Capital Gains Tax due on UK residential property, running from the completion date (the date you stopped being the owner), not from exchange of contracts
the same 60-day limit confirmed in HMRC's policy paper on late filing penalties for UK property disposal returns

date from which, where a residential property disposal is reported on a Self Assessment return, late filing penalties on the separate property return stop accruing once that Self Assessment return is submitted

scope.nation: UK-wide. Capital Gains Tax is not devolved, so the 60-day return applies to residential property anywhere in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: UK residents who dispose of UK residential property and have Capital Gains Tax to pay on it, and non-residents, who must report all sales and disposals of UK property or land by the deadline even if there is no tax to pay.
scope.excluded: UK residents do not need to report online if total gains are less than the tax-free allowance, so a disposal fully covered by reliefs or the annual exempt amount needs no 60-day return. The 60-day rule as set out on this page is about UK RESIDENTIAL property — a UK resident selling commercial property is not brought into it by this page and reports through Self Assessment instead. Non-residents get no equivalent let-off: they must report even with nothing to pay.
scope.from_when: Applies to disposals completing on or after 6 April 2020 and is a rolling 60-day clock, so a completion on 16 November 2026 falls due by 15 January 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Report through HMRC's Capital Gains Tax on UK property account and pay within the 60 days; the gain is then also reported again on the Self Assessment return for the year if you file one.

notes: The 60 days run from COMPLETION, not exchange — a November completion can fall due in January, in the middle of Self Assessment season. Three further points readers get wrong: it is a separate return from Self Assessment and filing the tax return does not replace it; the tax has to be PAID inside the 60 days, not just reported; and non-residents must file even where the gain is nil. Interest and late filing penalties run from the 60-day point, although from 28 October 2026 penalties stop accruing once a Self Assessment return covering the disposal is filed.

title: Inheritance Tax on unused pension funds and death benefits from 6 April 2027

figures.what: the measure takes effect in respect of deaths on or after this date, bringing most unused pension funds and pension death benefits into the value of a person's estate for Inheritance Tax
the share of death benefits potentially subject to Inheritance Tax that a beneficiary may access where personal representatives direct withholding
the period after the date of death for which that withholding of death benefits can apply

scope.nation: UK-wide. Inheritance Tax is reserved, so this applies in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: Estates within the scope of Inheritance Tax where the person who died held unused pension funds or where pension death benefits are paid, and the people who deal with them — beneficiaries, personal representatives and their advisers, plus pension scheme administrators who must share information.
scope.excluded: Death in service benefits payable from a registered pension scheme are excluded. So are dependants' scheme pensions from a defined benefit arrangement or a collective money purchase arrangement. Death benefits passing to a surviving spouse or civil partner, or to a registered charity, keep their existing exemption. And most estates are unaffected: HMRC states that most estates will continue to have no Inheritance Tax liability after 6 April 2027 and will have no extra interaction with HMRC.
scope.from_when: Deaths on or after 6 April 2027. Deaths before that date are not affected.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. Personal representatives are liable for reporting and paying any Inheritance Tax due on unused pension funds and death benefits; pension scheme administrators must provide information and support payment.

notes: The thing clients get wrong is thinking pensions are still outside the estate — from deaths on or after 6 April 2027 most unused pension funds count. But the headline must not be overstated: the spouse and civil partner exemption and the charity exemption survive, death in service benefits from a registered scheme are out, and HMRC itself says most estates will still pay no Inheritance Tax. The reporting and payment burden sits with personal representatives, not the pension scheme, so executors face a new information-gathering job. This is legislated policy with the detail still settling, so recheck before using any figure beyond the start date.

title: Telling HMRC about a company car: the quarterly P46(Car) dates

figures.what: deadline to tell HMRC about a company car provided, changed or withdrawn in the 6 October to 5 January quarter — so 2 February 2027 for changes up to 5 January 2027
deadline for changes in the 6 January to 5 April quarter
deadline for changes in the 6 April to 5 July quarter
deadline for changes in the 6 July to 5 October quarter

scope.nation: UK-wide. Company car benefit reporting is reserved and the dates are the same across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: Employers who provide, change or stop providing a car available for an employee's or director's private use and who do not payroll their employees' taxable benefits and expenses — HMRC's payrolling guidance states that employers who do not payroll benefits must continue to complete form P46(Car).
scope.excluded: You do not need to tell HMRC about pool cars used by more than one employee for business purposes and normally kept on your premises; cars adapted for employees with a disability where the only private use is home-to-work journeys; or emergency vehicles used only by on-call employees of the police, fire and rescue, ambulance or paramedic services. Employers who payroll car and car fuel benefit send the car data through their payroll submissions instead of a P46(Car).
scope.from_when: Continuing quarterly obligation. The next date is 2 February 2027, covering changes made between 6 October 2026 and 5 January 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Report online through HMRC's PAYE service, or complete the P46(Car) on screen, print it and post it to HMRC.

notes: Two things get missed. First, the duty is triggered by a CHANGE — a car starting, a car being swapped, or a car being taken away — not just by a new joiner, and a withdrawn car reported late means the employee keeps paying tax on a car they no longer have. Second, this is separate from the end-of-year benefit reporting and from paying Class 1A National Insurance on the car's value. From 6 April 2027 mandatory payrolling of car and car fuel benefit changes how most employers handle this, so the P46(Car) route should be rechecked for 2027-28.

title: Bank holidays over Christmas 2026 and New Year 2027, and what they do to payment timing

figures.what: Christmas Day — a bank holiday in England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland
Boxing Day substitute day — a bank holiday in England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland
New Year's Day — a bank holiday in England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland
substitute day for 2nd January — a bank holiday in SCOTLAND ONLY

figures.value: cleared funds by the due date
figures.what: HMRC's test for an electronic PAYE payment being on time and in full, which is why the number of banking days left matters over the holidays

scope.nation: England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland all have 25 December 2026, 28 December 2026 and 1 January 2027. Scotland additionally has Monday 4 January 2027. Northern Ireland has no extra bank holiday in this window.
scope.who: Anyone paying HMRC, a supplier or a payroll between mid-December 2026 and early January 2027, and employers planning pay dates and office closures.
scope.excluded: Monday 4 January 2027 is NOT a bank holiday in England, Wales or Northern Ireland — only in Scotland. Bank holidays are not an automatic entitlement to paid time off for workers; an employer's contracts decide that, so a reader should not treat this list as a statutory leave list.
scope.from_when: Dates confirmed for December 2026 and January 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. Use the dates to work backwards from HMRC deadlines of 19 December 2026, 22 December 2026, 19 January 2027, 22 January 2027 and 31 January 2027.

notes: Plain terms on the nation split: the Christmas and New Year holidays are the same across the UK this year, with one exception — Scotland gets Monday 4 January 2027 as the substitute for 2 January, England, Wales and Northern Ireland do not. The practical point for clients is banking days, not holidays: with 25 and 28 December shut and 1 January shut, a Bacs payment or a cheque posted in the Christmas week can easily miss a 19 or 22 December HMRC deadline, while Faster Payments usually still land the same or next day. Work backwards from the deadline rather than forwards from the date you intended to pay.

title: Company Tax Return: the 12-month filing deadline and HMRC's late filing penalties

figures.value: 12 months after the end of the accounting period
figures.what: deadline to file the Company Tax Return — so a 31 December 2025 year end must be filed by 31 December 2026

figures.value: 9 months and one day after the end of the accounting period
figures.what: the separate, earlier deadline to PAY Corporation Tax
HMRC penalty once the Company Tax Return is 1 day late
further HMRC penalty once the return is 3 months late
penalty at 6 months late, when HMRC estimates the Corporation Tax bill
penalty at 12 months late
the two £200 penalties rise to £1,000 each if the return is late three times in a row

scope.nation: UK-wide. Corporation Tax is reserved, so the deadline and penalties are the same for companies registered in England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
scope.who: A company or association that has received a notice to deliver a Company Tax Return from HMRC. You must still send a return if you made a loss or have no Corporation Tax to pay.
scope.excluded: You do not send a Company Tax Return if you are self-employed as a sole trader or a member of a partnership — you file a Self Assessment return instead. The penalties here are HMRC penalties on the tax return; they are not the Companies House penalties for late accounts, which are charged separately on a different deadline.
scope.from_when: Continuing obligation. In this window, companies with a 31 December 2025 year end must file by 31 December 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. File the Company Tax Return online with HMRC by the 12-month deadline, having already paid the Corporation Tax at 9 months and one day.

notes: Two separate mistakes to head off. First, paying and filing are different dates: for a 31 December 2025 year end the tax was due 1 October 2026 but the return is not due until 31 December 2026 — paying late accrues interest even if the return is on time. Second, a company filing late can be penalised TWICE, once by HMRC on the tax return and once by Companies House on the accounts; these are different regimes with different deadlines and different appeal routes. A loss-making or break-even company still has to file. Note the HMRC fixed penalties are £200, not the £100 figure that older write-ups still quote.

title: State Pension Rates Proposed for 2027 to 2028

figures.what: new State Pension full rate proposed for 2027 to 2028
new State Pension full rate for 2026 to 2027 (the rate it rises from)
old (basic) State Pension Category A or B rate proposed for 2027 to 2028
old (basic) State Pension Category A or B rate for 2026 to 2027
increase applied to State Pension increments and the statutory minimum increase for non-state pensions in 2027 to 2028 (3.80% in 2026 to 2027)

scope.nation: Great Britain. DWP sets these rates; Northern Ireland legislates its own matching rates separately through the Department for Communities.
scope.who: People who have reached State Pension age. The £250.70 full rate is the new State Pension, for people who reached State Pension age on or after 6 April 2016. The £192.10 rate is the Category A or B basic pension of the old scheme.
scope.excluded: Anyone who reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016 is on the old scheme and gets the £192.10 basic rate, not £250.70. Anyone who has not yet reached State Pension age gets nothing. The full rate is only paid where the National Insurance record is complete — a short record pays a proportion, not £250.70. These are PROPOSED rates and are not yet law, so nobody is entitled to them yet.
scope.from_when: Proposed for the 2027 to 2028 tax year, published 11 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: The uprating is automatic for people already being paid State Pension. A first claim must still be made — State Pension is not paid until it is claimed.

notes: This is a PROPOSED rates document published 11 November 2026, not final law: the figures take effect through a Social Security Benefits Up-rating Order that is normally laid in January or February and debated before April. The new State Pension rises about 3.9% (£241.30 to £250.70) while the separate increment and non-state-pension figure on the same page is 3.50% — do not confuse the two. The £250.70 headline is above the frozen personal allowance territory, so pensioners with any other income can be pushed into tax; the page says nothing about tax. Northern Ireland keeps parity but is a separate legal instrument. Scotland has devolved some disability benefits but NOT the State Pension.

title: Statutory Paternity Pay Rate and Threshold for 2027 to 2028

figures.what: Statutory Paternity Pay standard rate proposed for 2027 to 2028
Statutory Paternity Pay standard rate for 2026 to 2027 (the rate it rises from)
average weekly earnings threshold to qualify for Statutory Paternity Pay in 2027 to 2028 (up from £129.00)
what is paid instead of the standard rate where 90% of average weekly earnings is lower
continuous employment with the same employer needed up to any day in the qualifying week (the 15th week before the baby is due)

scope.nation: Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales). Northern Ireland runs its own equivalent scheme.
scope.who: An employee who is the father, the husband or partner of the mother or adopter, the child's adopter, or an intended parent in a surrogacy arrangement; who is on the employer's payroll up to the child's birth or placement; who has at least 26 weeks' continuous employment up to the qualifying week; and whose average weekly earnings reach the threshold.
scope.excluded: Anyone who is not classed as an employee — workers, contractors and the self-employed get no paternity leave and no paternity pay. Employees averaging less than the earnings threshold (£129 in 2026 to 2027, £133 proposed for 2027 to 2028) over the 8-week relevant period. Employees with under 26 weeks' continuous employment with that employer at the qualifying week. Employees who do not give the employer correct notice. Employees who are not taking the time off to care for the child or the mother, or who are not responsible for the child's upbringing.
scope.from_when: £201.11 proposed for the 2027 to 2028 tax year; £194.32 applies for 2026 to 2027
scope.how_to_claim: The employee must give the employer the correct notice and claim from the employer, who pays it through payroll. Tax and National Insurance are deducted from Statutory Paternity Pay.

notes: Two separate numbers move and clients mix them up: the pay rate (£194.32 to £201.11) and the earnings threshold to qualify at all (£129 to £133). An employee just above £129 this year may still be below £133 next year if their pay has not moved — they lose entitlement, not just value. Paternity leave itself needs no qualifying service (day one of employment), but paternity PAY needs 26 weeks — an employer who conflates the two underpays or overpays. The 2027 to 2028 figures are PROPOSED (published 11 November 2026) and take effect through an uprating order not yet made. Northern Ireland has a separate scheme at parity rates. Statutory Paternity Pay counts towards the benefit cap for the household.

title: Benefit Cap Held at the Same Level for 2027 to 2028

figures.what: benefit cap for a couple, or a single claimant with a child, in Greater London — unchanged from 2026 to 2027
benefit cap for a couple, or a single claimant with a child, in the rest of Great Britain — unchanged from 2026 to 2027
benefit cap for a single adult with no children in Greater London — unchanged from 2026 to 2027
benefit cap for a single adult with no children in the rest of Great Britain — unchanged from 2026 to 2027
combined household earnings after tax and National Insurance that exempt a Universal Credit household from the cap

scope.nation: Great Britain, with a higher cap inside Greater London and a lower one everywhere else. Northern Ireland operates its own benefit cap and its own mitigation arrangements.
scope.who: Households getting Universal Credit or Housing Benefit whose total capped benefits exceed the limit. The benefits counted towards the cap include Universal Credit, Housing Benefit, Child Benefit, Employment and Support Allowance, Jobseeker's Allowance, Maternity Allowance, Incapacity Benefit, Severe Disablement Allowance, Bereavement Allowance and Widowed Parent's Allowance.
scope.excluded: Not affected if you, your partner or a child under 18 living with you gets any of: Personal Independence Payment, Disability Living Allowance, Adult Disability Payment, Child Disability Payment, Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance, Pension Age Disability Payment, Attendance Allowance, Carer's Allowance, Carer Support Payment, Guardian's Allowance, Armed Forces Independence Payment, Armed Forces Compensation Scheme payments, Industrial Injuries Benefits, war pensions, War Widow's or War Widower's Pension, or the support component of Employment and Support Allowance. Also not affected if you are over State Pension age, if you have limited capability for work and work-related activity on Universal Credit, if you are caring for someone with a disability, or if combined household earnings are £881 or more a month after tax and National Insurance. A Universal Credit household with enough recent earnings also gets a delay of up to 9 months before the cap starts.
scope.from_when: Levels published 11 November 2026 as the proposed 2027 to 2028 figures, identical to 2026 to 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — the cap is applied automatically by DWP or the council. Exemption is also automatic once the qualifying benefit is in payment, so the action is to make sure that benefit is claimed.

notes: The news here is the freeze, not a figure: every one of the four cap levels is the same in 2027 to 2028 as in 2026 to 2027, while most benefits on the same page rise. A capped household therefore gets nothing from the uprating — the increase is clawed straight back. Greater London is a hard administrative boundary, so the same family a mile either side of it has a different cap. Birmingham and the West Midlands sit on the lower, rest-of-Great-Britain figures. Northern Ireland has domestic rates rather than council tax and runs its own cap, so do not quote these numbers there. The single quickest exemption route for a working household is getting combined take-home earnings to £881 a month.

title: Universal Credit Child Element and Childcare Costs for 2027 to 2028

figures.what: Universal Credit child element proposed for 2027 to 2028 for a first child born before 6 April 2017 (up from £351.88)
Universal Credit child element proposed for 2027 to 2028 for a first child born on or after 6 April 2017 and for subsequent children (up from £303.94)
maximum Universal Credit childcare costs amount for one child proposed for 2027 to 2028 (up from £1,071.09)
maximum Universal Credit childcare costs amount for two or more children shown for 2027 to 2028 (up from £1,836.16) — being replaced by an amount that rises with each additional child

scope.nation: Great Britain. Northern Ireland runs Universal Credit through the Department for Communities at parity rates.
scope.who: Universal Credit claimants responsible for a child or qualifying young person get the child element. The childcare costs amount is a separate element on top, for claimants paying for registered childcare.
scope.excluded: A first child born on or after 6 April 2017 gets the lower £314.58 rate, not £364.20 — the higher rate is closed to children born from that date. The childcare costs amount is not paid to households that are not getting Universal Credit, and the figures above are MAXIMUMS, not entitlements: a household paying less than the maximum gets the lower actual-cost figure, and the amount is capped as a percentage of the childcare actually paid for. The two-or-more-children figure of £1,900.43 is itself provisional — the page says this maximum is being replaced by one that rises for each additional child and that the table will be updated once the regulations are laid, so a household with three or more children cannot yet be told its figure.
scope.from_when: Proposed for the 2027 to 2028 tax year, published 11 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: The uprating is automatic. The childcare costs element must be claimed and the childcare costs reported through the Universal Credit account each assessment period, in arrears.

notes: The structural change matters more than the uprating: the current flat cap for two or more children is being replaced with an amount that increases per additional child, and the published table is explicitly incomplete until the regulations are laid. A family with three or more children in childcare should not be quoted a 2027 to 2028 figure yet. The 6 April 2017 birth-date split in the child element is the single most common thing clients get wrong — it is the child's date of birth that decides the rate, not the date of the claim. Childcare costs are paid in arrears against receipts, which is a cash-flow problem for low-paid clients and is not something an uprating fixes. These are PROPOSED figures, not yet law.

title: CSOP and EMI Share Option Limits Rise from April 2027

figures.what: new CSOP individual share option limit from 6 April 2027
current CSOP individual share option limit, in force since 6 April 2023 (£30,000 for options granted before that date)
new maximum CSOP exercise period from 6 April 2027 (current tax-free window is between 3 and 10 years after grant)
new window to exercise EMI options after a disqualifying event, from 6 April 2027
extended period for which certain shares and options reserved by third parties are excepted from the disguised remuneration rules

scope.who: Companies that operate a Schedule 4 Company Share Option Plan or an Enterprise Management Incentives scheme, and the employees and directors holding options under them. Also companies arranging to become controlled by an Employee Ownership Trust, where the existing EMI exception is being extended.
scope.excluded: A company that does not operate a tax-advantaged CSOP or EMI scheme gets nothing from this — it is not a relief you claim, it is a change to scheme limits. Options granted before 6 April 2027 stay under the current £60,000 CSOP limit until the change takes effect; there is no retrospective uplift. The £120,000 is not per plan: the CSOP limit is tested on the aggregate market value at grant across the individual's subsisting options under that scheme AND under any other Schedule 4 CSOP run by the same company or an associated company, so running a second plan does not double it. The limit is fixed at grant and is not recalculated if the share price later falls. The measure does not change the EMI individual option limit or the EMI company size and trade qualifying tests, so a company too large for EMI is still too large for EMI.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim, but scheme rules, option agreements and the plan's exercise-period drafting will need amending to use the higher limit and longer window. The change is to be legislated in Finance Bill 2026-27 and is not yet law.

notes: The policy paper was first published at Budget on 28 October 2026 and UPDATED on 12 November 2026 (impacts table added) — the 12 November update is what is new this week. The figures are not on the policy paper itself; they are in the Budget 2026 Overview of Tax Legislation and Rates, measure 1.6. Doubling the CSOP individual limit to £120,000 and stretching the exercise window to 15 years makes CSOP a realistic option for owner-managed companies that outgrew EMI, which is the practical point for clients. Two traps: the limit is aggregated across associated companies, and the removal of the CSOP/EMI limit interaction only takes effect from 6 April 2027, so an option granted in, say, February 2027 is still caught by the old interaction. Nothing should be granted on the new basis before the Finance Bill is enacted.

title: Partnership Tax Return: 31 January 2027 Deadline and the Separate Penalty Each Partner Gets

figures.what: Online filing deadline for the 2025-26 Partnership Tax Return (SA800), tax year 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026
Paper filing deadline for the same 2025-26 SA800 (already passed)
Automatic fixed late-filing penalty charged on EACH relevant partner under TMA 1970 s93A(2) when the partnership return is late - not £100 for the partnership
Further fixed penalty on each relevant partner if the failure continues beyond six months from the filing date (s93A(4)) - so £200 per partner in total

scope.who: The nominated partner files one SA800 for the partnership for 2025-26. Every individual partner then reports their share on their own SA100 partnership pages by the same 31 January 2027 date.
scope.excluded: Sole traders (no SA800 exists for them). Limited companies, which file a CT600 instead. A partnership that has not been issued a notice to file. A person who was not a partner at any time in the period covered by the return is not a 'relevant partner' and gets no penalty. Partnerships that include a company as a partner do NOT get the 31 October / 31 January dates - HMRC sets different filing dates for them. Partnerships issued a notice to file after 31 July 2026 also get a different date.
scope.from_when: 2025-26 return, due 31 January 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Nominated partner files SA800 online by 31 January 2027 (HMRC online service does not support SA800 - commercial software or an agent is needed). Each partner separately files their own return by the same date.

notes: The trap clients get wrong: a late partnership return multiplies. HMRC charges the £100 on all persons who were partners at any time in the return period, so a four-partner firm one day late is £400, and £800 once six months pass. EM4585 also confirms partners get no capping or reduction where their own tax liability is lower than the penalty - unlike individuals and trustees. Only the nominated partner can appeal, and that one appeal covers every partner's penalty. Daily penalties under s93A(3) exist but need an authorised officer's agreement and are reserved for large cases.

title: Trust Registration Service: the 31 January Declaration and 90-Day Deadlines

figures.what: Date by which trustees of a taxable trust must declare on the Trust Registration Service that the trust's details are up to date, for a 2025-26 relevant UK tax liability
Window to register a trust created on or after 6 April 2021 from the date it becomes liable to a relevant UK tax; also the window to update the register after any change to trust details
Registration deadline for a pre-6 April 2021 trust with a FIRST-time Income Tax or CGT liability arising in 2025-26 (earlier than the 31 January date)

Separate deadline to report and pay CGT on a disposal of UK residential property by the trust, from the date of sale - the trust must be registered as taxable before the CGT on UK property account can be used

scope.nation: UK-wide (HMRC register under the Money Laundering Regulations). Trust law itself differs in Scotland and Northern Ireland but the registration duty is the same.
scope.who: Trustees of a UK express trust, and of a non-UK trust with UK tax liabilities or UK land. Trustees of a TAXABLE trust (liable to Income Tax, CGT, Inheritance Tax, SDLT, LBTT, LTT or Stamp Duty Reserve Tax) must also make the annual 31 January declaration that the register is current.
scope.excluded: Non-taxable trusts do NOT make the 31 January declaration - they only have to keep the register updated within 90 days of a change. Schedule 3A excluded trusts need no registration at all unless they become liable to UK tax: statutory trusts created by court order or by law, UK registered pension scheme trusts, life policy trusts paying out only on death, illness or disability, trusts for a registered UK charity, trusts set up to open a child's bank account, will trusts wound up within 2 years of death, pilot trusts holding under £100 set up before 6 October 2020, co-ownership trusts holding jointly owned property as tenants in common, client-money and professional-services trusts, trusts set up by a UK government body or public authority, and Scottish survivorship destination trusts.
scope.from_when: Annual duty; the next declaration date is 31 January 2027 for 2025-26 liabilities
scope.how_to_claim: Trustee or agent signs into the Manage your trust's details service on GOV.UK with the trust's Government Gateway credentials, checks the details and submits the declaration. Agents need an agent services account and the client's authorisation.

notes: Two things clients get wrong. First, the 31 January declaration is NOT the same thing as the SA900 Trust and Estate Tax Return - a taxable trust that files SA900 still has to go into TRS separately and declare the register is current, and HMRC will not issue the SA900 Unique Taxpayer Reference until the trust is registered. Second, a trust that was non-taxable and becomes taxable in a year moves onto the taxable-trust deadlines, so the 31 January declaration starts applying. TRSM40030 also warns that where more than one tax could set a deadline, the EARLIER deadline applies - that is how a pre-2021 trust with a first Income Tax liability ends up with a 5 October date rather than 31 January.

title: Corporation Tax Quarterly Instalments: £1.5 Million Threshold and the 14 January 2027 Payment

figures.what: Annual rate of taxable profits above which a company is 'large' and must pay Corporation Tax by quarterly instalments instead of 9 months and 1 day after the year end
Profits level at and above which a company is 'very large' and pays all its instalments inside the accounting period itself, on a different timetable
Ceiling for the first-year let-off: a company with profits no more than £10 million does not have to pay by instalments if it was not large in any accounting period ending in the previous 12 months
Third instalment for a large company with a 12-month accounting period running 1 January to 31 December 2026 (instalments 14 July 2026, 14 October 2026, 14 January 2027, 14 April 2027)
Gap from the start of a 12-month accounting period to the first instalment; the remaining three fall at 3-month intervals, the last one 3 months and 14 days after the period ends

scope.who: Companies and other Corporation Tax payers with taxable profits at an annual rate of more than £1.5 million but less than £20 million. Payment must be made electronically.
scope.excluded: Companies with profits at an annual rate of £1.5 million or less - they pay in one go 9 months and 1 day after the year end. Companies with profits up to £10 million in their first large year, where they were not large in any accounting period ending in the preceding 12 months, including a newly incorporated company that had no accounting period in that period. Very large companies with profits of £20 million or more are outside this timetable and follow the separate, earlier very-large schedule.
scope.from_when: Current rules; the £1.5m threshold reverted to being divided by the number of associated companies for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2023
scope.how_to_claim: Company estimates its own liability and pays each instalment electronically by the due date without waiting for a demand from HMRC.

notes: The trap is associated companies. Both the £1.5 million and the £10 million limits are divided by the number of associated or related 51% group companies plus the company itself, so a company in a group of five hits instalments at £300,000 of profits, not £1.5 million. The same associated-company count drives the marginal relief thresholds, so a client who has just picked up a second company can find itself paying in instalments on profits it would have paid annually the year before. Short accounting periods also get a proportionately reduced threshold, and a period of 3 months or less produces one payment rather than instalments. Nothing on this page is a filing deadline - the CT600 is still due 12 months after the period end.

title: Quarterly PAYE Payers: £1,500 a Month Rule and the 22 January 2027 Deadline

figures.what: Average monthly PAYE and NIC payment below which an employer can pay HMRC quarterly instead of monthly (less than £18,000 a year)
Electronic payment deadline for quarter 3, the tax period 6 October 2026 to 5 January 2027 - cleared funds must reach HMRC by this date
Deadline for the same quarter if paying by cheque through the post
Electronic deadline for the monthly period 6 November to 5 December 2026, for employers who pay monthly rather than quarterly (19 December 2026 by post)

scope.nation: UK-wide (PAYE is not devolved; Scottish and Welsh rate taxpayers are still paid over through the same PAYE scheme)
scope.who: Employers with reasonable grounds to believe their average monthly PAYE, NIC, student loan and CIS payment across the full tax year will be under £1,500. Quarters run to 5 July, 5 October, 5 January and 5 April.
scope.excluded: Employers paying £1,500 a month or more on average (£18,000 or more a year) cannot pay quarterly - they must pay monthly. The quarterly option does not change RTI reporting: the FPS is still due on or before each payday whatever the payment frequency. It is not available simply because one quarter happens to be small; the test is the expected average across the whole tax year.
scope.from_when: Current rules; quarter 3 of 2026-27 is payable by 22 January 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Employer contacts the HMRC payment helpline to confirm eligibility to pay quarterly, then pays by Faster Payments, Bacs, debit card or direct debit so cleared funds reach HMRC by the 22nd.

notes: Two traps. First, quarterly payment is a payment concession only - the RTI Full Payment Submission is still due on or before every payday, so an employer who stops filing monthly because they now pay quarterly collects late-filing penalties. Second, the 19th and 22nd are dates by which HMRC must have the money, not dates to send it: Faster Payments is same or next day but Bacs takes three working days, and 19 December 2026 falls on a Saturday, so anyone still posting a cheque for the November-December month needs to be clear of that weekend. The 22nd itself is a Friday in January 2027 and a Tuesday in December 2026, so there is no weekend shift on the electronic dates.

title: Employment Intermediary Report: 5 February 2027 Deadline and £250 to £1,000 Penalties

figures.what: Deadline to send the employment intermediary report for the quarter 6 October 2026 to 5 January 2027
Last date a report for that 6 October to 5 January quarter can be replaced or corrected
Penalty for the first late quarterly report in a 12-month period
Penalty for the second late report in a 12-month period
Penalty for the third and each later late report in a 12-month period
Daily penalty where a report stays outstanding: £300 after 30 days and a further £300 after 60 days, then daily penalties for that return stop

scope.who: An agency or intermediary that, at any time in the quarter, supplies the services of individuals to a client, has a contract with that client, provides MORE THAN ONE worker's services, provides those services in the UK, and makes one or more payments for the services including payments to third parties.
scope.excluded: You do not report if you only introduce workers to clients, or only supply workers to another intermediary rather than holding the client contract. Personal service companies that supply a client with only one worker do not report. Intermediaries that operate PAYE on the workers' payments do not report. Anyone who has told HMRC they are no longer an intermediary, or who for a whole year does not provide more than one worker's services or make payments for services, is out. Separately, workers you leave OUT of a report include your own employees, workers with no UK tax liability, workers you did not find work for or did not pay in the period, actors, singers, musicians, other entertainers and fashion, photographic or artist models, and anyone whose payment details are already in another organisation's payroll submission.
scope.from_when: Current quarterly duty; next deadline 5 February 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Upload a CSV report through the Submit an employment intermediary report service on GOV.UK using a Government Gateway account.

notes: The trap most often missed is the nil report. If you are a specified intermediary but supplied no workers in the quarter, you must still file a nil report by 5 February 2027 - silence is a late report and attracts the £250. Penalties escalate on a rolling 12-month count, so an intermediary already two quarters behind is at £1,000 per report.
