The replacement window runs to 5 May 2027, which means an error spotted in March can be corrected without a penalty for inaccuracy. Supplying workers to another intermediary rather than to the end client shifts the duty up the chain, which is why construction and care sector clients with layered contracts should check who actually holds the client contract.

title: Gift Aid Carry Back: Must Be in the Original Return by 31 January 2027

figures.what: Filing date for the 2025-26 return; a Gift Aid donation made on or after 6 April 2026 can only be carried back into the 2025-26 return if that return reaches HMRC before the filing date
Where the carry-back amount goes on the SA100 for 2025-26

scope.nation: UK-wide. Scottish and Welsh taxpayers can carry back in the same way, but the relief follows their own rates and bands.
scope.who: Self Assessment taxpayers who have made Gift Aid donations since 6 April 2026 and want the relief given against 2025-26 income instead, typically because they paid higher-rate tax in 2025-26 but not now. The claim must be made in the ORIGINAL 2025-26 return.
scope.excluded: HMRC cannot accept a first claim, or an increased claim, in an AMENDED return - so anyone who files by 31 January and then tries to add the carry-back later in the amendment window loses it. Anyone who did not pay enough Income Tax or Capital Gains Tax in 2025-26 to cover the tax the charity reclaims cannot carry back that amount. Anyone not in Self Assessment for 2025-26 has no return to make the claim in. Donations made in 2025-26 itself are relieved in 2025-26 anyway and need no carry-back election.
scope.from_when: 2025-26 return, claim must be in the return filed by 31 January 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Enter the donation in box 8 on page TR 4 of the 2025-26 SA100 (or the equivalent box in the online return) and file by 31 January 2027.

notes: This is the one 31 January election that cannot be fixed afterwards. Everything else on a tax return can normally be amended up to 31 January 2028, but a Gift Aid carry-back claim is lost the moment the original return is filed without it, and lost outright if the return goes in after the filing date. Two conditions both have to hold: the return must be the original one, and it must be in on time. It is worth the most where income dropped between the two years - a client who was a higher-rate taxpayer in 2025-26 and a basic-rate taxpayer now gets 40% relief instead of none by carrying back. HS342 as published also carries an apparent typo referring to 'the year ended 5 April 2025' in the carry-back paragraph; the surrounding text and the box reference make clear it means the 2025-26 return.

title: Stamp Duty Land Tax: 14 Days to File and Pay, £100 and £200 Penalties

figures.what: Time from the effective date of the transaction to send the SDLT return and pay any tax - the return is due even if no tax is owed
Automatic fixed penalty for filing the SDLT return up to 3 months after the filing date
Automatic fixed penalty for filing more than 3 months after the filing date

figures.value: Up to 100% of the tax due
figures.what: Additional tax-based penalty where the return is still not filed 12 months after the filing date, on top of the fixed penalty
Chargeable consideration at or above which a return is generally required; at £39,999 or less no return is needed

scope.who: The purchaser in a land transaction in England or Northern Ireland, within 14 days of the effective date - usually completion, but it can be earlier where the contract is substantially performed, for example on paying about 90% of the price, taking possession or making the first rent payment.
scope.excluded: Scotland (Land and Buildings Transaction Tax, Revenue Scotland) and Wales (Land Transaction Tax, Welsh Revenue Authority) are outside SDLT entirely and have their own returns and deadlines. No SDLT return is needed where no money or other consideration was given, where the property was left to you in a will, where the transfer arises from a divorce or dissolution of a civil partnership, or where the price or value is £39,999 or less.
scope.from_when: Current rules
scope.how_to_claim: File the SDLT return online (usually by the conveyancer) and pay within 14 days of the effective date.

notes: Two things clients get wrong. First, the 14-day clock can start before completion: substantial performance - paying roughly 90% of the price, taking possession, or paying the first rent - is the effective date, which catches long-delayed completions and some lease arrangements. Second, the return itself is the obligation. A £100 penalty lands on a nil-tax transaction filed late, which happens on transfers of equity and low-value purchases people assume need nothing. Interest on late-paid tax runs from the day after the due date at the HM Treasury rate, is not a penalty, and cannot be appealed - though the fixed penalties can be.

title: CT61: 20% Tax on Interest a Company Pays, Due 14 January 2027

figures.what: Basic rate Income Tax the company must deduct from yearly interest and certain other payments, using the rate in force on the date the payment is made
Time after the end of each return period to send the CT61 and pay the tax, without waiting for a demand
Due date for the CT61 return and payment for the return period ended 31 December 2026
The standard quarter dates on which CT61 return periods end; a company may also need an extra return period to match its accounting period end

scope.nation: UK-wide (Corporation Tax and Income Tax deduction at source, not devolved)
scope.who: A company that pays yearly interest to someone other than a UK bank - most commonly interest on a loan from a director, a family member or a private individual - and also certain royalties, annuities and other annual payments, alternative finance payments, and payments under non-charitable deeds of covenant. The company deducts 20%, pays it to HMRC and reports it on form CT61.
scope.excluded: No deduction and no CT61 where the recipient is a UK-resident company, or a listed tax-exempt body such as a charity, local authority or approved pension fund. Interest paid to a UK bank is outside it. Donations to charities and interest on quoted Eurobonds are not subject to deduction. Short interest - interest on a loan not capable of lasting a year or more - is not yearly interest and is not caught. A company that makes no such payments in a quarter has no CT61 to file for that quarter.
scope.from_when: Current rules; return period ended 31 December 2026 is due 14 January 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Request form CT61 from HMRC, complete it for the return period and send it with payment to the Accounts Office within 14 days of the period end.

notes: This is the deadline owner-managed companies miss most often, because nothing in the payroll or VAT cycle prompts it. If a company pays interest on a director's loan, or on a loan from a family member, it must withhold 20% and account for it quarterly on a CT61 - the director then shows the gross interest and the tax credit on their own Self Assessment return. Paying the director the gross amount and sorting it out at the year end is not an option: the obligation is quarterly and the 14-day window is short. There is no CT61 for interest paid to a UK bank or to another UK company, which is why most companies never meet the form. The deducted tax is not Corporation Tax and does not go on the CT600.

title: Flat Rate Tax Relief for Uniforms, Work Clothing and Tools

figures.what: default annual flat rate expense if your job is not on HMRC's industry list
actual tax saved on a £60 flat rate claim at the 20% basic rate — HMRC's own worked example
annual flat rate for nurses, midwives and certain other listed health roles
annual flat rate for uniformed fire fighters and fire officers
annual flat rate for cabin crew
annual flat rate for pilots, co-pilots, helicopter pilots and uniformed flight deck crew
maximum total job expenses per tax year that can be claimed on form P87; above this you must file a Self Assessment return instead
how far back a claim can go — it must be made within 4 years from the end of the tax year claimed for

scope.nation: UK-wide (Income Tax relief; the cash value differs because Scottish and Welsh taxpayers relieve at their own rates)
scope.who: Employees taxed under PAYE who use their own money to buy, clean, repair or replace a uniform, specialist work clothing or tools they need for the job and use only for work. No receipts are needed for a flat rate claim.
scope.excluded: Anyone whose employer repays the full cost or provides the item instead gets nothing — and if the employer pays part, you deduct that part first. Anyone who paid no Income Tax in the year claimed for gets nothing, because relief cannot exceed the tax paid. The self-employed are outside this scheme entirely (they deduct actual costs as business expenses). A claim over £2,500 in a year cannot use form P87. Ordinary everyday clothing worn to work is never allowable.
scope.from_when: Flat rates are set per tax year and apply for 2026-27 (6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027)
scope.how_to_claim: Check the industry table on the GOV.UK guidance page for your job's rate (£60 if not listed), subtract any employer contribution, then claim online through the HMRC job expenses service, by post on form P87, or in box 18 of SA102 if you file Self Assessment

notes: The commonest misunderstanding is that a £60 flat rate puts £60 in your pocket. It does not — it reduces taxable pay by £60, so a basic rate taxpayer saves £12 and a higher rate taxpayer £24. HMRC states the £12 figure itself. Second trap: once HMRC puts the allowance in your tax code it usually keeps rolling forward, so the win is really in the backdated years, not the current one. Third trap: only form P87 is accepted for postal claims — HMRC rejects claims sent on anything else. Flat rates are UK-wide but the saving is bigger for Scottish taxpayers in the higher bands.

title: Help to Save: 50% Government Bonus on Savings

figures.what: the government bonus rate
maximum you can pay in; the minimum is £1 and you do not have to pay in every month
the most you can save over the 4 years
the most you can earn in bonuses over 4 years
the take-home pay you must have had in your last monthly Universal Credit assessment period to qualify
the life of the account; it closes 4 years after opening and cannot be reopened or replaced

scope.nation: UK-wide — you must live in the UK
scope.who: People receiving Universal Credit who had take-home pay of £1 or more in their last monthly assessment period. On a joint claim the couple's pay is assessed together but each partner needs their own account and applies separately.
scope.excluded: Anyone not on Universal Credit. Anyone whose take-home pay was below £1 in their last monthly assessment period. Anyone living overseas, unless they are a Crown servant or a member of the British armed forces, or the spouse or civil partner of one. Anyone who has already had a Help to Save account — you cannot open a second. Savers whose highest balance does not rise in years 3 and 4 get no final bonus at all.
scope.from_when: Accounts run for 4 years from the date you open them
scope.how_to_claim: Apply through the Help to Save service on GOV.UK or the HMRC app; you need a Government Gateway account

notes: Two bonuses, not one, and the second is easy to lose. The first bonus is 50% of your HIGHEST balance in years 1 and 2. The final bonus is 50% of the difference between your highest balance in years 3 and 4 and your highest balance in years 1 and 2 — so if you withdraw and never save above the old peak again, the second bonus is zero. Bonuses are paid into your bank account, not back into the Help to Save account. Ending your Universal Credit claim does NOT shut the account: once open, you keep saving for the full 4 years. Because the bonus is based on the highest balance rather than the closing balance, money can be withdrawn without destroying the first bonus already banked.

title: Attendance Allowance Weekly Rates

figures.what: lower rate — for frequent help or constant supervision during the day, or supervision at night
higher rate — for help or supervision through both day and night, or if a medical professional has said you are nearing the end of life
how long you must have needed the help before you qualify (different rules if nearing the end of life)
how long you must have lived in Great Britain; does not apply to refugees or people with humanitarian protection

scope.nation: England and Wales. Scotland has replaced it with Pension Age Disability Payment; Northern Ireland runs its own Attendance Allowance through nidirect.
scope.who: People who have reached State Pension age with a physical disability (including sensory), a mental disability (including learning difficulties) or a health condition severe enough that they need help caring for themselves or supervision for their own or someone else's safety, for at least 6 months. It is not means-tested, so earnings and savings do not affect it, and you do not need to have anyone actually caring for you.
scope.excluded: Anyone living in Scotland must apply for Pension Age Disability Payment instead. Anyone already getting DLA, PIP, Adult Disability Payment, Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance or Armed Forces Independence Payment cannot have Attendance Allowance as well. People living in a care home where the local authority pays for their care usually cannot get it — you can claim if you pay all the care home fees yourself. Anyone subject to immigration control, unless a sponsored immigrant. Anyone not habitually resident in the UK, Ireland, the Isle of Man or the Channel Islands. It covers nothing for mobility needs. If you also get Constant Attendance Allowance, your Attendance Allowance is reduced by that amount.
scope.from_when: Rates as published on GOV.UK on 17 November 2026; uprated each April
scope.how_to_claim: Apply online on GOV.UK, or print the claim form, or call the DWP Attendance Allowance helpline number published on GOV.UK to be sent one. The claim starts on the day you apply online, the day DWP receives a posted form, or the day of your call if you return the form within 6 weeks.

notes: This is the single most under-claimed pensioner benefit and the reason is a wrong belief that it is means-tested. It is not: savings, a pension and a paid-off house make no difference. It is also not paid for having a diagnosis — it is paid for needing help or supervision, and you do not have to be getting that help from anyone. The big knock-on is that an Attendance Allowance award can unlock extra Pension Credit, Housing Benefit and Council Tax Reduction, so it is worth more than the headline rate. Call timing matters: ring the helpline for a form and the claim is backdated to the date of the call, provided you send it in within 6 weeks — applying straight online starts it the day you apply, with nothing before that. Scottish readers must not be sent to this page; Pension Age Disability Payment is a separate Social Security Scotland benefit.

title: Maternity Allowance for Those Who Cannot Get Statutory Maternity Pay

figures.value: £194.32 a week or 90% of average weekly earnings, whichever is less
figures.what: Maternity Allowance for up to 39 weeks for the employed or recently stopped working
range for the self-employed over 39 weeks, depending on Class 2 National Insurance contributions paid
the lower award for doing unpaid work in a spouse's or civil partner's self-employed business

figures.value: 26 of the 66 weeks before the due date
figures.what: how long you must have been employed or registered self-employed to get the 39-week award

figures.value: £30 a week in at least 13 weeks
figures.what: the earnings test — you must have earned, or been treated as earning, at least this much in 13 of those 66 weeks; the weeks need not be consecutive

scope.nation: Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales). Northern Ireland runs its own Maternity Allowance through nidirect on the same rules.
scope.who: Pregnant women who cannot get Statutory Maternity Pay: the self-employed, recent job-leavers, people who changed jobs or had gaps in work, and those doing unpaid work in a spouse's or civil partner's business. You may still qualify if the baby was stillborn from the start of the 24th week of pregnancy, or born alive at any point.
scope.excluded: Anyone entitled to Statutory Maternity Pay from an employer gets SMP instead, not Maternity Allowance. Anyone who cannot meet the 26-weeks-in-66 work test, or the 13-weeks-at-£30 earnings test, gets nothing. For the 14-week award you must NOT have been employed or self-employed yourself, and your spouse or civil partner must have been registered self-employed with HMRC and paying Class 2 National Insurance in the same 26 weeks. Jobseeker's Allowance stops if you get Maternity Allowance, and Universal Credit is reduced pound for pound by the Maternity Allowance paid. The benefit cap may apply.
scope.from_when: Rates as published on GOV.UK on 17 November 2026; uprated each April
scope.how_to_claim: Claim on form MA1, available on GOV.UK, with proof of income and your MATB1 maternity certificate

notes: This is the award for people the SMP rules leave out, and it is routinely missed by the newly self-employed. Read the difference carefully. SMP is paid by the employer and starts at 90% of average weekly earnings with no cap for the first 6 weeks; Maternity Allowance is paid by DWP and is capped at £194.32 from week one, so it can be worth materially less than SMP over the 39 weeks. The self-employed amount is not a single figure — it depends on Class 2 contributions, and someone with gaps can land near £27 a week rather than £194.32, which is why checking the Class 2 record before claiming is worth real money. The two-tier nature of the £27 route is also missed: 14 weeks, not 39, and only if you did unpaid work for a spouse's or civil partner's business. Finally, Maternity Allowance reduces Universal Credit pound for pound, so for a household on UC the net gain can be nil — but it still protects the National Insurance record.

title: Cold Weather Payment: £25 per Cold Week

figures.what: paid for each 7-day period of very cold weather

figures.value: zero degrees Celsius or below over 7 consecutive days
figures.what: the trigger — an average temperature recorded as, or forecast to be, at or below freezing for 7 days running at your local weather station
the scheme season

scope.nation: England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland is excluded — Scottish households get the annual Winter Heating Payment instead, paid regardless of the weather.
scope.who: People receiving Pension Credit; income-related Employment and Support Allowance in the work-related activity group or support group, or in neither group but with a severe or enhanced disability premium, a pensioner premium, a disabled child or a child under 5 living with them; Universal Credit where the claimant and any partner are not employed or gainfully self-employed and either has limited capability for work or has a child under 5, or where the claim includes a disabled child amount regardless of work; and Support for Mortgage Interest where treated as receiving a qualifying benefit.
scope.excluded: Anyone living in Scotland. Anyone not on one of those four benefits — so most low-income working households, and anyone on Housing Benefit or Council Tax Reduction alone, get nothing. Universal Credit claimants (or their partners) who are employed or gainfully self-employed, unless they have limited capability for work, a child under 5, or a disabled child amount. Income-related ESA claimants in neither group with none of the listed premiums or children. It is tied to your local weather station, so a cold spell in your town that does not average zero over 7 full days triggers nothing.
scope.from_when: 1 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — it is paid automatically into the account that receives your benefit. You should report a change if you have a baby or a child under 5 comes to live with you, because that can make you eligible.

notes: The thing readers get wrong is thinking this is paid for a cold winter. It is not. It needs a SEVEN consecutive day average at or below zero at the weather station linked to your postcode — a sharp two-day freeze pays nothing, and neighbouring postcodes can get different answers. Check the postcode checker on GOV.UK rather than guessing. Scotland must never be told to look for this: Winter Heating Payment there is a fixed annual sum, paid whether it is cold or not. Northern Ireland uses a separate checker. The action a reader can actually take is not claiming the £25 — it is making sure DWP knows about a new baby or a child under 5 in the household, and making sure a Pension Credit entitlement is actually claimed, because Pension Credit is the gateway.

title: Budgeting Advance: Interest-Free Help With Unexpected Costs

figures.what: maximum Budgeting Advance if you are single
maximum if you are part of a couple
maximum if you have children
the smallest advance you can get
the most you can have earned in the past 6 months and still qualify
the repayment period, taken from Universal Credit payments starting with the next one

scope.nation: Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales). Northern Ireland runs its own Universal Credit advances through nidirect.
scope.who: Universal Credit claimants who need money for an unexpected cost and who have either been on Universal Credit, Employment and Support Allowance or Pension Credit for 6 months or more, or need the money to help start a new job or stay in work.
scope.excluded: Anyone who earned more than £2,600 in the past 6 months, or £3,600 as a couple. Anyone who has not finished repaying a previous Budgeting Advance — you can only hold one at a time. Anyone who has been on Universal Credit for less than 6 months and is not using the money to start or keep a job. It is not a grant: every pound comes back out of future Universal Credit payments, so it reduces your monthly award for up to 24 months.
scope.from_when: Amounts as published on GOV.UK on 17 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Ask through your Universal Credit online journal or call the Universal Credit helpline; a work coach decides

notes: The headline is that it is interest-free, and that is the real value against a doorstep or high-cost lender — but it is a LOAN, not support, and that is the part people miss. The repayment is deducted at source for up to 24 months, which makes an already tight monthly award tighter. Two further traps. First, the £812 figure needs children in the claim, not just a partner. Second, the 6-month earnings test is cumulative over the whole half year, so someone who worked briefly and stopped can be refused. Do not confuse this with a Budgeting Loan, which is the older Social Fund loan for people on legacy benefits such as Pension Credit or income-related ESA rather than Universal Credit — and note Scotland also has the Scottish Welfare Fund crisis grants, which are grants rather than loans and are claimed from the council.

title: Disabled Facilities Grant for Home Adaptations

figures.what: maximum Disabled Facilities Grant in England
maximum in Wales
maximum in Northern Ireland
the savings level above which household savings are taken into account in the means test
the period within which a council may require a landlord to let the property to another disabled person if the tenant moves out

scope.nation: England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland does not have Disabled Facilities Grants at all — adaptations there are arranged through the council or housing association under separate Scottish schemes.
scope.who: Disabled people, or someone living with them, who need the home adapted — widening doors, ramps, a stairlift, a downstairs bathroom, improved heating or access to rooms. Applications go to the local council, which must be satisfied the work is necessary, appropriate and reasonably practicable. Some councils pay more than the statutory maximum.
scope.excluded: Anyone living in Scotland — there is no Disabled Facilities Grant there. Most applicants are means-tested on household income and on savings over £6,000, so a household with means may get only a contribution, or nothing, and has to pay towards the cost. There are two important carve-outs from the means test: disabled children under 18 get a grant without their parents' income being counted, and landlords get a grant without their income and savings being counted. Work already started or finished before the council approves the grant is normally not funded.
scope.from_when: Maximum amounts as published on GOV.UK on 17 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Apply to your local council; the council arranges an assessment, usually by an occupational therapist, before approving the work

notes: Three nations, three different ceilings, and Scotland is simply not in the scheme — getting that wrong sends a reader to a dead end. The most valuable fact for families is the children's carve-out: for a disabled child under 18 the parents' income and savings are not tested at all, so households that assume they earn too much are often entitled to the full amount. Landlords are in the same position, which matters for private tenants whose landlord will not pay for adaptations. Two practical traps: the grant is approved before the work, not after, so paying for a stairlift first usually forfeits it; and the £30,000 England figure is a statutory maximum, not an entitlement — many councils top it up under their own discretionary housing assistance policies, so always ask what local top-up exists. A referral to the council's occupational therapy service is the real first step, because the assessment drives what the grant will cover.

title: Unclaimed Child Trust Funds and the Free HMRC Tracing Service

figures.what: total value of matured Child Trust Funds sitting unclaimed
number of unclaimed matured accounts
average value of an unclaimed account
the age at which you can use the HMRC tool to trace your own Child Trust Fund
how long HMRC usually takes to reply to an online tracing request; postal requests take longer, and you should chase after 9 weeks

scope.nation: UK-wide (HMRC administers Child Trust Funds across the UK)
scope.who: Young adults who were children when Child Trust Funds were running and never claimed the matured account, and parents or guardians of a child still under 18 who have lost track of the provider. The HMRC tracing service is free and tells you which provider holds the account.
scope.excluded: The tool cannot be used to find a Junior ISA — only a Child Trust Fund. A parent or guardian can use it only while the child is under 18; after that only the account holder can apply. You cannot save the form and come back to it, so you need your National Insurance number before you start. HMRC does not pay out the money — it only names the provider, and you must then claim from that provider. Children born outside the Child Trust Fund years have no account to find.
scope.from_when: Figures from the HMRC and HM Treasury news story published 29 June 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Use the free Find a Child Trust Fund tool on GOV.UK with your National Insurance number, or the free Share Foundation service at findctf.sharefound.org. HMRC posts the provider's details. If nothing arrives within 9 weeks, write to Charities, Savings and International 1, HMRC, BX9 1AU, quoting any reference number.

notes: This is the easiest unclaimed money in the UK and the average is not small — around £2,200 a head across more than 750,000 people. The one warning worth shouting is that the search is FREE from HMRC and free from the Share Foundation: a trade in paid tracing services exists and takes a cut of an account you could have found yourself with a National Insurance number and ten minutes. Second point: HMRC gives you the provider's name, not the money, so finding the account is step one of two — the provider then has its own identity checks. Third: the tool will not find a Junior ISA, which is where many of these funds were later transferred, so if the provider says the CTF was moved, follow it to the Junior ISA provider rather than starting again. Note the editor's notes on the same GOV.UK story describe the total as hundreds of millions, which contradicts the £1.6 billion headline figure on the page — cite the headline figure and the URL, and recheck when HMRC next updates it.

title: Section 75: Your Credit Card Company Is Liable Too

figures.what: the lower limit — section 75(3)(b) excludes a claim relating to a single item with a cash price not exceeding £100
the upper limit — section 75(3)(b) excludes a claim relating to a single item with a cash price of more than £30,000
the effect of section 75(1): the creditor is liable alongside the supplier for misrepresentation or breach of contract, so you can claim the whole amount from the lender

scope.who: A debtor under a debtor-creditor-supplier agreement falling within section 12(b) or (c) of the Act — in practice a credit card, store card or point-of-sale credit purchase — who has a claim against the supplier for misrepresentation or breach of contract. The debtor has the same claim against the creditor, who is jointly and severally liable with the supplier.
scope.excluded: Claims under a non-commercial agreement. Claims relating to any single item with a cash price not exceeding £100, or more than £30,000 — so a £95 item and a £40,000 item are both outside section 75. Certain running-account credit agreements under section 75(3)(c), where payments fall in periods of no more than three months (if not secured on land) and the whole credit is repayable in a single payment per period — charge cards of that kind are outside it. Debit cards are not covered at all, because there is no credit agreement; and a payment made through a third-party intermediary rather than directly to the supplier can break the debtor-creditor-supplier link.
scope.from_when: In force; Consumer Credit Act 1974
scope.how_to_claim: Claim in writing to the card issuer or lender. If refused, complain to the firm and then to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

notes: The statutory wording trips people up both ways. The limits bite on the cash price of the SINGLE ITEM, not on what you actually put on the card — so a £3,000 sofa bought with a £50 deposit on a credit card and the rest in cash is still covered in full, because the item price is over £100 and under £30,000. Equally, buying ten £60 items in one £600 transaction is not covered, because each single item is under the limit. Debit cards get nothing under section 75 — the route there is chargeback, which is a card scheme rule rather than a legal right, is time-limited, and gives no claim against the lender. Section 75 has no fixed deadline of its own and runs for as long as the underlying contract claim does, which is why it still works against a retailer or airline that has gone bust. Section 75A, a separate provision, covers linked loans above £30,000 on different conditions.

title: Director's Loan Account: the Nine-Month Rule and the s455 Charge

figures.what: period after the end of the company's Corporation Tax accounting period within which an overdrawn director's loan must be repaid to avoid the charge
CTA 2010 s455 Corporation Tax rate on an unrepaid loan, for loans made on or after 6 April 2026 (it tracks the dividend upper rate in ITA 2007 s8(2))
s455 rate for loans made on or after 6 April 2022 and before 6 April 2026 - still the only rate shown on the public guidance page
s455 rate for loans made from 6 April 2016 to 5 April 2022
s455 rate for loans made up to 5 April 2016
amount owed at any time in the year above which the loan is also a benefit in kind on the director personally, with Class 1 NICs due and the loan reported on the director's Self Assessment return
bed-and-breakfasting rule: for a loan over £5,000, the charge still applies if another loan of £5,000 or more is taken up to 30 days before or after repaying it
loans over this amount: the charge applies if another loan was arranged when the original was repaid, with no 30-day let-out
Dividend upper rate 2026-27, which s455(2) imports to set the s455 rate - ITA 2007 s8(2), substituted for 2026-27 and later years by Finance Act 2026 s4(1)(b)
Dividend upper rate also listed for 2027-28, so the s455 rate holds at 35.75% into 2027-28
Time limit to claim s458 relief after repayment - CTA 2010 s458(3): the claim must be made within 4 years from the end of the financial year in which the repayment, release or writing off occurs

scope.nation: UK-wide (Corporation Tax is not devolved; the same rule applies in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland)
scope.who: Close companies that lend money to, or advance money to, a participator or an associate of a participator - in practice an owner-director who takes money out of the company other than as salary, dividend or expense reimbursement. The company, not the director, pays the s455 tax.
scope.excluded: The charge does NOT catch: a company that is not a close company when the loan is made; money drawn and properly recorded as salary through RTI payroll or as a lawfully declared dividend; reimbursed business expenses; a director's loan account that is in credit (the company owes the director); and any loan fully repaid, released or written off within 9 months of the accounting period end. Separately, the £10,000 benefit-in-kind charge does not bite where total loans stayed at £10,000 or below throughout the tax year, or where the director paid the company interest at or above HMRC's official rate. Note a written-off loan escapes s455 but is taxed on the director as a distribution instead - it is not a free way out. Express statutory exceptions in CTA 2010 s456 also take a loan outside s455 entirely: (a) a loan made in the ordinary course of a business that includes the lending of money (s456(1)); (b) a loan not exceeding £15,000 including other loans outstanding from the company or its associated companies, where the borrower works full-time for the close company or an associated company AND does not have a material interest in any of them - all three conditions must be met (s456(3)-(6)), and if the borrower later acquires a material interest while part of the loan is outstanding a new loan of the outstanding amount is deemed made (s456(7)); (c) ordinary trade credit from the company's supply of goods or services, unless the credit exceeds 6 months or is longer than normally given to customers (s456(2)); (d) a loan to trustees of a charitable trust applied to the purposes of the charitable trust only (s456(2A)).
scope.from_when: s455 has applied for decades; the 35.75% rate applies to loans made on or after 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim - the company self-assesses. Report the loan on the CT600A supplementary pages of the Company Tax Return and pay the s455 tax with the Corporation Tax for the period. Once the loan is repaid, the company reclaims the s455 tax under CTA 2010 s458, but it cannot be reclaimed until 9 months and one day after the end of the accounting period in which the repayment happened - so the cash sits with HMRC for a long time. The s458 claim must be made within 4 years from the end of the financial year in which the repayment, release or writing off occurs (s458(3)).

notes: The s455 rate question is settled at primary source and this entry is now publishable. CTA 2010 s455(2) does not state a percentage: it imports the dividend upper rate in ITA 2007 s8(2) for the tax year the loan is made. ITA 2007 s8(2) now reads 35.75%, substituted for 2026-27 onwards by Finance Act 2026 s4(1)(b). So 35.75% is the operative rate for a loan made on or after 6 April 2026 as a matter of statute, and HMRC manual CTM61505 is correct. The public gov.uk/directors-loans page still shows 33.75% (and 32.5% pre-April-2022): that page is simply out of date, and it is not a competing authority, because the rate is not set there. Do NOT publish 33.75% for a loan made in 2026-27. The citation chain is s455(2) -> ITA 2007 s8(2) -> FA 2026 s4(1)(b). The rate also holds at 35.75% for 2027-28 per Budget 2026 Annex A. The number people get wrong: the 9 months runs from the COMPANY accounting period end, not the tax year end, and not from when the money was taken. Asymmetry worth using: the tax falls due 9 months and a day after the accounting period in which the loan was MADE (s455(3)), but relief cannot be given until 9 months after the end of the accounting period in which the REPAYMENT happened (s458(5)) - that is what strands the cash. There are two different £15,000 figures in this subject doing opposite jobs: the £15,000 bed-and-breakfasting trigger on the guidance page, and the £15,000 s456 safe harbour for a full-time employee or director with no material interest. An owner-director almost always has a material interest, so the safe harbour will not help the typical reader - copy must not imply 'under £15,000 is fine'. No Scottish or Welsh variation. NOT RE-VERIFIED at primary source this pass: the claim that interest on the s455 tax is not refundable even when the tax is - do not publish that point until it is read at the CTM61600 series.

title: Staff Christmas Party: the £150 a Head Exemption

figures.what: maximum cost per person for an annual staff function to be exempt from tax and NICs (ITEPA 2003 s264)
combined per-head limit where an employer holds more than one annual event in the year - the total of all events must not exceed it

scope.who: Employers putting on an annual social function - a Christmas party, summer barbecue or equivalent, including a virtual or online party. The event must be annual, must be open to all employees, and must cost £150 or less per person attending. A one-director company counts: the director is an employee.
scope.excluded: The exemption does NOT cover: a one-off event that is not annual (a staff celebration of winning a contract, a leaving do, a birthday); an event open only to directors or to a selected group rather than all staff (separate departmental or site parties are fine so long as every employee can attend one of them); and anything provided under a salary sacrifice arrangement, which must be reported regardless. It does not apply to self-employed sole traders or partners entertaining themselves - they have no employment to exempt. And it gives no relief for entertaining customers or suppliers.
scope.from_when: ITEPA 2003 s264; the £150 figure has been unchanged since 2003
scope.how_to_claim: No claim and no reporting if the conditions are met. If they are not, the employer reports the full cost per head on form P11D (or payrolls the benefit) and pays Class 1A NICs - or covers it for staff through a PAYE Settlement Agreement.

notes: The trap, in HMRC's own words at EIM21690: 'The figure of £150 is not an allowance.' Spend £151 a head and the WHOLE £151 is taxable, not the £1 over. Cost per head is the total cost of the event divided by everyone who attended, including non-employee guests, and it includes VAT plus any transport or overnight accommodation laid on so people can get there. So if partners come, dividing by heads can actually help you. Where there are two events and the combined total is over £150, HMRC lets you apply the £150 to whichever combination of events uses it best and taxes the rest. This is separate from the trivial benefits exemption - a party is not a trivial benefit, and the two do not stack on the same spend. No Scottish or Welsh difference: s264 is a UK-wide exemption, so nothing is taxed and devolved rates never come into it.

title: Pre-Trading Expenses: the Seven-Year Rule

figures.what: period before the trade, profession or vocation starts within which qualifying revenue expenditure can be relieved

scope.who: Sole traders, partners and companies that incurred revenue expenses before the business began trading. ITTOIA 2005 s57 for income tax; CTA 2009 s61 for companies. The expense is treated as if it were incurred on the first day of trading and deducted in that first period.
scope.excluded: The seven-year rule does NOT give relief for: capital expenditure (no deduction at all under these rules - plant and machinery goes through capital allowances instead, where CAA 2001 s12 treats pre-trading capital spend as incurred on the day trading starts); the advance purchase of trading stock, which is relieved when it is sold, not when it is bought; anything that will already be deductible in a post-commencement period, such as rent paid in advance; and anything that would NOT have been deductible if the trade had already been running - so it fails the wholly and exclusively test, it fails here too. Client entertaining, fines and personal costs are still disallowed no matter when they were paid.
scope.from_when: ITTOIA 2005 s57 / CTA 2009 s61, long-standing
scope.how_to_claim: Include the expenditure in the accounts or tax computation for the first period of trading, as if it had been spent on day one. There is no separate claim form - but if the first return has already been filed without it, amend that return rather than putting the spend in a later year.

notes: The thing clients get wrong: they assume anything spent before they registered is lost, and they throw the receipts away. Seven years is generous - a laptop, a website, market research, professional fees, insurance, phone and travel from years before the first invoice can all land in the first period. But it only works if you can prove it, which is why this pairs with the record-keeping rule. Two further traps: the expense must have been incurred for the business that actually started, and the seven years run back from COMMENCEMENT of trading, which is not the date of incorporation and not the date HMRC was told. Setting up - writing the business plan - is not itself trading. No Scottish or Welsh variation in what qualifies; the deduction is a UK-wide income or corporation tax computation rule, though a Scottish taxpayer's saving will be at Scottish income tax rates and a company's at the Corporation Tax rate.

title: How Long to Keep Business Records, and the Penalty if You Do Not

figures.what: minimum period after the 31 January filing deadline for which a self-employed person must keep records (TMA 1970 s12B: the fifth anniversary of the 31 January following the tax year)
maximum penalty per failure to keep or preserve adequate records, under TMA 1970 s12B(5)
minimum retention period for someone NOT carrying on a business - the first anniversary of the 31 January following the tax year (TMA 1970 s12B(1)(b))
retention period from the date of sending the return, where a return is filed more than 4 years after the deadline

scope.who: Anyone who files a Self Assessment return. The five-year rule applies to a person carrying on a trade, profession or business - and HMRC's SALF211 is explicit that for a business the five-year limit covers ALL records, not only the business ones.
scope.excluded: The five-year rule does NOT apply to someone with no trade, profession or business - an employee or pensioner filing only because of, say, dividends keeps records for just one year after the 31 January deadline. But the shorter period is overridden if HMRC opens an enquiry or can still open one: records must then be kept until the enquiry is closed by a final closure notice. Nothing here excludes you from the separate Companies House and Corporation Tax record rules, which run for 6 years from the end of the accounting period, or VAT records, which run for 6 years.
scope.from_when: TMA 1970 s12B, long-standing
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. Keep the records - paper or digital, HMRC accepts scanned copies. If records are lost, stolen or destroyed and cannot be replaced, file using estimated or provisional figures and tell HMRC on the return which you have used; provisional figures must be followed up with the real ones.

notes: The miscount: five years from the FILING DEADLINE, not five years from the tax year or from when you filed. Records for 2025-26 (deadline 31 January 2027) must be kept until at least the end of January 2032. The £3,000 is per failure, and HMRC's manual wording is 'up to' - it is a maximum, rarely charged in full, and in practice the worse outcome is losing a deduction you cannot evidence. Note the separate point in the box above: a return filed more than four years late only needs records kept for 15 months afterwards, which sounds generous until you remember the late-filing penalties. Making Tax Digital for Income Tax changes HOW records are kept (digitally, quarterly) for those in scope but not how long. No Scottish or Welsh variation - record-keeping and the penalty are reserved UK tax administration, even for a Scottish taxpayer paying Scottish rates.

title: State Pension: Qualifying Years and How to Check Your Forecast

figures.what: minimum National Insurance record needed to get any new State Pension at all
years needed for the full rate of new State Pension, where the NI record started after April 2016
full rate of the new State Pension for 2026 to 2027
basic State Pension (Category A or B) for 2026 to 2027, the old system rate

scope.nation: UK-wide and reserved - the State Pension is not devolved to Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland
scope.who: Men born on or after 6 April 1951 and women born on or after 6 April 1953, claiming at State Pension age. Qualifying years come from years of paid National Insurance, from NI credits (unemployment, illness, caring for a child or a relative), and from voluntary contributions.
scope.excluded: The new State Pension does NOT apply to a man born before 6 April 1951 or a woman born before 6 April 1953 - they are on the old basic State Pension, with any Additional State Pension, and the 35-year test does not apply to them. Fewer than 10 qualifying years means no new State Pension at all, not a reduced one. And 35 years is NOT a guarantee of the full rate for everyone: HMRC and DWP confirm that where the NI record began before April 2016 and the person was contracted out of the additional State Pension, they will usually need MORE than 35 years. Nobody gets the full rate simply by reaching 35 years on a pre-2016 record.
scope.from_when: new State Pension rules apply from 6 April 2016; rates shown are 2026 to 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Check the forecast and the NI record free at https://www.gov.uk/check-state-pension - it shows the number of qualifying years so far, which years are incomplete, and the forecast amount. The pension itself must be claimed; it is not paid automatically on reaching State Pension age.

notes: This is the January question behind 'should I pay voluntary NI?' - and the forecast is the only honest way to answer it, because paying for a gap year is wasted money if the person is already on track for the full rate, or if they have fewer than 10 years and will not reach 10. Two things people get wrong: 35 years is the figure for a record that STARTED after April 2016, so anyone with a contracted-out pre-2016 history should read the Starting Amount on their own forecast rather than counting years; and NI credits count as qualifying years without a penny being paid, so a parent claiming Child Benefit or a carer may have years they did not know about. The £241.30 is the full new State Pension for 2026-27; the old basic rate of £184.90 is a different pension, not a reduced version of the same one. Same rules and same amounts in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

title: Business Travel or Commuting: the 24-Month Rule

figures.what: length of continuous work at one place beyond which it stops being a temporary workplace and becomes a permanent one, so travel there is ordinary commuting with no relief
proportion of working time at a place that makes the work there 'to a significant extent' - both this and the 24-month test must be met before the place becomes permanent
fixed-term appointment test: attending a place for more than this share of the likely employment period, at 40% or more of working time, also makes it a permanent workplace

scope.who: Employees and directors travelling to a temporary workplace - a place attended for a limited duration or temporary purpose. Relief covers the full cost of that travel, and the employer can reimburse it tax-free or the employee can claim relief.
scope.excluded: No relief for: ordinary commuting between home and a permanent workplace; travel between home and a place that is not a workplace at all; travel to another job's workplace; a site where the employee works, or expects to work, 40% or more of their time for a continuous period of more than 24 months - and crucially it becomes permanent from the moment the expectation changes, not after the 24 months have run; a fixed-term appointment caught by the 80% test; and a depot or base where the employee regularly starts work or is routinely allocated tasks, which is a permanent workplace however many sites they then drive to. HMRC is explicit that an employee's home being a workplace does not by itself make the journey from home relievable.
scope.from_when: ITEPA 2003, from 6 April 1998 in substance; booklet 490 is the current HMRC guidance
scope.how_to_claim: If the employer reimburses at or below the approved mileage rates or actual cost, nothing is reported. If not reimbursed, the employee claims relief - through the Self Assessment return if they file one, otherwise by a P87 claim to HMRC, which can go back the current tax year plus the 4 previous years.

notes: Two tests, not one, and people apply only the 24 months. Both the 40% of working time and the more-than-24-months conditions must be met before a site turns permanent - fail either and the workplace can still be temporary, so a two-day-a-week site visited for three years may well still qualify. The sharper trap runs the other way: relief stops as soon as it is EXPECTED that the period will exceed 24 months, so a contractor on a 'rolling' 18-month site that is clearly going to run for three years loses relief from the point the expectation changed, and a retrospective claim for the first 24 months is wrong. Driving to a depot to pick up a van is commuting, not business travel. Mileage reimbursement rates are a separate matter from whether the journey qualifies at all - this rule decides the latter. No Scottish or Welsh variation in the rules; the value of unreimbursed relief follows the taxpayer's own rates, so a Scottish intermediate or higher rate taxpayer gets relief at Scottish rates.

title: Working From Home Tax Relief Has Gone for Employees

figures.what: date from which employees can no longer claim tax relief for unreimbursed additional household costs of working from home
how far back a claim can still be made for years before the withdrawal
the flat rate that could be claimed without receipts for earlier years, and still the amount an employer may reimburse tax-free
the monthly equivalent an employer can pay a monthly-paid homeworking employee tax and NIC free, with no evidence of actual cost
individuals HMRC expects the withdrawal to affect

scope.nation: UK-wide (ITEPA 2003; new s360B inserted into Part 4 Chapter 11)
scope.who: Employees and directors who have to work from home and were not reimbursed by their employer. For 2026-27 onwards they can no longer claim; for 2022-23 to 2025-26 they still can, if they met the old conditions.
scope.excluded: The withdrawal does NOT affect: employers reimbursing homeworking household costs, which stays tax and NIC free at £6 a week or £26 a month under the s316A exemption where there is a homeworking arrangement and the employee works from home regularly; the self-employed, who continue to deduct use-of-home costs either on the simplified flat rate or by apportionment; or employer-provided equipment and services where private use is insignificant. And the relief it removes was never available to anyone who CHOSE to work from home - HMRC's guidance is blunt that there is no claim where the contract allows home working, or where the office exists but was full on the day.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 (tax year 2026-27 onwards)
scope.how_to_claim: For 2025-26 and the three years before it, claim through the Self Assessment return or a P87 claim. For 2026-27 there is nothing to claim: the route is to ask the employer to reimburse instead, within the £6 a week / £26 a month exemption.

notes: This is the single most common January question that now has a different answer from last year. The £6 a week claim is dead for 2026-27 but alive for the four earlier years, and a backdated claim for 2022-23 must reach HMRC by 5 April 2027 before that year falls out of time - so this January is the last practical window for it. Do not confuse the two £6s: the employee DEDUCTION has gone, the employer REIMBURSEMENT exemption has not. Also note the relief was always worth only tax at the claimant's rate - £6 a week claimed at 20% was about £62 a year, not £312 - which is why the figure clients quote from social media is usually wrong by a factor of five. Scottish and Welsh taxpayers: the relief that has been withdrawn was given at their own income tax rates, so a Scottish higher or advanced rate taxpayer loses slightly more than an English one; the employer exemption amounts are identical across the UK.

title: Telling HMRC Your Company Is Active: the Three-Month Deadline

figures.what: period from the start of the company's tax accounting period within which a company that is now active must tell HMRC
expected annual Corporation Tax liability at or below which HMRC may treat a club or unincorporated organisation run for its members' benefit as dormant

scope.who: Any limited company within the charge to Corporation Tax that has become active. HMRC treats a company as active when it is carrying on a trade or profession, or receiving any other income - including earning bank interest or managing investments, not only selling things.
scope.excluded: A company HMRC accepts as dormant does NOT have to file a Company Tax Return - but only once it has actually told HMRC and HMRC has confirmed it. A company that simply stops trading and says nothing is still required to submit a Corporation Tax return and faces penalties if it does not. Pre-trading setup steps - writing a business plan, choosing a name - do not by themselves make a company active. Being dormant for Corporation Tax does not exempt the company from Companies House obligations: dormant accounts and a confirmation statement are still due.
scope.from_when: current HMRC guidance; the notification duty sits in CTA 2009 / FA 2004 s55
scope.how_to_claim: Register for Corporation Tax online through the company's HMRC business tax account within 3 months, giving the date business activity started, the company's registered details and the accounting reference date. To go dormant, tell HMRC separately - do not assume filing dormant accounts at Companies House tells HMRC anything.

notes: Two registers, two bodies, two sets of forms - and that is the whole misunderstanding. Companies House knows the company exists; HMRC does not know it has started trading until told, and a notice to deliver a return arriving two years later is how most people find out. The answer to 'I set up a company but never traded, do I have to file?' is: at Companies House yes, dormant accounts are still due; at HMRC only if HMRC has not been told it is dormant, in which case a return is required. HMRC's test for active is wider than clients expect - interest on a company bank account is 'other income' and can take a supposedly dormant company back into charge. Same rules in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland: Corporation Tax is not devolved, and Companies House covers the whole UK including Northern Ireland.

title: Married Couple's Allowance 2026-27 - the allowance almost nobody claims

figures.what: Married Couple's Allowance, maximum amount, 2026-27
Married Couple's Allowance, minimum amount, 2026-27
The relief is a tax reduction of 10% of the allowance amount, so a maximum of £1,170 and a minimum of £453 of actual tax saved in 2026-27 - ITA 2007 s45(1) and s46(1)

Adjusted net income limit for 2026-27: above this the allowance is cut by half the excess, but never below the minimum amount. ITA 2007 ss.45(4) and 46(4) as substituted by SI 2026/38. This figure is NOT stated on any gov.uk guidance page - cite the legislation
The 2026-27 uprating, with effect for 2026-27 and later years - The Income Tax (Indexation of Blind Person's Allowance and Married Couple's Allowance) Order 2026, SI 2026/38, arts 1(2) and 2
The 2025-26 tax saving STILL being quoted on the live gov.uk 'What you'll get' page as at 18 November 2026 - the guidance is a tax year behind the rates table and the statute

scope.nation: UK - an income tax reducer under ITA 2007, so it applies to Scottish and Welsh taxpayers too
scope.who: A married couple or civil partners, living together, where one of them was born before 6 April 1935. For marriages before 5 December 2005 the allowance goes to the husband (ITA 2007 s45); for marriages and civil partnerships on or after that date it goes to the partner with the higher net income (s46), or to whoever a joint election specifies if incomes are equal
scope.excluded: Couples where NEITHER partner was born before 6 April 1935 - they get Marriage Allowance instead (ITA 2007 s45(2)(c) and s46(2)(c)). People living together who are not married or in a civil partnership. Anyone already claiming Marriage Allowance: you cannot get Marriage Allowance and Married Couple's Allowance at the same time. Anyone who fails the residence test in ITA 2007 s56 - you must be UK resident for the tax year or fall into one of the s56(3) categories (UK or EEA national, resident in the Isle of Man or Channel Islands, Crown servant and so on). And the LOWER-income partner in a post-5-December-2005 marriage or civil partnership, because the relief belongs to the higher earner (s46(2)(e)).
scope.from_when: 2026-27 tax year, from 6 April 2026, with amounts set by SI 2026/38
scope.how_to_claim: It must be claimed. If you file Self Assessment, complete the Married Couple's Allowance section of the return. If not, contact HMRC with details of the marriage or civil partnership ceremony and your spouse's or civil partner's date of birth. A joint election to switch who receives it, or to apply the post-2005 rules to a pre-2005 marriage, must be made not more than 4 years after the end of the tax year it relates to (ITA 2007 s46(6)(b)).

notes: This is NOT Marriage Allowance, and the two are constantly confused. Marriage Allowance transfers £1,260 of personal allowance between spouses; Married Couple's Allowance is a flat 10% tax reducer and needs a pre-6-April-1935 birth date. You cannot have both. The publishing trap: as at 18 November 2026 the live gov.uk guidance pages still quote the 2025-26 saving of £436 to £1,127, while the HMRC rates table and the statute carry the 2026-27 amounts of £4,530 to £11,700, i.e. £453 to £1,170 of tax saved. Quote the rates table or statute figures, and always say which tax year you are quoting. You can still claim if you cannot live together because of illness or old age (including a partner in residential care), working away, an armed forces posting, prison, or training. The allowance is pro-rated in the year of marriage and continues to the end of the tax year on death, divorce or separation.

title: The £10,000 small pot and the £30,000 trivial commutation lump sum

figures.what: Maximum 'small lump sum' per arrangement for payments made on or after 27 March 2014, up from £2,000 - reg 11A, Registered Pension Schemes (Authorised Payments) Regulations 2009 (SI 2009/1171), for schemes that are NOT occupational or public service schemes
Maximum number of reg 11A small lump sums: the condition is that the member has not previously received more than 2 payments under regulation 11A
The equivalent small pot limit for occupational and public service schemes, under regs 11 and 12
Share of a small lump sum from UNCRYSTALLISED rights that is free of income tax - the balance is taxed as pension income
Tax-free share where the lump sum represents CRYSTALLISED rights - the whole payment is taxable as pension income

Trivial commutation limit - the value of the member's pension rights under ALL registered pension schemes they belong to, valued at the nominated date, must not exceed this (para 7, Schedule 29, Finance Act 2004)
All trivial commutation payments must be made within the 12-month commutation period
Minimum age for a reg 11A small lump sum - the normal minimum pension age

HMRC's own worked warning: an offer of £9,990 that grows past £10,000 by the payment date cannot be paid as a small lump sum, because the limit applies to the sum actually paid, including intervening growth and contributions

scope.who: Members of UK registered pension schemes. Small pots under reg 11A: anyone aged 55 or over (57 from 6 April 2028) with an arrangement worth £10,000 or less in a non-occupational scheme, such as an old personal pension or stakeholder. Trivial commutation: members whose total pension rights are £30,000 or less across all registered schemes, holding defined benefit, collective money purchase, or an in-payment money-purchase in-house scheme pension
scope.excluded: Anyone under 55 (57 from 6 April 2028) who does not meet the ill-health condition or hold a protected pension age. An arrangement worth MORE than £10,000 at the date of payment - no part of it can be taken as a small lump sum. Anyone who has already had 3 reg 11A small lump sums. Any payment that does not extinguish the member's entitlement under that arrangement. For trivial commutation, ordinary money purchase and personal pension pots do NOT qualify at all - only defined benefit, collective money purchase and in-payment money-purchase in-house scheme pensions (before 16 September 2016 only defined benefit rights qualified). Anyone whose total pension rights exceed £30,000 at the nominated date. For trivial commutation, anyone with no lump sum allowance left. Crystallised rights get no 25% tax-free portion. And a payment made to someone other than the member, for example after death, is fully taxable as pension income.
scope.from_when: The £10,000 small pot limit applies to payments made on or after 27 March 2014; the £30,000 trivial commutation limit to commutation periods beginning on or after 27 March 2014. The HMRC guidance applies where the 12-month commutation period began on or after 6 April 2015. Both manual pages were last updated 2 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: The member has to ask the scheme administrator to pay the arrangement out as a small lump sum (reg 11, 11A or 12) or as a trivial commutation lump sum. The payer MUST operate PAYE on the taxable part, which routinely over-deducts tax on a one-off payment; the refund is then claimed separately from HMRC, online through the pension tax refund service at gov.uk/claim-pension-tax-refund or on paper form P53.

notes: Two separate reliefs, constantly confused. Small pots are per ARRANGEMENT, so up to three lots of £10,000 from non-occupational schemes plus separate reg 11 and 12 pots from occupational schemes, and they are NOT restricted by the size of your total pension savings. Trivial commutation looks at your WHOLE pension wealth against a single £30,000 ceiling. Small lump sums are not relevant benefit crystallisation events, so they do not use up any lump sum allowance or lump sum and death benefit allowance; trivial commutation does require available lump sum allowance. The money-people-are-owed hook is the PAYE over-deduction: because the scheme operates PAYE on a one-off payment, the tax taken is usually too much, and the refund has to be claimed. HMRC also confirms a scheme can consolidate many tiny arrangements into one, two or three arrangements to allow the maximum small pots to be taken, without that counting as setting up a new arrangement. The exclusions printed inside the P55, P53Z and P50Z claim forms themselves have NOT been verified - do not state them.

title: Challenging your Council Tax band - proposal versus band review, and the two different clocks

figures.what: The valuation date Council Tax bands are based on in England
The valuation date Council Tax bands are based on in Wales
You have a LEGAL RIGHT to challenge, by making a proposal, if you have been paying Council Tax on the property for less than 6 months, or the Valuation Office changed your band in the last 6 months
Number of similar lower-banded comparable properties you must supply as evidence for a band review

figures.value: 1 April 1989 to 31 March 1993 in England, 1 April 2001 to 31 March 2005 in Wales
figures.what: The sale-price window the Valuation Office will accept as evidence
England band thresholds at April 1991 values
Wales band thresholds at April 2003 values - note Wales has a band I and England does not
How long the Valuation Office may take just to acknowledge a challenge
Valuation Office decision time where you have a legal right to challenge (a proposal)
Valuation Office decision time for a band review, where there is no legal right to challenge

figures.value: 3 months in England, 4 months in Wales
figures.what: Time limit to appeal the decision to the Valuation Tribunal
It costs nothing to appeal to the Valuation Tribunal, though you pay your own costs such as travel or an agent

scope.nation: England and Wales - the Valuation Office. Scotland has a separate route and Northern Ireland does not have Council Tax at all
scope.who: The Council Tax payer, whether homeowner or tenant, for a property in England or Wales, or an appointed representative
scope.excluded: Scotland - challenges go to the assessor at the local Valuation Joint Board or council through the Scottish Assessors Association, not the Valuation Office. Northern Ireland - domestic rates apply, not Council Tax, so this route does not exist. Anyone wanting a property removed from the list merely for being in poor repair: gov.uk states outright you cannot have a property removed just because it is in poor repair, it must be derelict or in serious disrepair. Anyone who went down the BAND REVIEW route and disagrees with the outcome - you can only appeal the decision if you had a legal right to challenge, so there is no Valuation Tribunal appeal from a band review. Average house-price indices are excluded as evidence: the Valuation Office will not consider average house price information from property websites as strong evidence. Anyone wanting to use the online service to get a property removed from the list, or acting as someone else's representative, must use the paper form instead. And nobody gets to stop paying - you must continue paying Council Tax while the challenge is reviewed.
scope.from_when: Current process as published on 18 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: In England and Wales, use the Valuation Office online challenge service linked from gov.uk/challenge-council-tax-band, or the paper Council Tax challenge form, plus an Authority to act form if you are acting for someone else. In Scotland, go through the Scottish Assessors Association. If the band changes, the Valuation Office tells the council, which revises the bill and pays any refund due.

notes: The distinction that makes this worth publishing: a PROPOSAL - a legal right, available within 6 months of becoming the taxpayer or of a Valuation Office band change, or after a material change - gets a decision in up to 4 months AND carries a right of appeal to the Valuation Tribunal. A BAND REVIEW, which is all that is open to anyone who has been paying for more than 6 months, can take up to 12 months and has NO appeal right at all. Most people who talk about challenging their band are in the second category and do not know it. Wales has a band I above £424,000; England stops at H - do not reuse English band figures for a Welsh property. Removal from the list is a separate remedy from rebanding: demolition, dereliction or serious structural disrepair, major renovation affecting all or most of the property, or conversion to purely business use; if removal was for renovation, liability restarts from the completion or move-in date. Scotland's bands and valuation date have NOT been verified - do not state them. Only the Scottish route is verified, not the Scottish figures.

title: When an online platform reports you to HMRC - 30 sales and EUR 2,000

figures.what: The date the UK digital platform reporting rules started

figures.value: fewer than 30 sales of goods and less than EUR 2,000 (about £1,700)
figures.what: The two conditions that must BOTH be met in a calendar year for the platform not to report you
The reporting year - a CALENDAR year, not a tax year
The deadline by which the platform must send the previous calendar year's information to HMRC, so 2026 calendar-year data is due by 31 January 2027
The tax year you must convert the platform's calendar-year figures into if you need to report the income
The platform's report to you breaks the year's earnings into quarters, net of fees, commission and taxes the platform deducted

scope.who: Anyone registered on a digital platform to sell goods or services in the UK - sole traders, individuals, companies and partnerships. It covers personal services such as food delivery, driving and freelancing, renting out property or transport, and selling goods. The platform must collect your full name, home address, date of birth and tax identification number, which is your National Insurance number if you live in the UK; a UK company gives its company registration number and a UK partnership its partnership UTR; property renters must give the address of every property listed
scope.excluded: Sellers who make fewer than 30 sales of GOODS in a calendar year AND receive less than EUR 2,000 (about £1,700) for them - their details are not reported. Note the exemption is written for sales of goods only: it does not cover sellers of services, or people renting out property or transport, who have no equivalent de minimis on this page. And being reported is not the same as owing tax - HMRC states that you are unlikely to pay tax if you sell personal items from your home, like the contents of a loft or garage; tax arises only if you are trading or making a capital gain.
scope.from_when: 1 January 2024 onwards
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. The platform collects and reports without you doing anything, and must give you a copy of what it reported to HMRC. What is not automatic is any tax liability or the obligation to register for Self Assessment, which stays with you: if the income is taxable, convert the calendar-year figures to the 6 April to 5 April tax year and report it. HMRC provides a checker for whether you need to tell them about income from online platforms.

notes: The single most useful line, in HMRC's own words: a platform reporting your details to HMRC does not automatically mean you owe tax. A lot of people received a platform report and panicked. The year mismatch is the practical trap: platforms report on the calendar year while HMRC taxes the 6 April to 5 April year, so the figure on the platform statement will never tie to a tax return. The platform's figure is also NET of its fees, commission and taxes deducted, so it is neither your turnover nor your profit - HMRC says these reports do not replace your normal business records or tax calculations. This is a different subject from the trading allowance: that is about whether tax is due, this is about whether you get REPORTED, and the two thresholds are completely different numbers. HMRC will pass the information to the tax authority of your country of residence if you live abroad.

title: What makes a VAT invoice valid - the 11 items, and the £250 simplified invoice

figures.what: The details a full VAT invoice must show (VAT Notice 700 para 16.3.1): a sequential number uniquely identifying the document; the time of supply (tax point); the date of issue where different; your name, address and VAT registration number; the customer's name and address; a description sufficient to identify the goods or services; for each description the quantity or extent, the VAT rate and the amount payable excluding VAT; the gross total excluding VAT; the rate of any cash discount offered; the total VAT chargeable; and the unit price
The total VAT chargeable must be expressed in sterling even where the rest of the invoice is in another currency (paras 16.3.1 and 16.4)
You must normally issue a VAT invoice within 30 days of the tax point arising (para 16.2.3); an invoice issued under this 30-day rule does not itself create a tax point
You must be able to provide English translations of specific invoices within 30 days if an HMRC officer asks (para 16.2.4)

The value of supply at or below which you may issue a SIMPLIFIED VAT invoice if your customer agrees (para 16.6.1), and the same ceiling for a retailer's VAT invoice (para 16.6.2) and for a less-detailed petrol or diesel invoice (para 17.1)

What a simplified or retailer's VAT invoice must show: your name, address and VAT registration number; the time of supply (tax point); a description identifying the goods or services; and, for each applicable VAT rate, the total amount payable INCLUDING VAT and the VAT rate
Above this you must issue a FULL VAT invoice, and you must issue one at any value if the customer asks (para 16.6.2)

scope.nation: UK, with extra Northern Ireland rules: a Northern Ireland business cannot use a simplified or retailer's VAT invoice for a customer from an EU member state, and one zero-rating or exempting a supply of goods to an EU member state must show the reason on the invoice
scope.who: VAT-registered businesses making a taxable supply of goods or services to another VAT-registered person - they must give that person a VAT invoice (para 16.2.1)
scope.excluded: Zero-rated supplies - HMRC states you do not have to issue VAT invoices for zero-rated supplies (para 16.2.1). Supplies to customers who are NOT VAT registered need no VAT invoice, and HMRC notes you do not have to check a customer's registration before issuing one. Where your customer operates self-billing arrangements, or you issue authenticated receipts (para 16.2.2). Gifts of goods on which VAT is due (para 16.2.2). Goods sold under a VAT second-hand margin scheme - you must NOT issue VAT invoices for those, as the schemes have their own special invoices (para 16.2.2). Exempt supplies must not be included in a retailer's VAT invoice (para 16.6.2). A simplified invoice is not available where the customer does not agree, where the supply exceeds £250, or (for Northern Ireland businesses) where the customer is from an EU member state. And if you accept card payments and issue a receipt as well as the card voucher, only one of the two documents may be in the form of a VAT invoice (para 16.6.2).
scope.from_when: Current VAT guide, Notice 700, as published and read on 18 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. It is an obligation on the supplier: issue a compliant invoice within 30 days of the tax point. The customer needs the valid VAT invoice as evidence to reclaim input tax (para 16.2.1). An extension to the 30-day limit is automatic in four listed cases - awaiting supplier or subcontractor invoices, an approved extension of the 14-day rule, approved special accounting arrangements, and being newly registered and not yet notified of the VAT number, which gives 30 days from the date of advice of the number; otherwise you must write to HMRC's VAT Written Enquiries Team.

notes: The gap between a RECEIPT and a VAT INVOICE is where most input tax gets lost: a till receipt with no VAT number and no VAT rate is neither a full nor a simplified VAT invoice. HMRC is explicit that a retailer may be liable to a financial penalty for refusing to issue a VAT invoice when asked by a taxable person (para 16.6.2), but no penalty amount is stated on that page, so do not quote a figure. Fuel is the everyday example: a VAT-inclusive pump sale of £250 or less can be a less-detailed invoice, and above £250 the forecourt may show the vehicle registration number instead of the customer's name and address and need not show litres or the type of supply (para 17.1). The unit price can be omitted where it is not normally provided in that sector and the customer does not require it (para 16.3.2). Zero-rated and exempt items on a mixed invoice must clearly show no VAT payable and carry a separate total for their values (para 16.5). This is the invoice-CONTENT subject and does not overlap the existing VAT margin scheme or record-keeping subjects.

scope.who: Buyers of residential property in Scotland — houses, flats, dwellings under construction, buildings being converted into dwellings, and certain multiple-occupancy accommodation including school pupil, student and armed forces accommodation. Tax is worked out band by band and the amounts added together.
scope.excluded: Buyers anywhere outside Scotland — England and Northern Ireland pay Stamp Duty Land Tax to HMRC and Wales pays Land Transaction Tax to the Welsh Revenue Authority, so LBTT never applies to them. Within Scotland, purchases with chargeable consideration under £40,000 are generally not notifiable, and exempt transactions are outside the charge. University and college halls of residence are not treated as residential multiple-occupancy accommodation.
scope.from_when: Rates in force from 1 April 2021 and still current on the page as read on 19 November 2026.
scope.how_to_claim: The buyer, usually through their solicitor, submits an LBTT return to Revenue Scotland and pays the tax. First-time buyer relief must be claimed on that return — it is not applied automatically.

notes: Not the same tax as Stamp Duty Land Tax. SDLT covers England and Northern Ireland and is administered by HMRC; Wales has Land Transaction Tax, administered by the Welsh Revenue Authority. The three taxes have different bands, different thresholds and different first-time buyer treatment, so an England figure must never be quoted for a Scottish purchase. Scottish first-time buyer relief raises the nil rate band to £175,000, a different mechanism from the SDLT first-time buyer rules. The Additional Dwelling Supplement is a separate charge on top of LBTT.

Most purchases by non-individuals, such as companies and certain trusts, pay ADS even with no other residential property.
scope.excluded: ADS does not apply if you own only one dwelling at the end of the effective date; if the consideration is under £40,000; if your other property is worth less than £40,000; if your share in a jointly owned property is worth less than £40,000 for effective dates from 1 April 2024; or if you disposed of your only or main residence within the 36 months before buying the new one, 18 months for earlier transactions. It never applies outside Scotland — buyers in England and Northern Ireland face the SDLT higher rates and buyers in Wales the LTT higher rates.

scope.how_to_claim: ADS is calculated alongside LBTT, declared on the LBTT return and paid at the same time. A repayment is claimed separately from Revenue Scotland if the previous main residence is sold within 36 months, that property was the only or main residence in the 36 months before the purchase, and the buyer has lived in the new property as their only or main residence.
